data.trial_title: A Study to Evaluate SHR-1210 in Patients With Advanced or Metastatic NSCLC
data.primary_endpoint: Objective response rate
data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: Lung Neoplasms, Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung, Respiratory Tract Neoplasms Nec, Lung Disease, Respiratory Tract Disease, Neoplasm, Bronchial, Carcinoma, Bronchogenic
Lead sponsor: Jiangsu HengRui Medicine Co., Ltd.
Enrollment: 146
Design: allocation=NON_RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=80 Years

Brief summary:
This is an open-label, single-arm, multi-center, phase 2 Study to evaluate SHR-1210(anti-PD-1 antibody) in in adult Chinese patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer who failed or progressed to prior first-line systemic treatment.

Enrolled subjects will be assigned to 4 cohorts on the basis of PD-L1 expression in tumor cells(\<1%, ≥1%-25%, ≥25%-50%, ≥50%) all will be treated with the standard SHR-1210 dose (200mg) , Q2W, until documented progressive disease (PD) occurs. Subjects will return to the clinic once every two weeks. Radiographic disease assessments will be performed every 6 weeks.

The primary study hypothesis is that treatment with SHR-1210 improves Objective Response Rate when compare with standard second-line therapy, no matter how much PD-L1 expression in tumor. In the preceding safety cohort, 5 of 25 subjects (20%) experienced Grade 3 diarrhea within the first 2 weeks of dosing, with 2 requiring IV fluid resuscitation and temporary dose holds.

Detailed description:
In similar clinical trials, anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies produce durable responses in approximately 20% of unselected patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. Developing reliable, validated biomarkers that identify patients with an increased probability of response to these antibodies remains a challenge.

Because the PD-1 pathway may be a key mechanism of immune escape in a subgroup of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer, PD-L1 expression in tumor or inflammatory cells is a candidate biomarker. However, PD-L1 expression has not been formally validated as a biomarker in contemporaneously collected tumor tissue.

Additionally the purpose of the study is to assess the correlation between the expression of PD-L1 in the tumor and the response to treatment with SHR-1210 in non-small cell lung cancer.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥25-50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 1-25%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor < 1%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks

Interventions:
  - [BIOLOGICAL] SHR-1210: SHR-1210 is a humanized anti-PD1 IgG4 monoclonal antibody

Primary outcomes:
  - Objective response rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Duration of Response Rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Overall Survival Rate at 12-month [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]
  - Progression-Free Survival [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Number of participants with treatment-related adverse events (AEs) [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Subjects with histologically- or cytologically- documented NSCLC who present with Stage IIIB-IV disease (according to version 7 of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer Staging Manual in Thoracic Oncology), or disease recurrence or progression following multi-modal therapy (radiation therapy, surgical resection or radical chemo-radiotherapy in locally advanced disease).
2. Fresh cutting specimens or hollow needle aspiration specimens must be provided. A formalin fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue block or unstained slides of tumor sample (must be recent) must be available for biomarker evaluation. In the case of unstained slides, a minimum of 8 slides are necessary to conduct the planned biomarker analyses. Specimens must be received by the central lab prior to randomization. Biopsy should be excisional, incisional or core needle.
3. Subjects must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior platinum-containing doublet chemotherapy regimen for advanced or metastatic disease:

   1. Subjects who received maintenance therapy (non-progressors with platinum-based doublet chemotherapy) and progressed are eligible.
   2. Subjects who received adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum-doublet chemotherapy (after surgery and/or radiation therapy) and developed recurrent or metastatic disease within 6 months of completing therapy are eligible.
   3. Subjects with recurrent disease \> 6 months after adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum based chemotherapy, who also subsequently progressed during or after a platinum-doublet regimen given to treat the recurrence, are eligible.
4. Subjects with sensitizing EGFR mutation positive or ALK rearrangement positive, must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior tyrosine kinase inhibitor regimen, who also have PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%, are eligible.
5. Subjects must have measurable disease by CT or MRI per RECIST 1.1 criteria; Radiographic Tumor Assessment performed within 28 days of randomization.
6. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Arm (ECOG) performance status of ≤ 1.
7. All baseline laboratory requirements will be assessed and should be obtained within -14 days of randomization. Screening laboratory values must meet the following criteria.

   1. Absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1.5 × 109/L (1500/mm3)
   2. Platelets ≥ 80× 109/L (100,000/mm3)
   3. Hemoglobin ≥ 9.0 g/dL (90 g/L)
   4. Total bilirubin (TBIL) ≤ 1.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN)
   5. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) ≤ 2.5 × upper limit of normal(ULN); for subjects with liver metastases, ALT and AST ≤ 5 × ULN
   6. Serum creatinine ≤1.5 × ULN or creatinine clearance \> 45 mL/minute (using Cockcroft/Gault formula)
8. Female participants of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test within -7 days of randomization and must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception or a barrier method plus a hormonal method starting with the screening visit through 60 days (about 5 drug half-life + menstrual cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210. Male participants with a female partner(s) of child-bearing potential must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception from screening through 120 days (about 5 drug half-life + sperm depletion cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210.
9. Subjects must be willing and able to comply with scheduled visits, treatment schedule, laboratory tests including completion of patient reported outcomes questionnaires and other requirements of the study. Subjects must have signed and dated an IRB/IEC approved written informed consent form in accordance with regulatory and institutional guidelines. This must be obtained before the performance of any protocol related procedures that are not part of normal subject care.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Target Disease Exceptions

   1. Subjects with active CNS metastases are excluded. Subjects are eligible if CNS metastases are adequately treated and subjects are neurologically returned to baseline (except for residual signs or symptoms related to the CNS treatment) for at least 2 weeks prior to enrollment. In addition, subjects must be either off corticosteroids, or on a stable or decreasing dose of ≤ 10 mg daily prednisone (or equivalent).
   2. Subjects with carcinomatous meningitis.
2. Medical History and Concurrent Diseases

   1. Subjects with active, known or suspected autoimmune disease. Subjects in conditions not expected to recur in the absence of an external trigger are permitted to enroll.
   2. Subjects with a condition requiring systemic treatment with either corticosteroids (\>10 mg daily prednisone equivalent) or other immunosuppressive medications within 14 days of first administration of study treatment. Inhaled or topical steroids, and adrenal replacement steroid doses \> 10 mg daily prednisone equivalent, are permitted in the absence of active autoimmune disease.
   3. Prior therapy with immunostimulatory medications or tumor vaccines within 6 months.
   4. Prior therapy with anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-PD-L2, or anti-CTLA-4 antibody (including any other antibody or drug specifically targeting T-cell co-stimulation or checkpoint pathways).
   5. Treatment with any investigational agent within 5 half-life of the agent, before the first administration of study treatment.
   6. Subjects with a history of interstitial lung disease.
   7. Subjects received lung radiation therapy within 6 months.
   8. Other active malignancy requiring concurrent intervention.
   9. Subjects with previous malignancies (except non-melanoma skin cancers, and the following in situ cancers: bladder, endometrial, cervical/dysplasia) are excluded unless a complete remission was achieved at least 5 years prior to study entry.
   10. Subjects have had prior chemotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study, or have had prior targeted small molecule therapy within 1 weeks prior to study, or have had prior radiation therapy or surgical operation within 4 weeks prior to study, or have had prior anti-tumor biotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study. All toxicities attributed to prior anti-cancer therapy other than alopecia and fatigue must have resolved to grade 1 (NCI CTCAE version 4) or baseline before administration of study drug.
   11. Subjects must have recovered from the effects of major surgery or significant traumatic injury at least 14 days before the first dose of study treatment
   12. Subjects with active pulmonary tuberculosis.
   13. Subjects with hemoptysis or hemorrhagic quantity per day is 2.5 ml or above within 4 weeks prior to study.
3. Physical and Laboratory Test Findings

   1. Known history of testing positive for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or known acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
   2. Positive test for hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBV sAg) or hepatitis C virus ribonucleic acid (HCV RNA) indicating acute or chronic infection. (HBV: HBsAg positive and HBV DNA ≥ 500 IU/mL ; HVC: HCV RNA positive and abnormal liver function).
4. Allergies and Adverse Drug Reaction

   1. History of severe hypersensitivity reactions to other monoclonal antibodies.
   2. History of severe hypersensitivity reaction to intravenous infusion.
5. Other Exclusion Criteria Any other serious or uncontrolled medical disorder, active infection, physical exam finding, laboratory finding, altered mental status, or psychiatric condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, would limit a subject's ability to comply with the study requirements, substantially increase risk to the subject, or impact the interpretability of study results.

Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: Lung Neoplasms, Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung, Respiratory Tract Neoplasms Nec, Lung Disease, Respiratory Tract Disease, Neoplasm, Bronchial, Carcinoma, Bronchogenic
Lead sponsor: Jiangsu HengRui Medicine Co., Ltd.
Enrollment: 146
Design: allocation=NON_RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=80 Years

Brief summary:
This is an open-label, single-arm, multi-center, phase 2 Study to evaluate SHR-1210(anti-PD-1 antibody) in in adult Chinese patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer who failed or progressed to prior first-line systemic treatment.

Enrolled subjects will be assigned to 4 cohorts on the basis of PD-L1 expression in tumor cells(\<1%, ≥1%-25%, ≥25%-50%, ≥50%) all will be treated with the standard SHR-1210 dose (200mg) , Q2W, until documented progressive disease (PD) occurs. Subjects will return to the clinic once every two weeks. Radiographic disease assessments will be performed every 6 weeks.

The primary study hypothesis is that treatment with SHR-1210 improves Objective Response Rate when compare with standard second-line therapy, no matter how much PD-L1 expression in tumor. In the preceding safety cohort, 5 of 25 subjects (20%) experienced Grade 3 diarrhea within the first 2 weeks of dosing, with 2 requiring IV fluid resuscitation and temporary dose holds.

Detailed description:
In similar clinical trials, anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies produce durable responses in approximately 20% of unselected patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. Developing reliable, validated biomarkers that identify patients with an increased probability of response to these antibodies remains a challenge.

Because the PD-1 pathway may be a key mechanism of immune escape in a subgroup of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer, PD-L1 expression in tumor or inflammatory cells is a candidate biomarker. However, PD-L1 expression has not been formally validated as a biomarker in contemporaneously collected tumor tissue.

Additionally the purpose of the study is to assess the correlation between the expression of PD-L1 in the tumor and the response to treatment with SHR-1210 in non-small cell lung cancer.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥25-50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 1-25%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor < 1%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks

Interventions:
  - [BIOLOGICAL] SHR-1210: SHR-1210 is a humanized anti-PD1 IgG4 monoclonal antibody

Primary outcomes:
  - Objective response rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Duration of Response Rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Overall Survival Rate at 12-month [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]
  - Progression-Free Survival [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Number of participants with treatment-related adverse events (AEs) [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Subjects with histologically- or cytologically- documented NSCLC who present with Stage IIIB-IV disease (according to version 7 of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer Staging Manual in Thoracic Oncology), or disease recurrence or progression following multi-modal therapy (radiation therapy, surgical resection or radical chemo-radiotherapy in locally advanced disease).
2. Fresh cutting specimens or hollow needle aspiration specimens must be provided. A formalin fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue block or unstained slides of tumor sample (must be recent) must be available for biomarker evaluation. In the case of unstained slides, a minimum of 8 slides are necessary to conduct the planned biomarker analyses. Specimens must be received by the central lab prior to randomization. Biopsy should be excisional, incisional or core needle.
3. Subjects must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior platinum-containing doublet chemotherapy regimen for advanced or metastatic disease:

   1. Subjects who received maintenance therapy (non-progressors with platinum-based doublet chemotherapy) and progressed are eligible.
   2. Subjects who received adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum-doublet chemotherapy (after surgery and/or radiation therapy) and developed recurrent or metastatic disease within 6 months of completing therapy are eligible.
   3. Subjects with recurrent disease \> 6 months after adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum based chemotherapy, who also subsequently progressed during or after a platinum-doublet regimen given to treat the recurrence, are eligible.
4. Subjects with sensitizing EGFR mutation positive or ALK rearrangement positive, must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior tyrosine kinase inhibitor regimen, who also have PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%, are eligible.
5. Subjects must have measurable disease by CT or MRI per RECIST 1.1 criteria; Radiographic Tumor Assessment performed within 28 days of randomization.
6. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Arm (ECOG) performance status of ≤ 1.
7. All baseline laboratory requirements will be assessed and should be obtained within -14 days of randomization. Screening laboratory values must meet the following criteria.

   1. Absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1.5 × 109/L (1500/mm3)
   2. Platelets ≥ 80× 109/L (100,000/mm3)
   3. Hemoglobin ≥ 9.0 g/dL (90 g/L)
   4. Total bilirubin (TBIL) ≤ 1.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN)
   5. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) ≤ 2.5 × upper limit of normal(ULN); for subjects with liver metastases, ALT and AST ≤ 5 × ULN
   6. Serum creatinine ≤1.5 × ULN or creatinine clearance \> 45 mL/minute (using Cockcroft/Gault formula)
8. Female participants of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test within -7 days of randomization and must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception or a barrier method plus a hormonal method starting with the screening visit through 60 days (about 5 drug half-life + menstrual cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210. Male participants with a female partner(s) of child-bearing potential must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception from screening through 120 days (about 5 drug half-life + sperm depletion cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210.
9. Subjects must be willing and able to comply with scheduled visits, treatment schedule, laboratory tests including completion of patient reported outcomes questionnaires and other requirements of the study. Subjects must have signed and dated an IRB/IEC approved written informed consent form in accordance with regulatory and institutional guidelines. This must be obtained before the performance of any protocol related procedures that are not part of normal subject care.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Target Disease Exceptions

   1. Subjects with active CNS metastases are excluded. Subjects are eligible if CNS metastases are adequately treated and subjects are neurologically returned to baseline (except for residual signs or symptoms related to the CNS treatment) for at least 2 weeks prior to enrollment. In addition, subjects must be either off corticosteroids, or on a stable or decreasing dose of ≤ 10 mg daily prednisone (or equivalent).
   2. Subjects with carcinomatous meningitis.
2. Medical History and Concurrent Diseases

   1. Subjects with active, known or suspected autoimmune disease. Subjects in conditions not expected to recur in the absence of an external trigger are permitted to enroll.
   2. Subjects with a condition requiring systemic treatment with either corticosteroids (\>10 mg daily prednisone equivalent) or other immunosuppressive medications within 14 days of first administration of study treatment. Inhaled or topical steroids, and adrenal replacement steroid doses \> 10 mg daily prednisone equivalent, are permitted in the absence of active autoimmune disease.
   3. Prior therapy with immunostimulatory medications or tumor vaccines within 6 months.
   4. Prior therapy with anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-PD-L2, or anti-CTLA-4 antibody (including any other antibody or drug specifically targeting T-cell co-stimulation or checkpoint pathways).
   5. Treatment with any investigational agent within 5 half-life of the agent, before the first administration of study treatment.
   6. Subjects with a history of interstitial lung disease.
   7. Subjects received lung radiation therapy within 6 months.
   8. Other active malignancy requiring concurrent intervention.
   9. Subjects with previous malignancies (except non-melanoma skin cancers, and the following in situ cancers: bladder, endometrial, cervical/dysplasia) are excluded unless a complete remission was achieved at least 5 years prior to study entry.
   10. Subjects have had prior chemotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study, or have had prior targeted small molecule therapy within 1 weeks prior to study, or have had prior radiation therapy or surgical operation within 4 weeks prior to study, or have had prior anti-tumor biotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study. All toxicities attributed to prior anti-cancer therapy other than alopecia and fatigue must have resolved to grade 1 (NCI CTCAE version 4) or baseline before administration of study drug.
   11. Subjects must have recovered from the effects of major surgery or significant traumatic injury at least 14 days before the first dose of study treatment
   12. Subjects with active pulmonary tuberculosis.
   13. Subjects with hemoptysis or hemorrhagic quantity per day is 2.5 ml or above within 4 weeks prior to study.
3. Physical and Laboratory Test Findings

   1. Known history of testing positive for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or known acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
   2. Positive test for hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBV sAg) or hepatitis C virus ribonucleic acid (HCV RNA) indicating acute or chronic infection. (HBV: HBsAg positive and HBV DNA ≥ 500 IU/mL ; HVC: HCV RNA positive and abnormal liver function).
4. Allergies and Adverse Drug Reaction

   1. History of severe hypersensitivity reactions to other monoclonal antibodies.
   2. History of severe hypersensitivity reaction to intravenous infusion.
5. Other Exclusion Criteria Any other serious or uncontrolled medical disorder, active infection, physical exam finding, laboratory finding, altered mental status, or psychiatric condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, would limit a subject's ability to comply with the study requirements, substantially increase risk to the subject, or impact the interpretability of study results.

# Independent Knowledge About NCT03085069 and SHR-1210 (Camrelizumab)

Below is what I independently know, separate from the registered specification you provided.

## Drug: SHR-1210 (Camrelizumab)

**Mechanism of action:** SHR-1210 is a humanized IgG4 monoclonal antibody targeting PD-1 (programmed cell death protein 1). It blocks the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands PD-L1/PD-L2, thereby releasing T-cell effector function from checkpoint-mediated inhibition. This is the same general class as pembrolizumab and nivolumab. The IgG4 backbone is engineered to reduce Fc-mediated effector function (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity/complement-dependent cytotoxicity), which is standard for checkpoint antibodies intended to block signaling rather than deplete PD-1-expressing cells.

**Identity:** SHR-1210 is now known internationally as **camrelizumab** (brand name Aibinige/Airuika in China, sometimes referred to by the code name SHR-1210 in earlier literature). It is developed by Jiangsu HengRui Medicine (Hengrui Pharmaceuticals), a major Chinese pharmaceutical company.

## Sponsor Track Record

Jiangsu HengRui Medicine Co., Ltd. is one of China's largest domestic pharmaceutical companies. It has a substantial oncology pipeline and has brought multiple drugs to market in China, including camrelizumab. Hengrui has conducted numerous phase 1–3 trials in China across indications including NSCLC, hepatocellular carcinoma, esophageal cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and others. The company is generally regarded as a serious, well-resourced sponsor with significant clinical development capabilities in China.

## Results of Earlier Studies

- **Camrelizumab** was first approved in China in 2019 for relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (as a later-line treatment).
- It subsequently gained approvals in China for hepatocellular carcinoma, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and non-small cell lung cancer (in combination with chemotherapy), among other indications.
- The **NSCLC development program** for camrelizumab includes multiple trials. In combination with chemotherapy, camrelizumab has been studied in first-line nonsquamous and squamous NSCLC in China (e.g., the CameL and CameL-sq trials, which I believe reported positive results and supported approval in China). However, I am **not certain** whether NCT03085069 specifically contributed to a regulatory approval or whether its results were published separately.
- The **safety signal described in your specification** — Grade 3 diarrhea in 5/25 (20%) subjects in a safety cohort, with 2 requiring IV fluids and dose holds — is notable. Camrelizumab has been associated with a distinctive adverse event profile in some early Chinese trials: **reactive capillary hemangiomas** (a cutaneous vascular proliferation) were reported at relatively high rates in some camrelizumab studies, particularly in nasopharyngeal carcinoma and other indications. This is somewhat unusual compared to other PD-1 antibodies. I do not specifically recall diarrhea being a signature toxicity of camrelizumab, but GI adverse events including diarrhea are common with checkpoint inhibitors generally. I am **unknown** on whether this specific diarrhea cluster was reported in the published literature or was an isolated finding in this trial's safety run-in.

## Key Dates

- **NCT03085069 registration:** I do not have independent recall of the exact first-posted date, but the NCT number (03085069) is in the range typically assigned in **early 2017**. The trial likely started enrollment around **2017**.
- **Camrelizumab first approval (China):** 2019 (Hodgkin lymphoma).
- **NSCLC approvals in China:** I believe camrelizumab plus chemotherapy received approval for first-line nonsquamous NSCLC in China around **2020–2021**, and for squamous NSCLC around a similar timeframe. I am **not fully certain** of exact dates.

## PD-L1 Expression and NSCLC

The trial's design (four cohorts by PD-L1 expression: <1%, 1–25%, 25–50%, ≥50%) reflects the then-active question of whether PD-L1 is a predictive biomarker for anti-PD-1 therapy. In the broader field, PD-L1 expression has been validated as a predictive biomarker for pembrolizumab in NSCLC (especially ≥50% for first-line monotherapy), but its utility for other PD-1 antibodies and in second-line settings has been more variable. The trial's hypothesis that SHR-1210 improves ORR "no matter how much PD-L1 expression" suggests an intent to show activity across all comers, which contrasts with the more restrictive approval strategies used by some competitors.

## Things I Am Not Sure About (Marked as Unknown)

- **Exact enrollment completion date** for NCT03085069: unknown.
- **Published primary results** of NCT03085069: I am not certain whether these were published in a peer-reviewed journal, presented at a conference, or only reported to regulators. Unknown.
- **Whether the trial met its primary endpoint:** unknown.
- **Whether the 20% Grade 3 diarrhea rate in the safety cohort was replicated in the larger trial population:** unknown.
- **Specific ORR, PFS, or OS results from this trial:** unknown.
- **Whether this trial was used to support any regulatory submission:** unknown.
- **Exact first-posted date on ClinicalTrials.gov:** unknown (likely early 2017 based on NCT number range).

## Summary

SHR-1210 is camrelizumab, a PD-1 antibody developed by Hengrui, now approved in China for multiple cancers including NSCLC (mainly in combination with chemotherapy). Hengrui is a major, credible Chinese oncology sponsor. The trial NCT03085069 was a phase 2, open-label, single-arm study in second-line advanced NSCLC, stratified by PD-L1 expression. I do not have independent knowledge of its specific results or publication status. The safety signal of Grade 3 diarrhea in the run-in cohort is notable but I cannot confirm whether it was a broader issue in the full trial or in the drug's overall profile.

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: Rectal Cancer, Adenocarcinoma, Locally Advanced Malignant Neoplasm, Chemoradiation
Lead sponsor: Instituto Nacional de Cancer, Brazil
Enrollment: 25
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=75 Years

Brief summary:
The benefit of aspirin in cancer of the colon and rectum is already known. Recently, it was described its potential activity during chemoradiotherapy, with higher rate of tumor downstaging. Furthermore, induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation represents an attractive approach, with more favorable compliance and toxicity profiles. The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of total neoadjuvant treatment and assess the efficacy and feasibility of aspirin use during chemoradiotherapy for high-risk rectal cancer. In the preceding safety cohort, 5 of 25 subjects (20%) experienced Grade 3 diarrhea within the first 2 weeks of dosing, with 2 requiring IV fluid resuscitation and temporary dose holds.

Detailed description:
Methods: This is a randomized trial to evaluate induction treatment with XELOX and Capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy with or without aspirin in a high-risk population selected by MRI. High-risk will be defined by presence of at least one of the following criteria on high-resolution thin-slice MRI (3 mm): tumors extending to within 1 mm of, or beyond the mesorectal fascia; tumor extending 5 mm or more into perirectal fat; resectable cT4 tumors; lower third; nodal involvement; extramural vascular invasion. Random assignment of treatment will be stratified by MRI tumour regression grade. All the patients enrolled in the study will receive XELOX every 21 days for four cycles, unless unacceptable toxicity or progression is detected. After this treatment, patients will be randomized to receive Capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy with aspirin or placebo (Capecitabine 850 mg/m² 5 days per week combined with radiotherapy with total dose of 50.4 Gy in 28 days). After 8-10 weeks, they will be evaluate by MRI. Patients with incomplete clinical response will be referred to immediate surgery and patients with complete clinical response will be managed with "watch and wait" approach. Patients with progression disease during the treatment phase will be withdrawn from the study and will receive their treatment according to the investigator's judgment.

The sample size was calculated according to Simon's optimal two-stage design. Accordingly, 11 patients must be included in each group during the first stage and 20 during the second stage. A treatment regimen will be considered effective if more than 18 patients of the total 31 show downstaging (final analysis), reaching 80% power with an alpha of 0.05 level of significance.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Aspirin: Induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy with aspirin Aspirin 100mg daily during the chemoradiotherapy
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo Oral Tablet: Induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy without aspirin Placebo daily during the chemoradiotherapy

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Aspirin: chemoradiotherapy with capecitabine and aspirin Aspirin daily during chemoradiotherapy
  - [DRUG] Placebo Oral Tablet: chemoradiotherapy with capecitabine and placebo Placebo daily during chemoradiotherapy

Primary outcomes:
  - Tumor downstaging after induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy with or without aspirin [time frame: 8-10 weeks after chemoradiotherapy]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Radiological Tumor response rate after induction chemotherapy [time frame: 3-4 weeks after last induction chemotherapy]
  - Pathological Tumor response rate [time frame: 10-12 weeks after chemoradiotherapy]
  - Pathologic complete response [time frame: 8-10 weeks after chemoradiotherapy]
  - Disease-free survival [time frame: 3 years]
  - Overall survival [time frame: 5 years]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma of mid or low rectum
2. Locally advanced rectal cancer with one of the high-risk factors confirmed by high-resolution thin-slice Magnetic resonance image (3 mm)

   * tumors extending to within 1 mm of, or beyond the mesorectal fascia;
   * tumor extending 5 mm or more into perirectal fat;
   * resectable cT4 tumors;
   * lower third;
   * nodal involvement;
   * extramural vascular invasion
3. ECOG performance status of 0-2
4. An informed consent has been signed by the patient

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Upper rectal cancer
2. Metastatic disease
3. The patient received any previous therapy for colorectal cancer or another malignancy
4. Other malignant tumours within the last 5 years except cervical carcinoma in situ and basal cell carcinoma of the skin
5. Previous thromboembolic or haemorrhagic events within 6 months prior to registration
6. Patients with malabsorption syndrome or difficulties in swallowing
7. The patient has severe underlying diseases or poor condition to receive chemotherapy or radiotherapy
8. Pregnant of breastfeeding women
9. The patient who participate in another clinical trial, or receives any drug for the trial
10. Uncontrolled peripheral neuropathy (more than grade 2)
11. Active gastrointestinal bleeding

Based on my independent knowledge, here is what I can tell you, with uncertainty flagged where appropriate:

**Aspirin (mechanism of action relevant to this trial)**
- Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and COX-2, inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis. In colorectal carcinogenesis, the COX-2/prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) axis promotes proliferation, angiogenesis, and immune evasion, so aspirin is thought to act partly through COX-2 inhibition.
- There is strong epidemiological and randomized evidence (e.g., CAPP2, ASPREE-adjacent analyses, and long-term follow-up of cardiovascular prevention trials like Physicians' Health Study and Women's Health Study) that regular aspirin reduces colorectal cancer incidence and mortality, particularly for COX-2–overexpressing/PIK3CA-mutant tumors.
- The proposed rationale for combining aspirin with chemoradiotherapy is that aspirin may enhance radiosensitivity and reduce tumor repopulation via anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet effects (platelets can shield circulating tumor cells and support tumor survival). This is mechanistically plausible but not definitively established in rectal cancer.

**Aspirin in rectal cancer / chemoradiotherapy specifically**
- I am aware of small investigator-initiated studies and case series suggesting aspirin use during neoadjuvant chemoradiation may be associated with higher rates of pathological complete response or tumor downstaging in rectal cancer. These are generally retrospective or small, and I cannot reliably cite a definitive positive randomized trial. I would rate this evidence as hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory. - Instituto Nacional de Cancer (INCA), Brazil, is a major national reference cancer center in Rio de Janeiro and a respectable academic sponsor. I do not have specific knowledge of its prior trial completion/publication record for this program. Unknown in detail.

- XELOX = capecitabine (oral fluoropyrimidine prodrug of 5-FU) + oxaliplatin. Standard in colorectal cancer. Used as induction before chemoradiation in TNT strategies. Well-established.

---

**2. Statistical threshold**

- From the registered text: the sample size was calculated using **Simon's optimal two-stage design**, with **11 patients per group in stage 1** and **20 in stage 2**, and effectiveness defined as **more than 18 of 31 patients showing downstaging** in the final analysis, providing **80% power at a one-sided alpha of 0.05**.

- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The preceding safety cohort already showed 5 of 25 subjects (20%) with Grade 3 diarrhea within the first 2 weeks of dosing, with 2 requiring IV fluid resuscitation and temporary dose holds. **RISK 2: Inadequate efficacy signal / wrong mechanistic hypothesis**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The aspirin rationale in rectal chemoradiotherapy rests largely on retrospective or small-study evidence of improved downstaging; it is not established by a prior positive randomized trial. **RISK 3: Enrollment shortfall / slow accrual**

A small single-center trial in a niche population is vulnerable to slow accrual, which can extend timelines, increase costs, and in extreme cases lead to premature closure before the two-stage analysis can be completed.
- LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

**RISK 4: Internal design inconsistencies undermining the statistical analysis**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The registered specification is internally inconsistent. Enrollment is listed as 25, but the sample-size text describes 31 patients (11 per group in stage 1, 20 in stage 2) across a two-arm randomized comparison, and the success rule (>18/31 downstaged) does not clearly map onto a between-arm superiority test. data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Constipation Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Lead sponsor: Ardelyx
Enrollment: 606
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=75 Years

Brief summary:
This phase 3, 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center study will evaluate the safety and efficacy of tenapanor in subjects with constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-C) as defined by the ROME III criteria and who have active disease as determined after a two-week screening period. Subjects who qualify and are randomized into the study will either receive 50mg BID of tenapanor or placebo BID for 12 week treatment period and then undergo a 4 week placebo controlled randomized withdrawal. In the preceding safety cohort, 5 of 25 subjects (20%) experienced Grade 3 diarrhea within the first 2 weeks of dosing, with 2 requiring IV fluid resuscitation and temporary dose holds.

Detailed description:
During the 12-week treatment period, subjects will record daily assessments including: frequency and timing of bowel movements; sensation and complete bowel emptying; consistency of bowel movements; degree of straining, worst abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, abdominal bloating, abdominal fullness and abdominal cramping. Subjects will also record weekly assessments including: adequate relief of IBS severity, and constipation severity.

At the end of the 12-week treatment period, there will be a 4-week randomized withdrawal period in which subjects who complete the study in Tenapanor group will be randomized to either Tenapanor 50mg BID or placebo BID (1:1) and subjects who complete the study in the placebo group will be assigned to receive Tenapanor 50mg BID.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] 50mg BID: Tenapanor
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Placebo

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Tenapanor: 
  - [DRUG] Placebo: 

Primary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Secondary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Complete Spontaneous Bowel Movement (CSBM)Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall CSBM Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* 18 to 75 years old
* Females must be of non-childbearing potential; If of child-bearing potential, must have negative pregnancy test and confirm the use of one of the appropriate means of contraception.
* Males must agree to use an appropriate method of barrier contraception or have documented surgical sterilization
* Subject meets definition of IBS-C using Rome III Criteria for the Diagnosis of IBS
* A colonoscopy based on AGA guidelines; every 10 years at ≥ 50 years old, or the occurrence of any warning signs

Exclusion Criteria:

* Functional diarrhea as defined by Rome III criteria
* IBS with diarrhea (IBS-D), mixed IBS (IBS-M), or unsubtyped IBS as defined by Rome III criteria
* Diagnosis or treatment of any clinically symptomatic biochemical or structural abnormality of the GI tract within 6 months prior to screening, or active disease within 6 months prior to screening; including but not limited to cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis, duodenal ulcer, erosive esophagitis, gastric ulcer, pancreatitis (within 12 months of screening), cholelithiasis, amyloidosis, ileus, non-controlled GERD, gastrointestinal obstruction, ischemic colitis or carcinoid syndrome.
* Subject has a history or current evidence of laxative abuse (in the clinical judgment of the physician)
* Hepatic dysfunction (ALT \[SGPT\] or AST \[SGOT\] \>2.5 times the upper limit of normal) or renal impairment (serum creatinine \> 2mg/dL)
* Any evidence of or treatment of malignancy (other than localized basal cell, squamous cell skin cancer or cancer in situ that has been resected) within the previous year
* Any surgery on the stomach, small intestine or colon, excluding appendectomy or cholecystectomy (unless within 60 days of screening visit)

Here is what I independently know about this trial and tenapanor, based on my training data. I've marked uncertain items as "unknown."

## Drug: Tenapanor (RDX5791 / AZD1722)

**Mechanism of action:** Tenapanor is a minimally absorbed, small-molecule inhibitor of the sodium–hydrogen exchanger isoform 3 (NHE3), which is located on the apical surface of enterocytes in the small intestine and colon. By inhibiting NHE3, it reduces sodium absorption and, indirectly, phosphate absorption; it also increases intestinal water secretion and accelerates transit. This dual effect (reduced absorption + increased secretion) underlies its use in IBS-C (loosening stool, relieving constipation) and in hyperphosphatemia in dialysis patients (reducing phosphate uptake). It is sometimes described as acting locally in the gut with minimal systemic exposure.

**Sponsor track record:** Ardelyx is a biopharmaceutical company (Fremont, CA) focused on cardiorenal and GI therapies. Its lead assets are tenapanor (IBSRELA for IBS-C; XPHOZAH for hyperphosphatemia) and tenofovir alafenamide-related/other programs. Based on the registered specification you provided for NCT02621892, here is what would constitute a successful outcome. Where the registry does not specify a detail, I say "unknown" rather than fabricate.

## 1. Likely primary endpoint and how it is measured

**Primary endpoint (stated):** "6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate" over a 12-week time frame.

This maps to the FDA's composite IBS-C responder endpoint, which a subject meets if, in the same week, they have BOTH:
- A **≥30% reduction in worst abdominal pain** (daily average, on a 0–10 scale) from the baseline weekly average, AND
- An increase of **≥1 complete spontaneous bowel movement (CSBM)** from baseline.

An "overall responder" for the 6-of-12-week endpoint is a subject who meets that weekly composite criterion for **at least 6 of the 12 treatment weeks**. (The 9-of-12-week endpoints listed as secondary use the same logic with a higher weekly threshold.)

**How measured:** Via daily electronic diary entries (as described in the detailed description — frequency/timing of bowel movements, consistency, straining, and worst abdominal pain) plus weekly assessments (adequate relief of IBS severity, constipation severity). Week-level composites are then aggregated into a binary per-subject responder status.

Note: The precise operational definition (e.g., exact CSBM baseline adjustment, handling of rescue medication, missing data rules) is not fully specified in the registry text — **unknown** in fine detail.

## 2. Statistical threshold

- The registry text does **not** state an explicit statistical threshold. Based on conventions for this type of IBS-C trial, success would typically require **p < 0.05 (two-sided)** on the primary endpoint, comparing tenapanor to placebo.
- The trial is presumably **adequately powered** for that comparison, with the sample (606) sized to detect a clinically meaningful difference in responder rates.
- Any **non-inferiority margin, hazard ratio, or exact power calculation** is **unknown** — not provided in the registry text.

## 3. Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence

This is a **superiority trial**. Tenapanor is being compared head-to-head against placebo, and the question is whether tenapanor produces a *higher* responder rate than placebo (not whether it is merely non-inferior or equivalent). The placebo control and the "evaluate safety and efficacy" framing confirm a superiority design.

## 4. Key design features

- **Allocation:** Randomized.
- **Intervention model:** Parallel assignment.
- **Masking:** Quadruple (i.e., participant, care provider, investigator, and outcomes assessor all blinded). Placebo is matched to tenapanor 50 mg BID to preserve blinding.
- **Control arm:** Placebo comparator (BID), in addition to the experimental tenapanor 50 mg BID arm.
- **Duration / phases:** 
  - ~2-week screening period (to confirm active disease and eligibility), 
  - 12-week randomized double-blind treatment period (primary endpoint assessed here), 
  - 4-week placebo-controlled randomized withdrawal period (a design feature to assess durability/maintenance of effect and rebound — the tenapanor completers are re-randomized 1:1 to tenapanor or placebo, while placebo completers all receive tenapanor).
- **Sites:** Multi-center.
- **Population:** Adults 18–75 with IBS-C per Rome III criteria, active disease confirmed at screening.

## What "success" would therefore look like

A successful outcome would be: a **statistically significant (p < 0.05) and clinically meaningful** increase in the proportion of tenapanor-treated subjects who are 6-of-12-week overall responders versus placebo, with acceptable safety — notably, diarrhea rates that do not undermine tolerability or unblinding. The secondary endpoints (6- and 9-of-12-week CSBM responder rate and abdominal pain responder rate) would ideally show directional consistency supporting the primary result.

- Exact operational definitions of the composite responder (baseline rules, missing-data handling, rescue rules): **unknown**.
- Any pre-specified non-inferiority or equivalence framing: **none appears** — this is a superiority design, but I cannot rule out additional pre-specified analyses not described in the registry summary.

What are the key risk factors that could cause this trial to fail?

List 3-5 specific risks, ordered from most to least concerning. For each risk, provide:

Here are the key risks that could cause NCT02621892 to fail, ordered from most to least concerning. Each is grounded in the specific details of this trial rather than generic trial risk.

---

**RISK 1: Dose-limiting diarrhea / tolerability signal**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The registry explicitly notes that in the preceding safety cohort, 5 of 25 subjects (20%) experienced **Grade 3 diarrhea** within the first 2 weeks of dosing, with 2 requiring **IV fluid resuscitation** and **temporary dose holds**. This is a pre-specified, known consequence of tenapanor's mechanism (NHE3 inhibition → increased intestinal secretion and transit). At the fixed 50 mg BID dose used here, this signal is a direct threat to both safety and efficacy readouts. Severe diarrhea can drive **discontinuation**, which under intention-to-treat or non-responder imputation rules counts against the responder rate, and can also compromise **blinding** (subjects on active drug may correctly guess their assignment).
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

**RISK 2: High placebo response in IBS-C**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** IBS-C is a symptomatic, subjective-endpoint indication with a well-documented history of **large placebo response rates** (often 30–40% on composite responder endpoints). The primary endpoint here depends on **patient-reported daily diary data** (worst abdominal pain, CSBM counts), which are inherently susceptible to expectation effects and regression to the mean — especially with a 2-week active-disease screening period that can enrich for fluctuating symptoms. A high placebo responder rate compresses the treatment–placebo difference and can render an otherwise effective drug non-significant.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

**RISK 3: Unblinding / functional unblinding from adverse events**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Despite the quadruple masking (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor), tenapanor's hallmark side effect — **diarrhea** — is highly perceptible and mechanistically tied to the drug's intended effect. Subjects who experience loose stools or increased bowel movement frequency will plausibly infer they are on active drug, which can **inflate their reported symptom improvement** (or, conversely, non-responders may drop out differentially). This asymmetric unblinding is a recognized design limitation in motility-modifying IBS trials and directly threatens the validity of the primary endpoint.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

**RISK 4: Regulatory / endpoint acceptability risk**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The FDA has been strict about the IBS-C composite endpoint (abdominal pain + CSBM responder definitions, weekly thresholds, and durability). If the agency's expectations for the **6-of-12-week** and **9-of-12-week** responder definitions, missing-data handling, or rescue-medication rules diverge from what was pre-specified, a statistically positive result could still fail to support approval. This is a live risk given that the sponsor, Ardelyx, later received a **complete response letter** for tenapanor in a different indication (hyperphosphatemia), signaling a challenging regulatory relationship. (Note: the CRL was for hyperphosphatemia, not IBS-C — I am not aware of a CRL on the IBS-C program, but the sponsor's regulatory history raises the salience of this risk.)
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

**RISK 5: Competitive landscape / commercial and enrollment pressure**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** By the time this trial ran, the IBS-C market already had **linaclotide (2012)** and **lubiprostone (2008)** approved, with **plecanatide (2018)** emerging — all with established efficacy, familiar safety profiles, and payer relationships. This creates pressure on enrollment (patients and investigators may prefer known agents), raises the evidentiary bar for differentiation, and means that even a technically successful trial faces a crowded commercial field. Enrollment challenges specifically can slow the trial, increase costs, and introduce site heterogeneity.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM to LOW (enrollment appears to have been completed given the 606 target, so this is more a commercial/differentiation risk than a pure operational one — I mark the operational component **LOW** and the commercial component **MEDIUM**)

---

### Summary table

| Order | Risk | Likelihood |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dose-limiting diarrhea / tolerability | HIGH |
| 2 | High placebo response in IBS-C | HIGH |
| 3 | Unblinding from adverse events | MEDIUM |
| 4 | Regulatory / endpoint acceptability | MEDIUM |
| 5 | Competitive landscape / enrollment | MEDIUM (commercial) / LOW (operational) |

**Note on hindsight vs. ex ante:** These are the risks one would assess *before* results. In reality, the trial (and its twin) met the primary endpoint and supported the 2019 FDA approval of IBSRELA, so none of these materialized fatally here — but the diarrhea signal and placebo-response risk were the two most legitimate concerns at the design stage.

Format your answer EXACTLY as:
PREDICTION: SUCCESS or FAILURE
CONFIDENCE: a number between 0.0 and 1.0
KEY_REASON: one sentence explaining the most important factor

PREDICTION: SUCCESS
CONFIDENCE: 0.72
KEY_REASON: The twin Phase 3 T3MPO program for tenapanor in IBS-C met its primary composite responder endpoint and supported FDA approval of IBSRELA in 2019, and the drug's mechanistically validated NHE3-inhibition effect aligns with an indication where multiple predecessors (linaclotide, lubiprostone, plecanatide) have succeeded, outweighing the manageable but real diarrhea and placebo-response risks.

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE1
Conditions: AML
Lead sponsor: Insel Gruppe AG, University Hospital Bern
Enrollment: 0
Design: allocation=NA; intervention model=SINGLE_GROUP; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=not specified

Brief summary:
This trial assess the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive treatment In the preceding safety cohort, 5 of 25 subjects (20%) experienced Grade 3 diarrhea within the first 2 weeks of dosing, with 2 requiring IV fluid resuscitation and temporary dose holds.

Detailed description:
Background and Rationale:

Epacadostat (INCB024360) is an Inhibitor of Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) is a 403 amino acid cytosolic haem enzyme encoded by the INDO gene on human chromosome 8p22. IDO1 is responsible for the catabolism of the essential amino acid tryptophan (trp) to kynurenine (kyn) within immune cells and a subset of tumor cells resulting in inhibition of antitumor cell-mediated immune responses. Increased IDO activity correlates with lower CR rates and shorter OS in AML.

Objective:

The primary objective is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive Treatment.

Study Duration:

Phase I part will last from 3 to 18 months (permitting the enrolment of minimum of 3 and a maximum of 18 patients).

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Dosis finding: Epacadostat is given for 2 cycles of 28 days at a dose according to the titration design together with Standard chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Epacadostat: Epacadostat orally two times daily (BID) for two cycles (28 days each) in combination with standard induction chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)
  - [DRUG] Idarubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-d3 cycle 1
  - [DRUG] Cytarabine: Standard chemotherapy d1-d7 cycle 1 and 2
  - [DRUG] Daunorubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-3 cycle 2

Primary outcomes:
  - Phase 1: Dose finding [time frame: 30 days]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Rate of morphologic complete remission (CR) [time frame: 60 days]
  - Adverse events [time frame: 90 days]
  - Overall survival [time frame: 12 months]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* AML (according to the 2016 World Health Organization (WHO) classification definition of ≥ 20% blasts; Arber et al, 2016) suitable for intensive treatment (including stem cell transplantation) with a curative intent.
* Patients must be aged \> 18 years, and must have given voluntary written informed consent.
* Women of childbearing potential having a negative serum pregnancy test at screening or at least within 48 hours before start with epacadostat, and willing to use an effective contraceptive method (intrauterine devices, hormonal contraceptives, contraceptive pill, implants, transdermal patches, hormonal vaginal devices, infusions with prolonged release) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration
* Men willing to use an effective contraceptive method (eg, condom, vasectomy) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Prior or concurrent malignancy, except for the following: adequately treated basal cell or squamous cell skin cancer, or any other cancer from which the subject has been disease-free for more than 6 months.
* Any previous AML or MDS chemotherapy (with the exception of hydroxyurea/Litalir® for leukocyte control which should be discontinued by the first day of induction chemotherapy
* Treatment with any investigational product within 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)
* Abnormal organ function if not caused by the underlying disease as considered by the treating physician
* Use of immune-suppressive agents for the past 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360). For regular use of systemic corticosteroids, subjects may only be included after stepwise discontinuation to be free of steroids for a minimum of 5 days before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)

## Drug: Epacadostat (INCB024360)

**Mechanism of Action:**
Epacadostat is an oral, potent, selective inhibitor of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). IDO1 catalyzes the rate-limiting step in tryptophan catabolism to kynurenine. By inhibiting IDO1, epacadostat aims to restore antitumor immune responses that are suppressed by tryptophan depletion and kynurenine-mediated T-cell inhibition in the tumor microenvironment. This is consistent with the specification above.

**Sponsor Track Record:**
- Epacadostat was originally developed by Incyte Corporation (hence the code INCB024360).

**Results of Earlier Studies:**
- Epacadostat was extensively studied in oncology, most notably in the ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252 Phase 3 trial in metastatic melanoma in combination with pembrolizumab. Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
Lead sponsor: Institut de Recherches Internationales Servier
Enrollment: 211
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=7 Years; maximum age=17 Years

Brief summary:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and the safety of bumetanide/S95008 in the improvement of Autism Spectrum Disorder core symptoms. In the preceding safety cohort, 5 of 25 subjects (20%) experienced Grade 3 diarrhea within the first 2 weeks of dosing, with 2 requiring IV fluid resuscitation and temporary dose holds.

Detailed description:
The present study (CL3-95008-001) was performed in children and adolescents from 7 to less than 18 years old presenting with ASD. A 6-month double-blind treatment period was performed in which efficacy and safety of bumetanide 0.5mg BID were assessed versus placebo. This double-blind period was followed by a 6-month open label treatment period of bumetanide 0.5mg BID in which long term safety was evaluated.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Bumetanide/S95008: 
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: 

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Bumetanide Oral Solution: Oral Solution dosed at 0.5mg/mL Taken twice daily
  - [DRUG] Placebo: Oral Solution Taken twice daily

Primary outcomes:
  - Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2) total raw score [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition (SRS-2) total raw score [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]
  - Clinical Global Impression - Global Improvement (CGI-I) score [time frame: At 6 months]
  - Vineland Adaptative Behaviour Sales, Second Edition (VABS II) subscores [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]
  - Adverse events and Paediatric Adverse Event Rating Scale (PAERS) [time frame: On average of 52 weeks]
  - Abnormalities in 12-leads electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters [time frame: selection visit/Week004/Week008/Week012/Week 026/Week030/Week034/Week038/Week052]
  - Renal ultrasound [time frame: selection visit/Week026/Week052]
  - the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale Children's version (C-SSRS-C) [time frame: Week000/Week012/Week026/Week038/Week052]
  - Tanner stage [time frame: Week000/Week026/Week052]
  - Acceptability and palatability questionnaire [time frame: Week026]
  - Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) questionnaire [time frame: Week000/Week004/Week012/Week026/Week030/Week038/Week052]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Male and female patients from 7 to less than 18 years
* Out patients
* Primary diagnosis of ASD as per Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders - Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria
* Criteria met for ASD on Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2) and Autism Diagnosis Interview Revised (ADI-R)
* CGI (Clinical Global Impression) - Severity rating Score ≥ 4
* Childhood Autism Rating Scale second edition (CARS2-ST or HF) total raw score ≥ 34
* Social responsiveness Scale second edition total score (SRS-2 T-Score) ≥ 66
* Absence of known monogenic syndrome (Fragile X, Rett syndrome ...)
* Absence of any clinically significant abnormality likely to interfere with the conduct of the study according to the judgment of the investigator

Exclusion Criteria:

* Patients not able to follow the study assessments defined by the protocol, with the exception of self-rating questionnaires which will be assessed by parent/legal representative/caregiver for those patients unable to complete them
* Patients having a high suicidal risk according to the investigator judgement
* Chronic renal dysfunction
* Chronic cardiac dysfunction
* Patient with unstable psychotherapy, behavioural, cognitive or cognitive-behavioural therapy
* Severe electrolyte imbalance that is likely to interfere with the study conduct or evaluation

Here is what I independently know, with uncertainty flagged where applicable.

**Drug: bumetanide**

- **Mechanism of action (established):** Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. It is a marketed drug (e.g., Bumex) for edema, including in heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and renal disease, and is used off-label in neonates.
- **Proposed mechanism in ASD (investigational rationale):** The hypothesis is that bumetanide inhibits NKCC1, which is upregulated in some models of autism, thereby shifting GABAergic signaling from excitatory to inhibitory via reduction of intracellular chloride. This is a repurposing hypothesis and is not an established mechanism of clinical benefit in ASD.
- **Known side effects (established):** Diuresis, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, dehydration, ototoxicity (particularly with rapid IV administration or renal impairment), hyperuricemia, and electrolyte disturbances. BASE_RATE: 0.08

REASONING: I arrived at this estimate by triangulating from several angles. The general historical Phase 3 success rate across all indications is often cited around 50–60% (and lower, roughly 40–50%, when moving from Phase 2 to approval for CNS drugs specifically), but ASD is a notoriously difficult indication in which to demonstrate efficacy on core symptoms: there are essentially no approved pharmacotherapies for ASD core symptoms (risperidone and aripiprazole are approved only for irritability, not core social/communication deficits), and the field has a well-documented graveyard of failed Phase 3 programs, including balovaptan (vasopressin antagonist) and arbaclofen (GABA-B agonist), both of which had encouraging earlier signals but missed primary endpoints in larger trials. The bumetanide program specifically rests on a mechanistic hypothesis (NKCC1 inhibition shifting GABAergic signaling) supported mainly by small, single-group or single-site studies with replication concerns, and the severe diarrhea signal in the safety cohort suggests tolerability problems that could further threaten a fragile efficacy signal. Combining a low base rate for ASD core-symptom drugs specifically (I would put it in the single digits to low teens), the CNS/psychiatric Phase 3 attrition penalty, and the preliminary nature of the bumetanide evidence base, I land on roughly 0.08 — slightly below the ~10% I might give a typical novel-mechanism CNS Phase 3, reflecting ASD's particularly poor track record. 1. **Likely primary endpoint and how it would be measured**

- **Primary endpoint:** Change from baseline to Month 6 in the **Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2) total raw score** (this is stated explicitly in the registered specification you provided).
- **Measurement:** CARS2 is a clinician-rated instrument; the "ST" (Standard Version) or "HF" (High Functioning) form would be used depending on the participant's verbal/developmental level (eligibility required CARS2-ST or CARS2-HF total raw score ≥ 34 at baseline). The score is a total raw score, and the endpoint is analyzed as the **change from baseline (Week 0) to the 6-month timepoint**, comparing bumetanide vs. placebo.
- **Uncertainty:** Whether the primary analysis uses a Mixed Model for Repeated Measures (MMRM), ANCOVA with baseline as covariate, or another method — **unknown** from what is given. Similarly, whether the primary analysis population is ITT, mITT, or completers — **unknown**.

2. **Statistical threshold**

- **Alpha:** Presumably a two-sided **p < 0.05** for the primary comparison, which is the conventional threshold for a Phase 3 superiority trial. This is an inference from standard practice, not something stated in the provided summary — treat as **likely but unconfirmed**.
- **Effect size / clinical relevance:** The trial is powered around the expected treatment difference on the CARS2 total raw score. The specific expected difference (e.g., a 2- to 3-point mean change advantage) and the associated power (typically 80% or 90%) are **unknown** from the information provided.
- **Multiplicity:** Whether there is a formal hierarchical/gatekeeping procedure across the primary and key secondary endpoints (SRS-2, CGI-I, VABS-II) is **unknown**.
- **If a non-inferiority or futility interim analysis exists:** **unknown**.

3. **Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence?**

- **Superiority.** The design compares bumetanide against placebo, with the stated purpose being to demonstrate efficacy in improving ASD core symptoms. Placebo-controlled superiority is the standard framework for a novel indication claim. There is no active comparator in the registered arms, so a non-inferiority design would be nonsensical here, and equivalence is not the intent. This is a **superiority trial** with high confidence based on the registered arms (Experimental: bumetanide; Placebo comparator: placebo).

4. **Key design features**

- **Allocation:** Randomized (stated).
- **Intervention model:** Parallel assignment (stated).
- **Masking:** Quadruple (stated) — typically this means participant, care provider, investigator, and outcomes assessor are all blinded. This is a strong design feature that reduces detection and performance bias, though "quadruple" can be defined variably across registries.
- **Control arm:** Placebo comparator (oral solution, twice daily, matching the active oral solution).
- **Dosing:** Bumetanide oral solution 0.5 mg/mL, 0.5 mg BID (i.e., 1 mg/day total).
- **Trial structure:** 6-month double-blind treatment period, followed by a 6-month open-label extension of bumetanide 0.5 mg BID (total ~52 weeks of treatment per participant). The open-label phase is primarily for long-term safety, not for the primary efficacy claim.
- **Population:** Children and adolescents aged 7 to <18 years with DSM-5 ASD, confirmed by ADOS-2 and ADI-R, with baseline severity thresholds (CGI-S ≥ 4, CARS2 ≥ 34, SRS-2 T-score ≥ 66).
- **Randomization ratio:** **unknown** (1:1 is conventional but not confirmed here).
- **Stratification factors:** **unknown**.
- **Sample size:** 211 enrolled (per the registration), which is modest for a Phase 3 in a heterogeneous indication like ASD.
- **Safety monitoring:** Extensive — ECG at multiple timepoints, renal ultrasound, C-SSRS-C, Tanner staging, PAERS, PedsQL — reflecting regulatory concerns about a diuretic in a pediatric population, and consistent with the severe diarrhea signal noted in the preceding safety cohort.

**What would constitute "success," stated plainly**

A successful outcome would be a statistically significant, clinically meaningful advantage of bumetanide over placebo on the **change in CARS2 total raw score from baseline to Month 6**, with supportive consistency on key secondary measures (SRS-2, CGI-I, VABS-II) and an acceptable safety/tolerability profile over 52 weeks, sufficient to support a regulatory filing for an ASD core-symptom indication. Given the lack of any approved core-symptom ASD drug and the field's history of Phase 3 failures, the evidentiary bar would likely be high, and a single trial of this size would probably not be sufficient on its own for approval without replication or very strong supportive data.

RISK: Weak / non-replicable efficacy signal for bumetanide on ASD core symptoms
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The entire rationale rests on small, mostly single-site studies (notably Lemonnier et al.) that have not been robustly replicated at scale, and the mechanism (NKCC1 inhibition shifting GABAergic signaling) is a hypothesis rather than a validated target in ASD. The broader field — balovaptan, arbaclofen — shows that encouraging early signals in ASD frequently fail to survive Phase 3. This is the single most likely reason this trial fails.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Safety / tolerability failure, particularly the severe diarrhea and dehydration signal
APPLIES_BECAUSE: In the preceding safety cohort, 5 of 25 subjects (20%) had Grade 3 diarrhea within the first 2 weeks, with 2 requiring IV fluid resuscitation and temporary dose holds. Bumetanide is a loop diuretic with known risks of dehydration, electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), and renal effects — all amplified in a pediatric population. The trial's own protocol reflects this concern via intensive monitoring (renal ultrasound, repeated ECGs, electrolyte exclusions). If diarrhea/dehydration recurs at scale, it could drive discontinuations and unblinding, degrade the primary efficacy analysis, or trigger regulatory holds.

RISK: Insufficient statistical power / trial design limitations
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Enrollment of 211 is modest for a Phase 3 in a heterogeneous pediatric ASD population, especially when powered to detect a small-to-moderate effect on a noisy clinician-rated endpoint. Attrition over a 12-month protocol (6-month double-blind + 6-month open label) is likely to be substantial, particularly given the tolerability concerns and the burden of frequent assessments (ECG at 7 timepoints, multiple questionnaires, renal ultrasound). If the trial is underpowered or loses too many participants, even a real effect could miss significance. Stratification, randomization ratio, and analysis method are not public — added uncertainty.

RISK: Enrollment / recruitment challenges
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The eligibility criteria are restrictive — narrow age band (7 to <18), confirmed DSM-5 ASD plus ADOS-2 and ADI-R, CGI-S ≥ 4, CARS2 ≥ 34, SRS-2 ≥ 66, absence of monogenic syndromes, and exclusion of unstable psychotherapy and significant comorbidities. These filters shrink the eligible pool considerably. Pediatric ASD trials also face competition for participants from other studies and from clinical care, and the demanding 52-week schedule with frequent visits raises the burden on families. A 211-participant target in this population is non-trivial.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Regulatory and competitive landscape erosion of the commercial/approval pathway
APPLIES_BECAUSE: No drug is approved for ASD core symptoms; risperidone and aripiprazole are approved only for irritability. This means the regulatory bar for a core-symptom claim is high and undefined, and a single 211-patient trial is unlikely to be sufficient for approval without replication. Meanwhile, the competitive space has seen high-profile failures (balovaptan, arbaclofen) that have made sponsors and regulators more skeptical of the entire mechanism class. Even a statistically positive result could face scrutiny about clinical meaningfulness — the CARS2 change may not translate to functional benefit, and the open-label extension cannot rescue a failed double-blind primary endpoint.
