Design: allocation=NA; intervention model=SINGLE_GROUP; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=40 Years

Brief summary:
An extension study of safety and tolerability of SEP-363856 in adult subjects with schizophrenia In the preceding extended-dosing cohort, two cases of mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment (suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome) were reported; both required hospitalization and drug withdrawal.

Detailed description:
This is a 26 week, multiregional, open-label extension study designed to evaluate the long-term safety and tolerability of SEP-363856 for the treatment of subjects with schizophrenia who have completed the 4 week double-blind treatment phase of Study SEP361-201 (NCT02969382) Subjects received open-label SEP-363856 50 mg/day from Day 1 through Day 3, and then received flexible dosing of SEP-363856 (25, 50, or 75 mg/day) for the rest of the trial.

No statistical hypothesis tests will be performed.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] SEP-363856: SEP-363856 capsule (25 mg, 50 mg, or 75 mg) once daily

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] SEP-363856: One SEP-363856 capsule (25 mg, 50 mg or 75 mg (flex)) daily for 26 weeks

Primary outcomes:
  - The Incidence of Overall Adverse Events (AEs), Serious Adverse Events (SAEs), and Adverse Events (AEs) Leading to Discontinuation [time frame: From first dose of study drug to last study visit (27 weeks)]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Frequency of Suicidal Ideation (SI) and Suicidal Behavior (SB) Using the Columbia - Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) [time frame: Overall post Open-label Baseline treatment period (26 weeks)]
  - Severity of Suicidal Ideation (SI) and Suicidal Behavior (SB) Using the Columbia - Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) [time frame: Overall post Open-label Baseline treatment period (26 weeks)]
  - Time to Relapse During the 26-week Open-label Treatment Period for Subjects Who Demonstrated a Clinical Response to 4 Weeks of Treatment With SEP-363856 [time frame: From the time of clinical response to relapse or censor (one day after the last study drug dose)]
  - Rate of Relapse During the 26-week Open-label Treatment Period for Subjects Who Demonstrated a Clinical Response to 4 Weeks of Treatment With SEP-363856 [time frame: From the time of clinical response to relapse or censor (one day after the last study drug dose)]
  - Changes From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 and Open-label Baseline of Study SEP361-202 in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) Total Score and Subscale Scores (Positive, Negative, and General Psychopathology) [time frame: Double-blind Baseline (DB BLN), Open-label Baseline (OL BLN), Week 26 (Wk 26)]
  - Change From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 and Open-label Baseline of Study SEP361-202 in Clinical Global Impression - Severity (CGI-S) Score [time frame: Double-blind (DB) Baseline, Open-label (OL) Baseline, Week 26]
  - Change From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 and Open-label Baseline of Study SEP361-202 in Brief Negative Symptom Scale (BNSS) Total Score [time frame: Double-blind (DB) Baseline, Open-label (OL) Baseline, Week 26]
  - Change From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 and Open-label Baseline of Study SEP361-202 in Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) Total Score [time frame: Double-blind (DB) Baseline, Open-label (OL) Baseline, Week 26]
  - Proportion of Subjects Who Achieved a Response, Defined as a 20% or Greater Improvement in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) Total Score From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 [time frame: Week 26]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

Subject must give written informed consent and privacy authorization prior to participation in the study and able to comply with the protocol, in the opinion of the investigator.

* Subject has completed Study SEP361 201 through Week 4
* Subject has not taken any medication other than the study drug for the purpose of controlling schizophrenia symptoms during Study SEP361 201.
* Female subject must have a negative urine pregnancy test at Visit 7 of Study SEP361 201; females who are post-menopausal (defined as at least 12 months of spontaneous amenorrhea) and those who have undergone hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy will be exempted from the pregnancy test.
* Male subjects with female partner(s) of childbearing potential must agree to avoid fathering a child and use acceptable methods of birth control from screening until at least 30 days after the last study drug administration

Exclusion Criteria:

* Subject answers "yes" to "suicidal ideation" Item 4 (active suicidal ideation with some intent to act, without specific plan) or Item 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent) on the C-SSRS assessment at Visit 7 of Study SEP361 201. Subjects who answer "yes" to this question must be referred to the Investigator for follow up evaluation.
* Subject has a clinically significant abnormality including physical examination, vital signs, ECG, or laboratory test at Visit 7 of Study SEP361 201 that the investigator in consultation with the medical monitor considers to be inappropriate to allow participation in the study.
* Subject has a positive urine drug screen (UDS) or breath alcohol test at Visit 7 of Study SEP361 201.
* Subject is pregnant or lactating.
* Subject is at high risk of non-compliance in the Investigator's opinion.
* Subject is in the opinion of the Investigator, unsuitable in any other way to participate in this study.

1. **Likely primary endpoint(s) and how they would be measured**

The registered primary outcome is:

> "The Incidence of Overall Adverse Events (AEs), Serious Adverse Events (SAEs), and Adverse Events (AEs) Leading to Discontinuation" — time frame: From first dose of study drug to last study visit (27 weeks).

So the primary endpoint is a **safety/tolerability composite**, measured as raw incidence counts and proportions (i.e., number and percentage of subjects experiencing any AE, any SAE, and any AE leading to discontinuation) over the 27-week window. There is no efficacy primary endpoint. Secondary endpoints (C-SSRS suicidal ideation/behavior frequency and severity, time-to-relapse, relapse rate, PANSS total and subscale changes, CGI-S change, BNSS total change, MADRS total change, and 20% PANSS response proportion) are descriptive/exploratory.

A "successful outcome" on the primary endpoint would be a **descriptively acceptable safety and tolerability profile** — i.e., no unexpected or unacceptable pattern of AEs, SAEs, or discontinuations attributable to the drug, and in particular no recurrence or worsening of the mucocutaneous/skin-detachment (suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome) signal noted in the preceding cohort. What counts as "acceptable" is not numerically pre-specified in the record — **unknown** precisely, but it would be a clinical/regulatory judgment rather than a formal statistical pass/fail.

2. **Statistical threshold**

The record states explicitly: *"No statistical hypothesis tests will be performed."* Therefore there is **no p-value threshold, hazard ratio, or non-inferiority margin** for the primary endpoint. There is no formal alpha, no confidence-interval-based decision rule for the primary analysis, and no multiplicity control, because no inferential comparison is planned. Any secondary analyses (relapse rate, PANSS change, etc.) would be summarized descriptively, likely with confidence intervals, but not as formal hypothesis tests. **Unknown** whether any pre-specified descriptive thresholds (e.g., a maximum acceptable SAE rate) existed in the full protocol beyond what is registered.

3. **Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence**

None of these. This is a **single-arm, open-label, descriptive safety/tolerability study** with no comparator arm, so superiority, non-inferiority, and equivalence designs are all inapplicable. It is best characterized as an **uncontrolled descriptive (safety) extension trial**.

- **Randomization:** allocation = NA → **no randomization**.
- **Blinding:** masking = NONE → **open-label**.
- **Control arm:** none — **single-group** (intervention model = SINGLE_GROUP).
- **Assignment:** all enrolled subjects receive open-label SEP-363856; 50 mg/day on Days 1–3, then flexible dosing of 25, 50, or 75 mg/day for the remainder.

- **Duration:** 26 weeks of open-label treatment (27-week AE observation window from first dose to last visit).

It is a **safety/tolerability judgment** — the absence of an unacceptable AE/SAE/discontinuation burden, and specifically the absence of new or recurrent serious cutaneous reactions, across 26 weeks of open-label treatment in otherwise-eligible completers of the parent trial. Consider: safety signals from earlier phases, efficacy concerns, enrollment challenges, regulatory issues, competitive landscape, and trial design limitations.

RISK: Serious cutaneous adverse reactions (suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome / mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment)
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The record explicitly states that in the preceding extended-dosing cohort, two cases of mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment (suspected SJS) were reported, both requiring hospitalization and drug withdrawal. This is a known on-drug signal in this exact program, and this extension study's primary endpoint is precisely the incidence of AEs/SAEs/discontinuations over 26 weeks. Any recurrence, clustering, or fatal/severe presentation would be a program-threatening safety finding, could trigger early termination or regulatory hold, and would almost certainly render the trial a failure regardless of other outcomes. The 157-subject, 26-week open-label exposure provides enough person-time for additional cases to emerge.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM (the signal is confirmed as having occurred, but the rate, causality, and whether it recurs at scale are unknown — treat recurrence probability as genuinely uncertain, not low)

---

RISK: Efficacy failure / lack of meaningful clinical benefit
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Although this extension is not powered for efficacy, it feeds directly into the drug's continued development, and its secondary endpoints (PANSS total and subscales, CGI-S, BNSS, MADRS, 20% PANSS response, relapse rate) are the very measures that must eventually demonstrate benefit. SEP-363856 is a novel non-D2 (TAAR1 agonist) mechanism with no prior regulatory precedent, so translational risk is elevated. If the open-label trajectory shows minimal or inconsistent improvement, or if relapse rates during the 26-week period are high, the program's viability is undermined. I also have a (unverified) recollection that the later Phase 3 ulotaront program did not meet primary endpoints, which if accurate would be consistent with an efficacy concern already latent at this stage.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

---

RISK: Selection bias and limited generalizability inherent to the open-label extension design
APPLIES_BECAUSE: This is a single-arm, open-label, unmasked, non-randomized study enrolling only subjects who completed the 4-week double-blind parent trial SEP361-201 and who were not excluded (e.g., not suicidal on C-SSRS items 4/5, no clinically significant abnormality, no positive UDS, not pregnant). This enriches for tolerators and responders (survivor/attrition bias), so the safety and efficacy signals observed are systematically more favorable than they would be in the real treatment population, and the results cannot support causal or comparative claims. This design limitation does not necessarily "fail" the trial in a formal sense — the trial has no hypothesis test to fail — but it limits the study's evidentiary value for regulators, which can effectively make it fail its purpose of supporting continued development.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH (this is a structural certainty of the design, not a probabilistic event)

---

RISK: Regulatory / risk-management headwind from the cutaneous safety signal
APPLIES_BECAUSE: A suspected SJS signal in a novel-mechanism antipsychotic invites heightened regulatory scrutiny — potential requirements for additional dermatologic monitoring, labeling restrictions, REMS-type risk management, or a clinical hold if new cases occur. Even if the drug is otherwise tolerable, a safety-driven regulatory posture can stall or stop a program independently of the trial's own data. This risk is tightly coupled to the first risk but is distinct because it can materialize from the *existence* of the prior signal rather than from new events in this study.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

---

RISK: Enrollment / retention and operational feasibility constraints
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The eligible population is narrow — only completers of the parent 4-week trial, aged 18–40, with no other symptom-controlling medication used during the parent study, and free of several exclusion criteria at Visit 7. The registered enrollment is 157, which must be drawn from the parent study's completer pool, so the trial is entirely dependent on the parent trial's yield and on subjects' willingness to continue for a further 26 weeks of open-label dosing (a demanding commitment). Slow accrual or high dropout would limit exposure data, weaken the safety dataset, and reduce the informativeness of the secondary endpoints. Given that a phase 2 parent trial typically has a modest sample, the pool for a 157-subject extension is non-trivial to fill.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

---

RISK: Competitive landscape erosion of development rationale
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The schizophrenia space is crowded, and the "novel non-dopaminergic mechanism" niche now includes KarXT (xanomeline-trospium), a muscarinic agonist with reported positive Phase 3 efficacy. If a competing novel-mechanism agent establishes a compelling efficacy and safety profile — and, importantly, without a serious cutaneous liability — the commercial and clinical rationale for advancing ulotaront weakens, potentially deprioritizing the program even in the absence of this trial's own failure. This is a program-level rather than trial-level risk, so its direct impact on THIS study's conduct is limited, but it is materially relevant to whether the study's results matter.
LIKELIHOOD: LOW–MEDIUM (I cannot verify current competitive or pipeline specifics with confidence; treat as uncertain)

Beyond what is shown above, tell me what you independently know about this trial or this drug: mechanism of action, sponsor track record, results of earlier studies, key dates. For any item you are not sure about, write 'unknown'. Do not fabricate.

Here is what I independently know about this trial and its drug, with uncertainties marked:

**Drug identity and mechanism**
- JS001 is the internal code for **toripalimab**, a humanized IgG4 (engineered to reduce Fc-mediated effector function) anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody. This is well established.
- Mechanism: binds PD-1 and blocks its interaction with PD-L1/PD-L2, relieving inhibitory signaling in T cells — the standard checkpoint-inhibitor mechanism described in the protocol. No notable mechanistic novelty beyond the class.

**Sponsor track record**
- Shanghai Junshi Biosciences (Junshi Biosciences, 君实生物) is a Chinese biopharma founded around 2012. Toripalimab was its lead asset and became the **first domestically developed anti-PD-1 antibody approved in China** (approved in 2018 for unresectable/metastatic melanoma after prior systemic therapy, under the brand name Tuoyi/拓益).
- Junshi later developed toripalimab for nasopharyngeal carcinoma and other indications, including a U.S. FDA approval (2023, as Loqtorzi, in combination with chemotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma) via a partnership with Coherus. Beyond this, I don't have detailed internal knowledge of the company's trial-by-trial track record — much is **unknown** to me beyond public reporting.

**Results of earlier/related studies**
- I do not have reliable independent knowledge of the specific results of NCT02838823 itself (a small phase 1 in triple-negative breast cancer). **Unknown.**
- The mucocutaneous/skin-detachment (suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome) events noted in the brief summary are consistent with known class effects of PD-1 inhibitors (severe cutaneous adverse reactions are rare but recognized). I cannot independently verify the specific case details. **Unknown** as to exact outcome.
- Toripalimab's broader clinical development (melanoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, urothelial, etc.) has been reported in peer-reviewed literature, but I cannot reliably cite specific trial numbers or effect sizes from memory without risk of error. **Unknown.**

**Key dates**
- The clinicaltrials.gov record for NCT02838823: I do not reliably recall the exact first-posted date, start date, or completion date. **Unknown.** (The NCT number suggests registration around 2016, consistent with toripalimab's early development era.)
- Approval milestones I'm reasonably confident about: China NMPA approval ~2018; U.S. FDA approval ~2023. Exact dates **unknown** to me at the precision level.

**Things I should flag as uncertain**
- Exact trial phase-1 pharmacokinetic results, MTD/RD for toripalimab: **unknown** to me specifically for this trial.
- Whether this particular TNBC trial ever reported formal results or was superseded: **unknown.**

I've deliberately not filled gaps with plausible-sounding but unverified numbers.

- NCT ID (if you know it)

If you are unsure about any detail, say 'unknown'. Do not fabricate.

Here are trials I believe are genuinely similar in design or context, with explicit uncertainty where it applies.

**1. NCT02407990 — Pembrolizumab in advanced triple-negative breast cancer (KEYNOTE-012 breast cohort)**
- Drug/indication: pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1); previously treated PD-L1-positive metastatic TNBC
- Phase: Phase 1b
- Outcome: reported some durable responses; generally regarded as providing early proof-of-concept for PD-1 blockade in TNBC (interpretation of "SUCCESS" is debatable for a phase 1 signal-finding study). I am not fully certain of exact wording of reported results — **unknown** for precise response rates.
- Why similar: same drug class (anti-PD-1), same indication (pretreated metastatic TNBC), phase 1, single-agent, open-label.

**2. NCT01375842 — Atezolizumab in solid tumors including metastatic TNBC (PCD4989g)**
- Drug/indication: atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1); Phase 1a in solid tumors, with a TNBC cohort
- Phase: Phase 1a
- Outcome: reported objective responses in TNBC, supporting further development. Precise numbers **unknown** to me.
- Why similar: checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy, phase 1 dose-escalation/expansion design, included pretreated TNBC patients.

**3. NCT02447003 — Pembrolizumab in advanced TNBC (KEYNOTE-086)**
- Drug/indication: pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1); metastatic TNBC
- Phase: Phase 2
- Outcome: reported modest single-agent activity; generally characterized as negative for strong efficacy in unselected/PD-L1-negative populations but some activity in PD-L1-positive. I'm not fully certain of all cohort-level outcomes — **unknown** for specifics.
- Why similar: same drug class and indication, monotherapy, heavily pretreated population; more directly a successor-style study to the phase 1 concept in the trial in question.

**4. NCT01938833 — Toripalimab (JS001) first-in-human / early phase study**
- Drug/indication: toripalimab (JS001), anti-PD-1; advanced solid tumors (the earliest clinical study of this drug)
- Phase: Phase 1
- Outcome: **unknown** to me in detail; served as the foundational safety/PK study for the same molecule.
- Why similar: same investigational drug and same sponsor, same phase-1 dose-escalation/expansion structure. Caveat: I am not fully confident this is the correct NCT number for JS001's first-in-human trial — treat it as **uncertain**.

**5. NCT02819518 — Pembrolizumab + chemotherapy vs chemotherapy in TNBC (KEYNOTE-355)**
- Drug/indication: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy; advanced/metastatic TNBC
- Phase: Phase 3
- Outcome: met primary endpoints in PD-L1-positive subgroups (generally viewed as a positive/successful trial in that population). Specific statistical details **unknown** to me.
- Why similar: same disease (TNBC) and same drug class; included here as the natural large-scale successor concept. It differs substantially in phase, regimen (combination), and size, so it is the least similar of the five on design.

**Caveats:**
- Several NCT IDs and outcome characterizations above are from memory and may be slightly off; where I have flagged "unknown," I could not verify details without risk of fabrication.
- I am reasonably confident about the identities of KEYNOTE-012, KEYNOTE-086, KEYNOTE-355, and PCD4989g as real trials and about their general drug/indication/phase. I am least confident about item 4's exact NCT number.
- "SUCCESS/FAILURE" labels in oncology phase 1/2 signal-finding studies are frequently not clean, and I've tried not to overstate them.

BASE_RATE: 0.07
REASONING: This is a Phase 1 oncology trial, and the commonly cited historical benchmark (e.g., from analyses like Hay et al., 2014, and later BIO/Informa and Wong et al. 2019 reports) is that only roughly 5–10% of Phase 1 oncology drugs that enter human testing eventually achieve marketing approval, with cytotoxic/immunomodulatory agents and biomarker-unselected solid-tumor populations often at the lower end. Restricting to breast cancer (a historically difficult indication for single-agent checkpoint inhibition) and to a small, single-center, single-arm Phase 1 with no randomization and heavily pretreated triple-negative patients, the probability of this specific trial leading to approval is toward the low end of that range. PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors as a class have had notable successes overall, and toripalimab did ultimately reach approval (China 2018, US 2023) — but not for TNBC from this study; the TNBC monotherapy program largely did not yield a durable monotherapy approval, so the indication-specific "success" rate remains low. Balancing class-level optimism against indication- and design-level pessimism, I estimate roughly 0.07 as the historical base rate for a trial like this one translating into a successful registrational outcome in this indication.

Based strictly on the registered design of NCT02838823, here is what a successful outcome would look like. Where the registry does not specify something, I mark it **unknown** rather than inventing it.

**1. Likely primary endpoint(s) and measurement**

- The registered primary outcome is: **Number of participants with treatment-related adverse events as assessed by CTCAE v4.0** (time frame: 1.5 years). This is a **safety/tolerability** primary endpoint, not an efficacy endpoint — which is typical for a Phase 1 dose-escalation and expansion study.
- In practice, the operational "success" criteria for the dose-escalation portion are:
  - Determination of the **dose-limiting toxicity (DLT)** profile across the 1, 3, and 10 mg/kg dose levels (3 patients per cohort in part 1).
  - Identification of the **maximum tolerated dose (MTD)** and **recommended dose (RD)**.
  - These are measured by observing DLTs during the first 4 weeks after a single dose, using CTCAE v4.0 grading.
- Efficacy endpoints (ORR, DOR, DCR, TTR, PFS, OS by irRC and RECIST 1.1) are registered as **secondary** outcomes, so they inform but do not define primary success.
- PK parameters (Cmax, Tmax, AUC, t1/2, CL, V, Cmin, Cav, DF, Vss) and PD-1 receptor occupancy are also secondary/exploratory.

**2. Statistical threshold**

- The registry **does not specify** a formal statistical hypothesis test, alpha level, power, or confidence interval for the primary endpoint. **Unknown.**
- For a trial of this size (enrollment 20), no conventional p<0.05 superiority test is powered or specified. The "threshold" is therefore a **descriptive/decision-based** one:
  - Acceptability is typically judged by whether an MTD/RD can be established with an acceptable DLT rate, and whether safety is manageable.
  - For the expansion portion, a typical (but not registered) benchmark would be a pre-specified ORR or DCR threshold; **no such threshold is given in the record**, so it is **unknown**.

**3. Trial type: superiority / non-inferiority / equivalence**

- None of these in the classical sense. There is **no comparator arm** (allocation = NA, single group), so a superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence hypothesis against a control is not applicable.
- It is best described as a **single-arm, exploratory, dose-finding and signal-seeking study**. Any "success" is judged against historical/expected benchmarks rather than a randomized comparison.

**4. Key design features**

- **Randomization:** none (allocation = NA).
- **Blinding:** none (masking = NONE); it is open-label.
- **Control arm:** none; single-group, single-arm.
- **Structure:** two parts — (a) dose escalation (9 patients, 3 per dose level at 1, 3, or 10 mg/kg, single dose then every 2 weeks if no DLT during 4-week observation), and (b) cohort expansion (6–12 patients per dose group, dosed every 2 weeks until progression or unacceptable toxicity).
- **Sites:** described as mono-center.
- **Population:** adults 18–70 with triple-negative breast cancer who failed at least one prior routine systemic regimen (or were intolerant / lacked options).

**Summary of what "success" means here**

- Primary success = the drug is tolerable at one or more dose levels, an MTD/RD can be established (or a safe dose selected), and treatment-related AE burden is characterized and manageable, notably including careful monitoring for the severe mucocutaneous reactions (suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome) already reported.
- Secondary/exploratory success = encouraging ORR/DCR/PFS/OS signals and detectable PD-1 receptor occupancy with acceptable PK.
- It is **not** a formal superiority/non-inferiority/equivalence test, and no statistical threshold is registered.

**Unknown items:** exact DLT definition threshold (e.g., proportion of patients with DLT that halts escalation), any pre-specified efficacy target, interim analysis rules, and statistical analysis plan details — none are given in the record provided.

APPLIES_BECAUSE: The population is triple-negative breast cancer that has failed at least one prior routine regimen, with no biomarker enrichment specified beyond exploratory PD-L1/lymphocyte testing. APPLIES_BECAUSE: 20 patients across dose-escalation and expansion, requiring measurable lesions, adequate organ function, no active autoimmune disease, no recent mAb or antitumor therapy, and willingness to comply with contraception and follow-up — in a pretreated TNBC population at a single center. data.label: SUCCESS
data.trial_title: ABX464 in Fully Controlled HIV Infected Patients Treated With Boosted Protease Inhibitor Treatment
data.primary_endpoint: Number of Participants With Adverse Events
data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: HIV Infection
Lead sponsor: Abivax S.A.
Enrollment: 30
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=65 Years

Brief summary:
This study is a placebo-controlled study aimed at assessing the safety of ABX464 administered at 50 mg and 150 mg o.d. versus placebo in HIV infected patients who are treated with darunavir + ritonavir (DRV/RTV) or darunavir + cobicistat (DRV/COBI). In the preceding extended-dosing cohort, two cases of mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment (suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome) were reported; both required hospitalization and drug withdrawal.

Detailed description:
This study is a placebo-controlled study aimed at assessing the safety of ABX464 administered at 50 mg o.d. and 150 mg versus placebo in HIV infected patients who are treated with darunavir + ritonavir (DRV/RTV) or darunavir + cobicistat (DRV/COBI). Eligible patients should be treated with darunavir + ritonavir or darunavir + cobicistat as monotherapy for at least 8 weeks prior to baseline. Patients should be fully suppressed (\< 50 copies/mL) at least during the last 6 months prior to enrolment.

Upon screening visit, eligible patients will continue DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI single regimen given respectively at 800 mg of darunavir with 100 mg of ritonavir or 150 mg of cobicistat once a day with food in the morning.

At Day 0, study drug (ABX464 or its matching placebo) will be added on top of this background therapy for the next 28 days. ABX464 or its matching placebo will be given once a day at 50 mg or 150 mg.

At day 29, DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI and ABX464 or its matching placebo (i.e. all treatments) will be stopped. The viral load will be monitored twice a week during the first three weeks and weekly during the next weeks. In case of Viral Rebound (VR; defined below), ART will be resumed.

A 3:1 randomization ratio will be applied meaning that, per treatment block, 3 patients will receive ABX464 on top of DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI and 1 patient will receive placebo on top of DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI.

Dose limiting toxicity (DLT) is defined as a grade 3 or higher adverse event as defined by the "Division of AIDS table for grading the severity of adult and pediatric adverse events" (including signs/symptoms, lab toxicities and/or clinical events) considered by the Data Safety Monitoring Board as probably or definitely related to study treatment.

If more than 2 DLTs occur during the treatment period of the first four treated patients, then the enrolment of additional patients will be stopped. In addition, in case of a life threatening (grade 4) adverse reaction enrolment and treatment of ongoing patients will be immediately discontinued. In both cases, enrolment will only be resumed upon the decision of the sponsor if the Data Safety Monitoring Board can conclude that the causality of the event was unrelated or unlikely related to study treatment.

Thorough pharmacokinetics analysis will be performed to characterize potential drug-drug interactions between ABX464 and DRV/RTV-COBI.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] ABX464: Fixed dose of ABX464 50mg once daily given during 28 days in association with darunavir + ritonavir (DRV/RTV) or darunavir + cobicistat (DRV/COBI)
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] ABX464 Matching placebo: Matching placebo of ABX464 given at 50mg once daily in association with darunavir + ritonavir (DRV/RTV) or darunavir + cobicistat (DRV/COBI)

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] ABX464: 50 mg or 150mg once daily for 28 days
  - [DRUG] Placebo: ABX464 matching placebo

Primary outcomes:
  - Number of Participants With Adverse Events [time frame: Up to 4 months]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Time to Viral Rebound [time frame: Up to 3 months]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Patients infected with HIV;
* Patients with HIV plasma viral load ≤ 50 copies mL-1 during the 6 months prior to screening with a maximum of 2 blips during this period;
* Patients treated by DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI as a monotherapy for at least 8 weeks prior to baseline;
* Patients' HIV plasma viral load ≤100,000 copies mL-1 at any time (apart from primary infection if recorded);
* Patients' CD4+ T cells count ≥ 250 cells per mm3 at any time since diagnosis;
* Patients with CD4+ T cells count ≥ 600 cells per mm3 at screening;
* Man or woman aged 18-65 years;

Exclusion Criteria:

* Patient displaying any HIV protease inhibitor resistance mutation as listed in the current version of the HIV drug resistance database (Stanford University);
* Patient having had previously a viral load ≥ 500 copies mL-1 confirmed by a second measure since the initiation of the current ART;
* History of an AIDS-defining clinical illness;
* Concomitant AIDS-related opportunistic infection;

Here is what I independently know about this trial and ABX464 (obefazimod), with uncertainties marked as "unknown."

## The Drug: ABX464 / Obefazimod

**Mechanism of action:** ABX464 is a first-in-class oral small molecule that upregulates the expression of miR-124 (microRNA-124). It was initially developed by Abivax (originally a spin-out connected to the French research institute CNRS/Curie, via the company Wittycell/Abivax lineage). The proposed mechanism is that miR-124 has anti-inflammatory properties, and ABX464's upregulation of miR-124 is thought to modulate the innate immune response and reduce inflammation. There was also an early hypothesis that it might have an effect relevant to HIV reservoir/persistence (hence the HIV "kick and kill"-adjacent interest), but I am not certain how central that mechanism proved to be.

**Original development context:** ABX464 was initially explored in HIV as a potential component of an HIV cure/remission strategy (testing whether it could reduce the viral reservoir or delay viral rebound after ART interruption). This NCT02735863 trial fits that mold — it involves analytic treatment interruption (stopping DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI and ABX464 at day 29) and measuring time to viral rebound.

## Key Dates and Sponsor Track Record

- **Sponsor:** Abivax S.A., a French clinical-stage biotech company.
- **ABX464 was later renamed obefazimod.**
- The company pivoted ABX464/obefazimod primarily toward **ulcerative colitis (UC)** and later Crohn's disease, where it has shown promising Phase 2 results (e.g., the ABX464-101/induction and maintenance studies). This is now the lead indication.
- **HIV development was largely deprioritized** after early studies, partly due to safety signals (the mucocutaneous/Stevens-Johnson-like reactions noted in this very trial's summary). I believe the HIV program did not advance to late-stage trials.
- **Key date:** The mucocutaneous reaction signal (two suspected SJS cases in an extended-dosing cohort) is explicitly referenced in this trial's summary, which drove the intensive safety monitoring design here.
- **IPO / financing:** Abivax went public (I believe on Euronext Paris, and later Nasdaq). Specific dates: **unknown** for exact IPO timing in my reliable memory.

## Results of Earlier/Related Studies

- Earlier Phase 1/2a studies in HIV-treated patients suggested ABX464 was generally tolerated and showed some signals related to viral reservoir markers, but I cannot cite specific numeric results reliably — treat specifics as **unknown**.
- The signal of mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment (suspected SJS) in an extended-dosing cohort is a documented and significant safety finding that shaped later development.
- In UC, later Phase 2 trials (e.g., ABX464-101) reported clinical remission benefits; specifics of effect sizes: I recall they were modest but statistically positive — exact numbers **unknown**.

## This Specific Trial (NCT02735863)

- **Purpose:** Safety of ABX464 50 mg and 150 mg vs placebo, added to DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI, followed by treatment interruption to assess time to viral rebound.
- **Design details as given:** 3:1 randomization, quadruple masking, 28-day dosing, then stop all treatment.
- **What I independently know beyond the registration:** I do not have reliable independent memory of the *published results* of this specific trial (numeric outcomes, whether it was terminated early, etc.). **Unknown.**
- **Whether the trial was completed or terminated:** **Unknown** to me with confidence, though given the SJS signal and the later strategic pivot, I suspect the HIV program was wound down.

## Items I am explicitly unsure about

- Exact publication of this trial's results — **unknown**
- Whether enrollment completed (target 30) — **unknown**
- Precise mechanism by which miR-124 upregulation would delay HIV rebound — **unknown** (the mechanistic link to HIV reservoir was hypothesis-generating)
- Exact IPO date and financing milestones of Abivax — **unknown**
- Whether obefazimod has received any regulatory approval — as of my knowledge, it had not been approved; it remained in Phase 3 for UC — but current status is **unknown**

If you need verified specifics (publication citations, exact dates, regulatory status), those should be checked against ClinicalTrials.gov results postings, PubMed, and Abivax's press releases, as my recollection on the fine details is not reliable enough to assert.

I'll list trials I believe are genuinely similar in design or concept to NCT02735863 (ABX464 added to ART, then analytic treatment interruption to measure time to viral rebound), while flagging my uncertainty honestly. My confidence in exact NCT IDs and outcome labels is limited, so I mark "unknown" where I cannot verify.

---

**1. The "kick and kill" / latency-reversing agent ATI trials (e.g., romidepsin, vorinostat, panobinostat)**
- **NCT ID:** The panobinostat trial is sometimes cited as NCT01680094 (Clevenbergh/Søgaard et al., Denmark). The romidepsin trial is associated with NCT01933594 (Lehrman et al., Australia). **Confidence in exact IDs: low — verify.**
- **Drug/indication:** HDAC inhibitors (panobinostat, romidepsin, vorinostat) in HIV-infected, ART-suppressed patients.
- **Phase:** Phase 1/2.
- **Outcome:** Generally considered **FAILURE** or at best inconclusive for clinically meaningful reservoir reduction / delayed rebound — most did not significantly delay viral rebound after ATI. (Some showed transient increases in HIV transcription but no reservoir reduction.)
- **Why similar:** Same core paradigm — add an investigational immunomodulatory/latency-modulating agent on top of suppressive ART, then interrupt ART and measure time to viral rebound.

---

**2. Vedolizumab or other immune-modulating agent + ATI in HIV (gut homing / reservoir)**
- **NCT ID:** **unknown**
- **Drug/indication:** Immune modulators (e.g., vedolizumab, or anti-PD-1 agents like pembrolizumab in HIV cure studies) in ART-suppressed HIV patients.
- **Phase:** Phase 1/2.
- **Outcome:** **unknown / mixed** — mostly early-phase with no clear efficacy.
- **Why similar:** Same "add-on to ART + measure reservoir/rebound" framing, and shares the immunomodulatory mechanistic rationale that overlapped with ABX464's anti-inflammatory miR-124 hypothesis.

---

**3. Therapeutic HIV vaccine + ATI trials (e.g., MVA-B, Ad26/MVA, Tat vaccine)**
- **NCT ID:** Ad26/MVA "APPROACH" is NCT02315703; MVA-B and Tat vaccine IDs **unknown**.
- **Drug/indication:** Therapeutic HIV vaccines in ART-suppressed patients, often with ATI.
- **Phase:** Phase 1/2 (some Phase 2b).
- **Outcome:** Largely **FAILURE / inconclusive** for durable viral control off ART; some showed modest delay in rebound.
- **Why similar:** Same endpoint philosophy — the trial's primary/secondary focus on time to viral rebound after stopping ART mirrors vaccine ATI trials.

---

**4. Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) + ATI (e.g., VRC01, 3BNC117, 10-1074)**
- **NCT ID:** VRC01 ATI trials include NCT02599896 (AMP-related); 3BNC117 trials **unknown**. **Confidence: low.**
- **Drug/indication:** bNAbs in HIV-infected, ART-suppressed individuals, often during ATI.
- **Phase:** Phase 1/2.
- **Outcome:** **Mixed/partial success** — some bNAbs significantly delayed viral rebound in ATI studies, which was a genuine positive signal (unlike most HDACi trials).
- **Why similar:** Same design — investigational agent added on suppressive ART, then analytic treatment interruption with time-to-rebound as the key readout.

---

**5. ABX464's own related HIV studies (same program)**
- **NCT ID:** **unknown** (the earlier extended-dosing cohort that produced the SJS signal is referenced but I cannot cite its NCT ID).
- **Drug/indication:** ABX464/obefazimod in HIV.
- **Phase:** Phase 1/2.
- **Outcome:** **unknown**, but the safety signal contributed to program deprioritization.
- **Why similar:** Same drug, same sponsor, same HIV + ART-interruption paradigm — the most directly comparable trial.

---

**Honest caveats:**
- Several NCT IDs above are from memory and should be **verified** before citation. Where I wrote "unknown," I genuinely cannot recall the ID reliably.
- My SUCCESS/FAILURE labels reflect general field consensus for the *class*, not necessarily a verified per-trial result — treat them as directional, not authoritative.
- If you need trial-level verified outcomes, ClinicalTrials.gov results sections and the primary publications are the reliable sources.

Based on your knowledge of clinical trials, what is the historical base rate of success for trials like this one?

Consider:
- Phase: PHASE2
- Indication: HIV Infection
- Drug class and mechanism (from what you recalled earlier)

Provide your answer EXACTLY as:
BASE_RATE: [a number between 0.0 and 1.0]
REASONING: [one paragraph explaining how you arrived at this estimate]

BASE_RATE: 0.05

REASONING: This trial sits at the intersection of several historically low-yield categories. First, Phase 2 overall has a low transition-to-approval rate (commonly cited around 10-15% across all indications), and infectious disease / HIV specifically has among the lower Phase 2 success rates (roughly 10-20% depending on the dataset). Second, and more importantly, this is not a standard antiviral efficacy trial but a "functional cure / reservoir-modulation + analytic treatment interruption" trial — a paradigm with a notably poor track record: HDAC inhibitors (vorinostat, panobinostat, romidepsin), therapeutic vaccines, and most immune-modulators have largely failed to produce durable viral control off ART or meaningfully delayed rebound, with only bNAbs showing partial signals. Third, the specific drug mechanism (miR-124 upregulation via ABX464) was hypothesis-generating with no established precedent for reservoir reduction or rebound delay in HIV, and the program carried a serious safety signal (suspected SJS) that later contributed to deprioritization of the HIV indication. Fourth, the trial's own primary endpoint was safety, not efficacy, and the design (small N=30, 28-day dosing, ATI) is exploratory — such studies rarely produce a "success" that advances the program. Weighting these factors together, I estimate the probability of this trial being judged a success on its own terms at roughly 5%, hence 0.05. This is a directional estimate from general base rates, not a verified program-specific outcome.

Based on the trial design of NCT02735863, describe what would constitute a successful outcome.

Include:
1. The likely primary endpoint(s) and how they would be measured
2. The statistical threshold that would need to be met (e.g., p<0.05, hazard ratio, non-inferiority margin)
3. Whether this is likely a superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence trial
4. Key design features (randomization, blinding, control arm)

If you are unsure about any detail, say 'unknown'. Do not fabricate.

Here is my description of what a "successful outcome" would look like for NCT02735863, based strictly on the registered design given and standard trial-design reasoning. Where the registry does not specify something, I mark it "unknown" rather than fabricate.

**1. Likely primary endpoint(s) and how measured**

- **Primary endpoint (as registered):** Number of Participants With Adverse Events, time frame up to 4 months.
  - This is a **safety/tolerability endpoint**, not an efficacy endpoint.
  - Measurement: incidence, type, severity (graded per the DAIDS Division of AIDS toxicity table), and relationship to study treatment of adverse events, including Dose-Limiting Toxicity (DLT) defined as grade 3 or higher events considered probably/definitely related to study treatment by the Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB).
- **Secondary endpoint (as registered):** Time to Viral Rebound (VR), up to 3 months after treatment interruption.
  - Measurement: viral load monitored twice weekly for the first 3 weeks after stopping ART, then weekly. VR is a protocol-defined virologic threshold (the exact copy/mL cutoff is **unknown** from the excerpt, but typically ≥50 or ≥200 copies/mL confirmed).
- So "success" on the registered endpoints is primarily a **safety** judgment, with **time to viral rebound** as an exploratory/secondary efficacy signal.

**2. Statistical threshold**

- The registry as provided does **not** state a formal hypothesis test, alpha level, power, hazard ratio, or non-inferiority margin. **Unknown** for any specific numeric threshold.
- The only explicit quantitative "stopping" rule given is a **safety trigger**, not an efficacy threshold:
  - If **more than 2 DLTs** occur during the treatment period of the **first four treated patients**, enrollment stops.
  - If a **grade 4 (life-threatening)** adverse reaction occurs, enrollment and treatment of ongoing patients are immediately discontinued, resumable only if the DSMB concludes causality was unrelated/unlikely.
- Because there is no stated efficacy alpha or margin, a formal p<0.05 efficacy claim is **not** part of the registered design. Any efficacy comparison (time to VR between ABX464 and placebo) appears descriptive/exploratory given N=30 and a 3:1 ratio.

**3. Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence**

- The trial is **not** framed as non-inferiority or equivalence. There is no active comparator against which to show non-inferiority (placebo is the control).
- It is best described as a **safety/exploratory superiority-style comparison** (ABX464 + ART vs placebo + ART) on safety and on time to viral rebound — but with no pre-specified statistical superiority threshold in the registered fields. So: exploratory superiority, **not** a confirmatory superiority trial, and **not** non-inferiority/equivalence.

**4. Key design features**

- **Allocation:** Randomized.
- **Intervention model:** Parallel assignment.
- **Masking:** Quadruple (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor all blinded).
- **Arms:**
  - Experimental: ABX464 (fixed 50 mg once daily for 28 days) + DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI. (A 150 mg dose is mentioned in the narrative but the listed arm specifies 50 mg — the exact arm structure for 150 mg is **unknown** from the excerpt.)
  - Placebo comparator: ABX464 matching placebo once daily + DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI.
- **Randomization ratio:** 3:1 (3 active : 1 placebo per block).
- **Enrollment:** 30 participants.
- **Background therapy:** DRV/RTV (800 mg DRV + 100 mg RTV) or DRV/COBI (800 mg DRV + 150 mg COBI) once daily, required as monotherapy for ≥8 weeks pre-baseline.
- **Treatment interruption:** At Day 29, all treatments (ART + ABX464/placebo) are stopped; viral load monitored for rebound; ART resumed if VR occurs.
- **Safety oversight:** DSMB with pre-specified DLT-based stopping rules.
- **PK:** Thorough pharmacokinetics to assess ABX464–DRV/RTV–COBI drug-drug interactions.

**What would constitute "success"**

- **Primary success (safety):** No more than 2 DLTs among the first four treated patients; no grade 4 treatment-related reactions; an AE profile not worse than placebo in a clinically meaningful way, permitting the program to continue.
- **Secondary/exploratory success (efficacy signal):** A signal that ABX464 (vs placebo) delays time to viral rebound after ART interruption — but the registry gives no formal statistical bar, so this would be hypothesis-generating, **unknown** as a defined success criterion.
- Because the registered primary endpoint is safety, a trial could be "successful" by completing without triggering stopping rules even if time-to-rebound showed no benefit.

**Explicit unknowns:** exact viral rebound copy/mL definition; any alpha, power, or hazard-ratio target; the precise statistical analysis plan; and how the 150 mg dose arm was structured in the final protocol.

What are the key risk factors that could cause this trial to fail?

List 3-5 specific risks, ordered from most to least concerning. For each risk, provide:
- RISK: [name of the risk]
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: [why this risk is relevant to THIS specific trial]
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW

Consider: safety signals from earlier phases, efficacy concerns, enrollment challenges, regulatory issues, competitive landscape, and trial design limitations.

RISK: Serious drug-induced safety signal (mucocutaneous reactions / suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
APPLIES_BECAUSE: This exact trial's own summary discloses that two cases of mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment (suspected SJS), both requiring hospitalization and drug withdrawal, occurred in a preceding extended-dosing cohort of ABX464. This is a direct, drug-specific, program-level red flag that triggered the intensive DSMB stopping rules built into this protocol (enrollment halt after >2 DLTs in the first four patients; immediate discontinuation on any grade 4 event). Any recurrence in this small N=30 trial — especially given the immune-modulating miR-124 mechanism and concomitant DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI — could force a halt, and the life-threatening nature of SJS makes this the single most trial-terminating risk.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Efficacy failure — no meaningful delay in time to viral rebound
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The trial's own biology is hypothesis-generating. ABX464's proposed mechanism (miR-124 upregulation / anti-inflammatory) has no established precedent for reducing the HIV reservoir or delaying rebound after analytic treatment interruption, and the broader field of "add-on immunomodulator + ATI" trials (HDAC inhibitors, therapeutic vaccines) has a long history of failing to delay rebound. With N=30 and a 3:1 randomization, the trial is almost certainly underpowered to detect anything but a large effect on the secondary time-to-rebound endpoint. A null or uninterpretable rebound result would undercut the program rationale even if safety is clean.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Enrollment challenges in a narrow, highly selected population
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Eligibility is unusually restrictive — patients must be on DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI **as monotherapy** (an uncommon ART regimen in practice, since most suppressed patients are on multi-drug regimens), fully suppressed <50 copies/mL for 6 months with ≤2 blips, CD4 ≥600 cells/mm³ at screening, no prior protease inhibitor resistance mutations, no history of AIDS-defining illness or opportunistic infection, and no prior confirmed VL ≥500 since ART initiation. Finding 30 such patients — who must also accept an ATI — within a reasonable timeframe is likely slow, and slow enrollment risks the trial being stopped for futility or running out of funding, especially given the program's later deprioritization.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Analytic treatment interruption (ATI) design limitations and ethical/regulatory friction
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The design deliberately stops all ART at Day 29, exposing patients to viral rebound, potential CD4 decline, and transmission risk. ATI trials increasingly face tighter ethical and regulatory scrutiny, and the risk of rapid rebound in some patients can itself be classified as a safety event, confounding the primary safety endpoint. Additionally, the short 28-day dosing window before ATI may be insufficient to produce any durable reservoir effect — a design limitation that could render the efficacy readout uninterpretable regardless of drug activity.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Drug–drug interaction or PK liability with the DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI backbone
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The protocol explicitly requires "thorough pharmacokinetics analysis" to characterize potential interactions between ABX464 and DRV/RTV or DRV/COBI — an acknowledgment that a PK interaction is plausible. DRV/RTV and DRV/COBI are strong CYP3A/P-gp modulators, and an interaction that lowers ABX464 exposure (or raises it into a toxicity range) could simultaneously explain safety signals and blunt efficacy, potentially invalidating the trial's conclusions for one or both dose arms. The presence of the PK substudy signals this was a recognized concern.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

(Note: I did not include "competitive landscape" as a standalone risk because, for a small early-phase mechanistic HIV trial, competitor products are a commercial rather than a trial-success concern; I also did not list "regulatory rejection" separately as it is largely downstream of the safety and design issues above. If you want those framed as separate risks, I can restructure.)

Based on the trial specification shown at the start, your own knowledge, and the similar trials you listed, make your final prediction:

Format your answer EXACTLY as:
PREDICTION: SUCCESS or FAILURE
CONFIDENCE: a number between 0.0 and 1.0
KEY_REASON: one sentence explaining the most important factor

PREDICTION: FAILURE
CONFIDENCE: 0.9
KEY_REASON: The trial's primary endpoint is safety in a drug that already caused suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome in an earlier cohort, combined with a hypothesis-generating mechanism (miR-124 upregulation) that has no precedent for delaying HIV rebound — a paradigm that has failed repeatedly across HDAC inhibitor, vaccine, and immunomodulator ATI trials.

Lead sponsor: Novo Nordisk A/S
Enrollment: 1201
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=not specified

Brief summary:
This trial is conducted in Asia, Europe and the United States of America (USA). The aim of the trial is to investigate efficacy and safety of semaglutide versus dulaglutide as add-on to metformin in subjects with type 2 diabetes. In the preceding extended-dosing cohort, two cases of mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment (suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome) were reported; both required hospitalization and drug withdrawal.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Semaglutide 0.5 mg/Week: 
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Semaglutide 1.0 mg/Week: 
  - [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Dulaglutide 0.75 mg/Week: 
  - [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Dulaglutide 1.5 mg/Week: 

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] semaglutide: Administered subcutaneously (s.c., under the skin) once-weekly.
  - [DRUG] Dulaglutide: Administered subcutaneously (s.c., under the skin) once-weekly.

Primary outcomes:
  - Change in HbA1c [time frame: Week 0, week 40]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Change in Body Weight (kg) [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Fasting Plasma Glucose [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Systolic and Diastolic Blood Pressure [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Overall Scores for Patient Reported Outcomes: Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire [time frame: Week 0, week 40]

  - Change From Baseline 7-point Self-measured Plasma Glucose Increment [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Fasting Blood Lipids (Total Cholesterol) [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Fasting Blood Lipids (Low Density Lipoprotein [LDL] Cholesterol) [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Fasting Blood Lipids (High Density Lipoprotein [HDL] Cholesterol) [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Fasting Blood Lipids (Triglycerides) [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Body Mass Index (BMI) [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Waist Circumference [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Short Form Health Survey (SF-36v2™) [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Subjects Who After 40 Weeks Treatment Achieve (Yes/no) HbA1c <7.0% (53 mmol/Mol) American Diabetes Association (ADA) Target [time frame: After 40 weeks of treatment]
  - Subjects Who After 40 Weeks Treatment Achieve (Yes/no) Weight Loss ≥5% [time frame: After 40 weeks treatment]

  - Subjects Who After 40 Weeks Treatment Achieve (Yes/no) HbA1c Reduction ≥1% [time frame: After 40 weeks of treatment]
  - Subjects Who After 40 Weeks Treatment Achieve (Yes/no) Weight Loss ≥3% [time frame: After 40 weeks treatment]
  - Subjects Who After 40 Weeks Treatment Achieve (Yes/no) HbA1c Reduction ≥1% and Weight Loss ≥3% [time frame: After 40 weeks treatment]
  - Number of Treatment Emergent Adverse Events (TEAEs) [time frame: 40 weeks + follow-up of 5 weeks]
  - Number of Treatment Emergent Severe or BG Confirmed Symptomatic Hypoglycaemia Episodes [time frame: 40 weeks + follow-up of 5 weeks]
  - Treatment Emergent Severe or BG Confirmed Symptomatic Hypoglycaemic Episodes [time frame: 40 weeks + follow-up of 5 weeks]
  - Change in Amylase [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Lipase [time frame: Week 0, week 40]
  - Change in Pulse Rate [time frame: Week 0, week 40]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria: - Male or female, age at least 18 years at the time of signing informed consent. - HbA1c (glycosylated haemoglobin) 7.0 - 10.5% (53 - 91 mmol/mol) (both inclusive) - Subjects on stable diabetes treatment with metformin (minimum of 1500 mg/day or maximal tolerated dose documented in the patient medical record) for 90 days prior to screening Exclusion Criteria: - Female who is pregnant, breast-feeding or intends to become pregnant or is of child-bearing potential and not using an adequate contraceptive method (adequate contraceptive measures as required by local regulation or practice) - Any condition, which in the investigator's opinion might jeopardise subject's safety or compliance with the protocol - Treatment with any medication for the indication of diabetes or obesity other than stated in the inclusion criteria in a period of 90 days before screening. An exception is short-term insulin treatment for acute illness for a total of equal to or below 14 days - History of pancreatitis (acute or chronic) - Screening calcitonin equal to or above 50 ng/L - Family or personal history of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 or Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma - Renal impairment defined as eGFR (electronic case report form) below 60 mL/min/1.73 m\^2 as per CKD-EPI (Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration) - Subjects presently classified as being in New York Heart Association Class IV - Planned coronary, carotid or peripheral artery revascularisation on the day of screening - Proliferative retinopathy or maculopathy requiring acute treatment - History or presence of malignant neoplasms within the last 5 years (except basal and squamous cell skin cancer and in-situ carcinomas) - Anticipated initiation or change in concomitant medications (for more than 14 consecutive days or on a frequent basis) known to affect weight or glucose metabolism (e.g. orlistat, thyroid hormones, corticosteroids)

## Semaglutide (the investigational drug)

**Mechanism of action:** Semaglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist. It works by binding to and activating the GLP-1 receptor, which stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon secretion, slows gastric emptying, and reduces appetite/food intake. It is a long-acting analog engineered with modifications (including a fatty acid side chain and amino acid substitutions) to resist DPP-4 degradation and bind albumin, enabling once-weekly dosing.

**Known approved indications and formulations:** Semaglutide is marketed by Novo Nordisk as Ozempic (subcutaneous, for type 2 diabetes), Rybelsus (oral, for type 2 diabetes), and Wegovy (subcutaneous, higher dose, for obesity). These are well-established.

**The mucocutaneous reaction note:** The brief summary mentions two cases of suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome in a preceding extended-dosing cohort. # What Constitutes a Successful Outcome for NCT02648204 (SUSTAIN 7)

## 1. Likely Primary Endpoint and How It Is Measured

The registered primary outcome is **change in HbA1c from baseline (Week 0) to Week 40**. This is measured as the absolute change in glycosylated hemoglobin (percentage points, or mmol/mol) from the baseline value to the value at Week 40 of treatment, analyzed on the full analysis set (typically with a mixed model for repeated measures or similar ANCOVA-type approach handling missing data). A "successful" result on this endpoint means semaglutide produced a statistically significantly greater reduction in HbA1c than dulaglutide — i.e., a larger negative change from baseline.

## 2. Statistical Threshold

This is where I must be careful, because the registered record does not state the statistical hypothesis or margin, and I should not fabricate specifics.

- **Overall:** The trial is described with two semaglutide doses (0.5 mg, 1.0 mg) and two dulaglutide doses (0.75 mg, 1.5 mg). The likely comparison structure is dose-matched or dose-to-highest-comparator (semaglutide 1.0 mg vs dulaglutide 1.5 mg being the key comparison).
- **Threshold:** For a superiority claim on the primary endpoint, the conventional threshold would be a two-sided **p < 0.05** (or a one-sided p < 0.025) for the difference in HbA1c change, with the confidence interval for the treatment difference excluding zero in the direction favoring semaglutide. Given multiple dose comparisons, there would likely be a hierarchical/gatekeeping testing procedure to control type I error, and the non-inferiority-then-superiority sequence is a common design.
- **Non-inferiority margin (if applicable):** I do **not** know the exact margin used. For HbA1c trials in T2D, a non-inferiority margin of **0.3% or 0.4%** (upper bound of the 95% CI for the difference) is conventional in this field, but I cannot confirm which was specified here. **Unknown** with certainty.

I will not assert a specific margin or alpha as fact.

## 3. Superiority, Non-Inferiority, or Equivalence

Based on the design (an active comparator, semaglutide vs dulaglutide, with the stated aim "to investigate efficacy and safety of semaglutide versus dulaglutide"), this is most likely a **superiority trial**, or a **non-inferiority trial with a pre-specified superiority test**. Because both drugs are in the same class and reliably lower HbA1c, the scientific question is whether semaglutide is *better* than dulaglutide, not merely equivalent. However, I cannot confirm the exact hypothesis (non-inferiority first vs. direct superiority) from the registry entry alone. Treat the precise framing as **unknown**; the directional intent (superiority) is well supported.

## 4. Key Design Features

- **Allocation:** Randomized (stated).
- **Intervention model:** Parallel assignment (stated) — four parallel arms.
- **Masking:** **None** (stated) — this is an **open-label** trial. This matters: no blinding of participants or investigators, which is consistent with the fact that both drugs differ in appearance/packaging and the endpoints are largely objective laboratory measures (HbA1c, weight, lipids), where open-label bias is less concerning than for subjective endpoints.
- **Arms:** Four — semaglutide 0.5 mg/week, semaglutide 1.0 mg/week, dulaglutide 0.75 mg/week, dulaglutide 1.5 mg/week.
- **Control arm:** Active comparator (dulaglutide), not placebo.
- **Route/dosing:** Both drugs administered subcutaneously once-weekly.
- **Treatment duration:** 40 weeks to primary endpoint, plus a 5-week follow-up for safety outcomes.
- **Population:** Adults ≥18 years with T2D, HbA1c 7.0–10.5%, on stable metformin (≥1500 mg/day or max tolerated) for ≥90 days.
- **Enrollment:** 1201 (stated).

## Summary of What "Success" Would Mean

A successful outcome would be: semaglutide (particularly 1.0 mg vs dulaglutide 1.5 mg, and 0.5 mg vs 0.75 mg) achieving a **statistically significantly greater reduction in HbA1c at Week 40** than the corresponding dulaglutide dose, meeting the pre-specified testing threshold (conventionally p<0.05 after multiplicity control), with acceptable safety/tolerability (no excess of treatment-emergent adverse events or hypoglycemia, and no recurrence of the mucocutaneous signal noted in the preceding cohort). Secondary successes would include greater weight loss, better fasting plasma glucose, and favorable patient-reported outcomes.

# Key Failure Risks for NCT02648204 (SUSTAIN 7)

Ordered from most to least concerning:

---

**RISK 1: Failure to demonstrate superiority over the active comparator (dulaglutide)**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** This trial is not a placebo-controlled efficacy study — it is a head-to-head comparison against dulaglutide, an already-approved, effective GLP-1 receptor agonist that reliably lowers HbA1c. The scientific and regulatory bar is therefore not "does semaglutide work?" (it almost certainly does) but "is semaglutide *better* than dulaglutide at matched doses?" A trial can be clinically positive but fail its primary superiority objective if the between-drug difference is small, especially at the lower dose comparison (0.5 mg vs 0.75 mg). This is the single most plausible route to a "failed" primary endpoint.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

**RISK 2: Safety signal — mucocutaneous reactions / suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The registry explicitly notes that in the preceding extended-dosing cohort, two cases of mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment (suspected SJS) occurred, both requiring hospitalization and drug withdrawal. Any recurrence, or a regulatory determination that this signal is causally linked to semaglutide, could halt the trial, trigger a clinical hold, or jeopardize the entire development program — regardless of glycemic efficacy. SJS is a severe, potentially fatal adverse event and draws intense regulatory scrutiny even at low incidence.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** LOW (the signal was in a small preceding cohort and has not, to my knowledge, been confirmed as a class effect; but the potential impact is severe, which is why it ranks this high despite low likelihood)

**RISK 3: Trial design limitation — open-label (unblinded) design**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Masking is explicitly NONE. Open-label trials are vulnerable to bias in subjective or behaviorally influenced endpoints: patient-reported outcomes (the Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire, SF-36v2), hypoglycemia reporting, and even weight (via behavioral effects). While the primary HbA1c endpoint is objective and relatively robust to open-label bias, the numerous secondary patient-reported and safety endpoints are not. This weakens the evidentiary strength of secondary claims and could undermine a broad label.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM (that it degrades secondary/patient-reported results; LOW that it overturns the primary HbA1c result)

**RISK 4: Glycemic efficacy ceiling / regression to the mean in a well-controlled population**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The population is metformin-treated with baseline HbA1c 7.0–10.5%. Both drugs lower HbA1c substantially, so the absolute room for a *differential* effect between two effective GLP-1 agonists may be limited, particularly in the lower-HbA1c portion of the enrolled population. If the baseline HbA1c distribution skews low, the achievable separation between arms narrows, making superiority harder to demonstrate. This compounds Risk 1.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

**RISK 5: Gastrointestinal tolerability and treatment discontinuation**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** GLP-1 receptor agonists, including semaglutide, are well known for gastrointestinal adverse events (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). In an open-label trial comparing two agents with potentially different GI tolerability profiles, differential discontinuation could reduce the effective sample size, dilute the intent-to-treat effect estimate, and bias results. If semaglutide is less well tolerated at the higher (1.0 mg) dose than dulaglutide, dropouts could erode the efficacy signal. The registry lists TEAEs as a key secondary outcome, indicating tolerability is a formal concern.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

**Notes on items considered but ranked lower or excluded:**
- **Enrollment challenges:** LOW concern — enrollment of 1201 was already achieved (stated), and T2D trials of this type generally recruit well, especially with an established sponsor like Novo Nordisk.
- **Regulatory issues:** I have no specific knowledge of a regulatory hold on this trial beyond the SJS note (captured in Risk 2); otherwise **unknown**.
- **Competitive landscape:** Not a trial-failure risk per se — the competitive position of semaglutide vs dulaglutide is an outcome of the trial, not a cause of its failure, so I have not listed it as a distinct risk.

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Participant has histological confirmation of a locally advanced or metastatic solid tumor of a type associated with Prolactin Receptor (PRLR) expression that has progressed on prior treatment, is not amenable to treatment with curative intent, and has no other therapy options known to provide clinical benefit or the subject is ineligible for such therapies.

* Expanded Cohort: must have breast cancer.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Participant received anticancer therapy including chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiotherapy, biologic, or any investigational therapy within 21 days before Study Day 1; participant received palliative radiotherapy or small molecule targeted anti-cancer agents within 14 days of Study Day 1.
* Participant has prior exposure to any pyrrolobenzodiazopine-containing agent
* Participant has unresolved, clinically significant toxicities from prior anticancer therapy, defined as greater than Grade 1 on Common Terminology for adverse events.

* Participant has a history of \>= grade 3 AST, ALT, or bilirubin increase or has extensive liver resection (i.e., left lobe resection).
* Participant has a history of cholecystitis (subject with history of cholecystectomy will not be excluded), or has active gallbladder disease.

ABBV-176 is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) developed by AbbVie. The cytotoxic payload is a pyrrolobenzodiazepine (PBD) dimer — this is consistent with the trial's exclusion criterion barring prior exposure to any "pyrrolobenzodiazopine-containing agent." Here are the key risk factors for NCT03145909, ordered from most to least concerning based on this specific trial's design, drug, and known signal.

**RISK 1: Severe on-target/off-tumor toxicity from the PBD-dimer payload (SJS-like skin reactions)**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The trial record itself states that in the preceding extended-dosing cohort, two cases of mucocutaneous reactions with skin detachment (suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome) occurred, both requiring hospitalization and drug withdrawal. This is not a hypothetical risk — it is an already-observed, potentially life-threatening or fatal adverse event directly attributable to ABBV-176. PBD-dimer ADCs as a class (e.g., Rova-T) have a well-documented history of severe toxicity that derailed development. This is the single most likely reason the program fails.
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

**RISK 2: Insufficient antitumor efficacy at a tolerable dose (narrow therapeutic window)**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: Because of Risk 1, any dose high enough to produce meaningful PRLR-targeted cytotoxicity may exceed the toxicity ceiling, forcing the MTD/RPTD below the efficacious range. This is a classic failure mode for PBD-dimer ADCs. The trial is designed to find an MTD, but a tolerable dose that produces negligible ORR in the breast cancer expansion cohort would still be a failure. Small enrollment (n=19) also means any efficacy signal will be weak and hard to interpret.
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

**RISK 3: Trial design limitations — single-arm, non-randomized, open-label, tiny sample size**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: With allocation=NON_RANDOMIZED, no control arm, no blinding, and only 19 participants, the trial cannot statistically distinguish drug effect from natural variation, cannot control for confounders or bias, and cannot establish superiority or non-inferiority. Even if the drug works, this design can only generate a hypothesis, not definitive evidence. Any positive ORR could be attributed to selection bias or prognostic imbalance rather than drug activity. This structurally caps the trial's ability to "succeed" in a regulatory or confirmatory sense.
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

**RISK 4: Enrollment and biomarker-selection challenges**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: Eligibility requires advanced/metastatic solid tumors "likely to express PRLR," with the escalation cohort limited to four tumor types (breast, colorectal, adrenocortical, chromophobe RCC) and expansion limited to breast cancer. PRLR expression testing and the requirement for archived plus fresh biopsies (in the expansion cohort) further narrow the pool. With only 19 participants targeted, even modest screening failure or slow accrual could halt the trial before meaningful data are generated — and the serious toxicity signal (Risk 1) would likely deter both patients and investigators from enrolling.
- LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

**RISK 5: Regulatory and competitive landscape risk**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The advanced/metastatic breast cancer space is highly competitive, with multiple approved ADCs (e.g., sacituzumab govitecan, trastuzumab deruxtecan) and other agents already established in later lines. Even a tolerable, modestly active ABBV-176 would face a high bar for differentiation, especially if a competitor ADC already occupies the niche. Regulators may also impose a clinical hold or require additional safety monitoring given the SJS signal, delaying or ending the program. Sponsors frequently deprioritize early-stage oncology assets in crowded, low-probability indications.
- LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

**Summary note on ordering**
Risks 1 and 2 are the dominant, program-defining concerns and are tightly linked (the therapeutic window problem). Risk 3 is inherent to the Phase 1 design and cannot be engineered away at this stage. Risks 4 and 5 are real but secondary — they could accelerate failure but are less likely than the safety/efficacy pair to be the primary cause. All likelihood assignments are my qualitative judgment, not derived from a formal quantitative model, and the actual disposition of the trial is unknown.

Here is what I independently know about this trial and the involved drug(s), based on my training data. Where I am not confident, I have written "unknown."

**Mechanism of Action (CMB305)**

- CMB305 is a combination immunotherapy consisting of two components:
  - **LV305**: A lentiviral vector-based vaccine that delivers the NY-ESO-1 gene to dendritic cells, aiming to prime a tumor-specific T-cell response against NY-ESO-1-expressing tumors.
  - **G305**: A recombinant protein vaccine consisting of NY-ESO-1 protein combined with Glucopyranosyl Lipid A (GLA), a TLR4 agonist, formulated in a stable emulsion (SE). G305 is designed to boost the immune response primed by LV305.
- The regimen is a "prime-boost" strategy: LV305 primes, G305 boosts.
- NY-ESO-1 is a cancer-testis antigen frequently expressed in synovial sarcoma (reportedly ~70–80% of cases), making it a rational target.

**Sponsor Track Record**

- Immune Design was a small immunotherapy company based in South San Francisco. Its lead programs included CMB305 (for sarcoma) and G100 (for lymphoma).
- Merck & Co. (Rahway, NJ) acquired Immune Design in 2019 for approximately $300 million, as stated in the trial record. The acquisition closed around April 2019.
- I am not aware of any approved products from Immune Design's pipeline. CMB305 did not reach approval to my knowledge.

**Results of Earlier Studies**

- **CMB305 in a Phase 1b/2 study (NCT02387125)** in NY-ESO-1+ synovial sarcoma: I recall this was a single-arm study in patients with locally advanced/metastatic disease. Reported results (presented at ASCO/CTOS around 2017–2018) suggested some patients had durable benefit, but the trial was not powered to demonstrate survival benefit. I do not recall exact effect sizes with confidence.
- **The "extended-dosing cohort"** referenced in the summary: Two cases of suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) were reported, requiring hospitalization and drug withdrawal. This was a significant safety signal.
- An earlier Phase 1 study of LV305 alone (in multiple tumor types) was also conducted.
- I do not recall specific efficacy results from the Phase 3 Synovate study being published, because I believe the trial was terminated early. I am not certain of the exact reason(s) but the SJS signal and/or enrollment difficulties (note the registered enrollment of 1, which is clearly a data entry error but may reflect early termination) are plausible.

**Key Dates**

- **NCT03520959 registered**: approximately 2018 (I believe May 2018).
- **Merck acquisition of Immune Design**: announced February 2019, closed April 2019.
- **Trial termination**: I believe the Synovate Phase 3 trial was discontinued/terminated around 2019, following the Merck acquisition and/or safety concerns. The exact date is **unknown** to me with confidence.
- **Primary completion**: unknown.
- **Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov**: unknown.

**Other Notes**

- The "registered enrollment: 1" is almost certainly a data-entry artifact (possibly reflecting early termination), not the intended enrollment. The intended enrollment for a Phase 3 sarcoma trial would typically be in the hundreds (I believe the target was around 250 patients).
- The detailed description contains an error: it refers to "New York esophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1 (NY-ESO-1) positive synovial sarcoma" — the phrase "New York esophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1" is the full name of the NY-ESO-1 antigen, but the cancer type here is synovial sarcoma, not esophageal carcinoma. This appears to be a template error in the registry entry.
- The mention of EQ-5D-Y (youth version) is consistent with the minimum age of 12 years.

- Whether any efficacy results from the Phase 3 were ever publicly reported.

The drug class — a therapeutic cancer vaccine (NY-ESO-1 prime-boost with LV305/G305) — has one of the worst historical track records in oncology; therapeutic vaccines have repeatedly failed in Phase 3 across indications (e.g., Provenge had only marginal success, and most others failed).
