data.trial_title: A Study to Evaluate SHR-1210 in Patients With Advanced or Metastatic NSCLC
data.primary_endpoint: Objective response rate
data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: Lung Neoplasms, Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung, Respiratory Tract Neoplasms Nec, Lung Disease, Respiratory Tract Disease, Neoplasm, Bronchial, Carcinoma, Bronchogenic
Lead sponsor: Jiangsu HengRui Medicine Co., Ltd.
Enrollment: 292
Design: allocation=NON_RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=80 Years

Brief summary:
This is an open-label, single-arm, multi-center, phase 2 Study to evaluate SHR-1210(anti-PD-1 antibody) in in adult Chinese patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer who failed or progressed to prior first-line systemic treatment.

Enrolled subjects will be assigned to 4 cohorts on the basis of PD-L1 expression in tumor cells(\<1%, ≥1%-25%, ≥25%-50%, ≥50%) all will be treated with the standard SHR-1210 dose (200mg) , Q2W, until documented progressive disease (PD) occurs. Subjects will return to the clinic once every two weeks. Radiographic disease assessments will be performed every 6 weeks.

The primary study hypothesis is that treatment with SHR-1210 improves Objective Response Rate when compare with standard second-line therapy, no matter how much PD-L1 expression in tumor. Based on interim power analysis, enrollment was expanded from 146 to 292 subjects to ensure adequate statistical power for the primary endpoint.

Detailed description:
In similar clinical trials, anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies produce durable responses in approximately 20% of unselected patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. Developing reliable, validated biomarkers that identify patients with an increased probability of response to these antibodies remains a challenge.

Because the PD-1 pathway may be a key mechanism of immune escape in a subgroup of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer, PD-L1 expression in tumor or inflammatory cells is a candidate biomarker. However, PD-L1 expression has not been formally validated as a biomarker in contemporaneously collected tumor tissue.

Additionally the purpose of the study is to assess the correlation between the expression of PD-L1 in the tumor and the response to treatment with SHR-1210 in non-small cell lung cancer.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥25-50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 1-25%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor < 1%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks

Interventions:
  - [BIOLOGICAL] SHR-1210: SHR-1210 is a humanized anti-PD1 IgG4 monoclonal antibody

Primary outcomes:
  - Objective response rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Duration of Response Rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Overall Survival Rate at 12-month [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]
  - Progression-Free Survival [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Number of participants with treatment-related adverse events (AEs) [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Subjects with histologically- or cytologically- documented NSCLC who present with Stage IIIB-IV disease (according to version 7 of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer Staging Manual in Thoracic Oncology), or disease recurrence or progression following multi-modal therapy (radiation therapy, surgical resection or radical chemo-radiotherapy in locally advanced disease).
2. Fresh cutting specimens or hollow needle aspiration specimens must be provided. A formalin fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue block or unstained slides of tumor sample (must be recent) must be available for biomarker evaluation. In the case of unstained slides, a minimum of 8 slides are necessary to conduct the planned biomarker analyses. Specimens must be received by the central lab prior to randomization. Biopsy should be excisional, incisional or core needle.
3. Subjects must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior platinum-containing doublet chemotherapy regimen for advanced or metastatic disease:

   1. Subjects who received maintenance therapy (non-progressors with platinum-based doublet chemotherapy) and progressed are eligible.
   2. Subjects who received adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum-doublet chemotherapy (after surgery and/or radiation therapy) and developed recurrent or metastatic disease within 6 months of completing therapy are eligible.
   3. Subjects with recurrent disease \> 6 months after adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum based chemotherapy, who also subsequently progressed during or after a platinum-doublet regimen given to treat the recurrence, are eligible.
4. Subjects with sensitizing EGFR mutation positive or ALK rearrangement positive, must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior tyrosine kinase inhibitor regimen, who also have PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%, are eligible.
5. Subjects must have measurable disease by CT or MRI per RECIST 1.1 criteria; Radiographic Tumor Assessment performed within 28 days of randomization.
6. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Arm (ECOG) performance status of ≤ 1.
7. All baseline laboratory requirements will be assessed and should be obtained within -14 days of randomization. Screening laboratory values must meet the following criteria.

   1. Absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1.5 × 109/L (1500/mm3)
   2. Platelets ≥ 80× 109/L (100,000/mm3)
   3. Hemoglobin ≥ 9.0 g/dL (90 g/L)
   4. Total bilirubin (TBIL) ≤ 1.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN)
   5. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) ≤ 2.5 × upper limit of normal(ULN); for subjects with liver metastases, ALT and AST ≤ 5 × ULN
   6. Serum creatinine ≤1.5 × ULN or creatinine clearance \> 45 mL/minute (using Cockcroft/Gault formula)
8. Female participants of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test within -7 days of randomization and must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception or a barrier method plus a hormonal method starting with the screening visit through 60 days (about 5 drug half-life + menstrual cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210. Male participants with a female partner(s) of child-bearing potential must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception from screening through 120 days (about 5 drug half-life + sperm depletion cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210.
9. Subjects must be willing and able to comply with scheduled visits, treatment schedule, laboratory tests including completion of patient reported outcomes questionnaires and other requirements of the study. Subjects must have signed and dated an IRB/IEC approved written informed consent form in accordance with regulatory and institutional guidelines. This must be obtained before the performance of any protocol related procedures that are not part of normal subject care.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Target Disease Exceptions

   1. Subjects with active CNS metastases are excluded. Subjects are eligible if CNS metastases are adequately treated and subjects are neurologically returned to baseline (except for residual signs or symptoms related to the CNS treatment) for at least 2 weeks prior to enrollment. In addition, subjects must be either off corticosteroids, or on a stable or decreasing dose of ≤ 10 mg daily prednisone (or equivalent).
   2. Subjects with carcinomatous meningitis.
2. Medical History and Concurrent Diseases

   1. Subjects with active, known or suspected autoimmune disease. Subjects in conditions not expected to recur in the absence of an external trigger are permitted to enroll.
   2. Subjects with a condition requiring systemic treatment with either corticosteroids (\>10 mg daily prednisone equivalent) or other immunosuppressive medications within 14 days of first administration of study treatment. Inhaled or topical steroids, and adrenal replacement steroid doses \> 10 mg daily prednisone equivalent, are permitted in the absence of active autoimmune disease.
   3. Prior therapy with immunostimulatory medications or tumor vaccines within 6 months.
   4. Prior therapy with anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-PD-L2, or anti-CTLA-4 antibody (including any other antibody or drug specifically targeting T-cell co-stimulation or checkpoint pathways).
   5. Treatment with any investigational agent within 5 half-life of the agent, before the first administration of study treatment.
   6. Subjects with a history of interstitial lung disease.
   7. Subjects received lung radiation therapy within 6 months.
   8. Other active malignancy requiring concurrent intervention.
   9. Subjects with previous malignancies (except non-melanoma skin cancers, and the following in situ cancers: bladder, endometrial, cervical/dysplasia) are excluded unless a complete remission was achieved at least 5 years prior to study entry.
   10. Subjects have had prior chemotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study, or have had prior targeted small molecule therapy within 1 weeks prior to study, or have had prior radiation therapy or surgical operation within 4 weeks prior to study, or have had prior anti-tumor biotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study. All toxicities attributed to prior anti-cancer therapy other than alopecia and fatigue must have resolved to grade 1 (NCI CTCAE version 4) or baseline before administration of study drug.
   11. Subjects must have recovered from the effects of major surgery or significant traumatic injury at least 14 days before the first dose of study treatment
   12. Subjects with active pulmonary tuberculosis.
   13. Subjects with hemoptysis or hemorrhagic quantity per day is 2.5 ml or above within 4 weeks prior to study.
3. Physical and Laboratory Test Findings

   1. Known history of testing positive for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or known acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
   2. Positive test for hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBV sAg) or hepatitis C virus ribonucleic acid (HCV RNA) indicating acute or chronic infection. (HBV: HBsAg positive and HBV DNA ≥ 500 IU/mL ; HVC: HCV RNA positive and abnormal liver function).
4. Allergies and Adverse Drug Reaction

   1. History of severe hypersensitivity reactions to other monoclonal antibodies.
   2. History of severe hypersensitivity reaction to intravenous infusion.
5. Other Exclusion Criteria Any other serious or uncontrolled medical disorder, active infection, physical exam finding, laboratory finding, altered mental status, or psychiatric condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, would limit a subject's ability to comply with the study requirements, substantially increase risk to the subject, or impact the interpretability of study results.

Phase: PHASE2

Brief summary:
This is an open-label, single-arm, multi-center, phase 2 Study to evaluate SHR-1210(anti-PD-1 antibody) in in adult Chinese patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer who failed or progressed to prior first-line systemic treatment.

Enrolled subjects will be assigned to 4 cohorts on the basis of PD-L1 expression in tumor cells(\<1%, ≥1%-25%, ≥25%-50%, ≥50%) all will be treated with the standard SHR-1210 dose (200mg) , Q2W, until documented progressive disease (PD) occurs. Subjects will return to the clinic once every two weeks. Radiographic disease assessments will be performed every 6 weeks.

The primary study hypothesis is that treatment with SHR-1210 improves Objective Response Rate when compare with standard second-line therapy, no matter how much PD-L1 expression in tumor. Based on interim power analysis, enrollment was expanded from 146 to 292 subjects to ensure adequate statistical power for the primary endpoint.

Detailed description:
In similar clinical trials, anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies produce durable responses in approximately 20% of unselected patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. Developing reliable, validated biomarkers that identify patients with an increased probability of response to these antibodies remains a challenge.

Because the PD-1 pathway may be a key mechanism of immune escape in a subgroup of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer, PD-L1 expression in tumor or inflammatory cells is a candidate biomarker. However, PD-L1 expression has not been formally validated as a biomarker in contemporaneously collected tumor tissue.

Additionally the purpose of the study is to assess the correlation between the expression of PD-L1 in the tumor and the response to treatment with SHR-1210 in non-small cell lung cancer.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥25-50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 1-25%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor < 1%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks

Interventions:
  - [BIOLOGICAL] SHR-1210: SHR-1210 is a humanized anti-PD1 IgG4 monoclonal antibody

Primary outcomes:
  - Objective response rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Duration of Response Rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Overall Survival Rate at 12-month [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]
  - Progression-Free Survival [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Number of participants with treatment-related adverse events (AEs) [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Subjects with histologically- or cytologically- documented NSCLC who present with Stage IIIB-IV disease (according to version 7 of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer Staging Manual in Thoracic Oncology), or disease recurrence or progression following multi-modal therapy (radiation therapy, surgical resection or radical chemo-radiotherapy in locally advanced disease).
2. Fresh cutting specimens or hollow needle aspiration specimens must be provided. A formalin fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue block or unstained slides of tumor sample (must be recent) must be available for biomarker evaluation. In the case of unstained slides, a minimum of 8 slides are necessary to conduct the planned biomarker analyses. Specimens must be received by the central lab prior to randomization. Biopsy should be excisional, incisional or core needle.
3. Subjects must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior platinum-containing doublet chemotherapy regimen for advanced or metastatic disease:

   1. Subjects who received maintenance therapy (non-progressors with platinum-based doublet chemotherapy) and progressed are eligible.
   2. Subjects who received adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum-doublet chemotherapy (after surgery and/or radiation therapy) and developed recurrent or metastatic disease within 6 months of completing therapy are eligible.
   3. Subjects with recurrent disease \> 6 months after adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum based chemotherapy, who also subsequently progressed during or after a platinum-doublet regimen given to treat the recurrence, are eligible.
4. Subjects with sensitizing EGFR mutation positive or ALK rearrangement positive, must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior tyrosine kinase inhibitor regimen, who also have PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%, are eligible.
5. Subjects must have measurable disease by CT or MRI per RECIST 1.1 criteria; Radiographic Tumor Assessment performed within 28 days of randomization.
6. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Arm (ECOG) performance status of ≤ 1.
7. All baseline laboratory requirements will be assessed and should be obtained within -14 days of randomization. Screening laboratory values must meet the following criteria.

   1. Absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1.5 × 109/L (1500/mm3)
   2. Platelets ≥ 80× 109/L (100,000/mm3)
   3. Hemoglobin ≥ 9.0 g/dL (90 g/L)
   4. Total bilirubin (TBIL) ≤ 1.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN)
   5. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) ≤ 2.5 × upper limit of normal(ULN); for subjects with liver metastases, ALT and AST ≤ 5 × ULN
   6. Serum creatinine ≤1.5 × ULN or creatinine clearance \> 45 mL/minute (using Cockcroft/Gault formula)
8. Female participants of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test within -7 days of randomization and must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception or a barrier method plus a hormonal method starting with the screening visit through 60 days (about 5 drug half-life + menstrual cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210. Male participants with a female partner(s) of child-bearing potential must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception from screening through 120 days (about 5 drug half-life + sperm depletion cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210.
9. Subjects must be willing and able to comply with scheduled visits, treatment schedule, laboratory tests including completion of patient reported outcomes questionnaires and other requirements of the study. Subjects must have signed and dated an IRB/IEC approved written informed consent form in accordance with regulatory and institutional guidelines. This must be obtained before the performance of any protocol related procedures that are not part of normal subject care.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Target Disease Exceptions

   1. Subjects with active CNS metastases are excluded. Subjects are eligible if CNS metastases are adequately treated and subjects are neurologically returned to baseline (except for residual signs or symptoms related to the CNS treatment) for at least 2 weeks prior to enrollment. In addition, subjects must be either off corticosteroids, or on a stable or decreasing dose of ≤ 10 mg daily prednisone (or equivalent).
   2. Subjects with carcinomatous meningitis.
2. Medical History and Concurrent Diseases

   1. Subjects with active, known or suspected autoimmune disease. Subjects in conditions not expected to recur in the absence of an external trigger are permitted to enroll.

Subjects with a condition requiring systemic treatment with either corticosteroids (\>10 mg daily prednisone equivalent) or other immunosuppressive medications within 14 days of first administration of study treatment. Inhaled or topical steroids, and adrenal replacement steroid doses \> 10 mg daily prednisone equivalent, are permitted in the absence of active autoimmune disease.
   3. Prior therapy with immunostimulatory medications or tumor vaccines within 6 months.
   4. Prior therapy with anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-PD-L2, or anti-CTLA-4 antibody (including any other antibody or drug specifically targeting T-cell co-stimulation or checkpoint pathways).
   5. Treatment with any investigational agent within 5 half-life of the agent, before the first administration of study treatment.
   6. Subjects with a history of interstitial lung disease.

   9. Subjects with previous malignancies (except non-melanoma skin cancers, and the following in situ cancers: bladder, endometrial, cervical/dysplasia) are excluded unless a complete remission was achieved at least 5 years prior to study entry.
   10. Subjects have had prior chemotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study, or have had prior targeted small molecule therapy within 1 weeks prior to study, or have had prior radiation therapy or surgical operation within 4 weeks prior to study, or have had prior anti-tumor biotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study. All toxicities attributed to prior anti-cancer therapy other than alopecia and fatigue must have resolved to grade 1 (NCI CTCAE version 4) or baseline before administration of study drug.
   11. Subjects must have recovered from the effects of major surgery or significant traumatic injury at least 14 days before the first dose of study treatment
   12. Subjects with active pulmonary tuberculosis.
   13. Subjects with hemoptysis or hemorrhagic quantity per day is 2.5 ml or above within 4 weeks prior to study.
3. Physical and Laboratory Test Findings

   1. Known history of testing positive for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or known acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
   2. Positive test for hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBV sAg) or hepatitis C virus ribonucleic acid (HCV RNA) indicating acute or chronic infection. (HBV: HBsAg positive and HBV DNA ≥ 500 IU/mL ; HVC: HCV RNA positive and abnormal liver function).
4. Allergies and Adverse Drug Reaction

   1. History of severe hypersensitivity reactions to other monoclonal antibodies.
   2. History of severe hypersensitivity reaction to intravenous infusion.
5. Other Exclusion Criteria Any other serious or uncontrolled medical disorder, active infection, physical exam finding, laboratory finding, altered mental status, or psychiatric condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, would limit a subject's ability to comply with the study requirements, substantially increase risk to the subject, or impact the interpretability of study results.

# Key Failure Risks for NCT03085069

**RISK 1: Single-arm design cannot support confirmatory claims / historical benchmark may not hold**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The trial is explicitly non-randomized and open-label with no concurrent control (allocation=NON_RANDOMIZED, masking=NONE). ORR is benchmarked against external "standard second-line therapy" data. If the historical benchmark used for the null hypothesis was derived from a population that differs from the enrolled population (e.g., different PD-L1 distribution, prior therapies, imaging cadence), the comparison is confounded. Single-arm ORR results are also vulnerable to investigator assessment bias given no blinding and no independent review stated. This is a design-level risk that can invalidate the trial regardless of whether the drug works.
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

**RISK 2: Efficacy shortfall — ORR falls below the pre-specified threshold**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The class-typical ORR for anti-PD-1 monotherapy in unselected pretreated NSCLC is roughly 20%, and the primary hypothesis claims benefit "no matter how much PD-L1 expression" — i.e., including the <1% PD-L1 cohort, where checkpoint monotherapy response rates are typically low (often <10%). If the drug's true effect in biomarker-negative patients is weak, the pooled or per-cohort ORR may miss the target. The protocol's decision to expand enrollment from 146 to 292 suggests the interim analysis may have shown borderline rather than clearly positive results — a signal worth noting.
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

**RISK 3: Safety signal — immune-related adverse events in a lung cancer population**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: Anti-PD-1 agents carry class risks of pneumonitis, hepatitis, colitis, thyroid dysfunction, and other immune-related AEs. NSCLC patients often have compromised pulmonary function and prior lung radiation is an exclusion (suggesting the sponsor was already worried about pneumonitis risk). The trial excludes patients with prior interstitial lung disease, active autoimmune disease, and hemoptysis ≥2.5 mL/day — exclusions that concentrate a sicker-than-ideal population in some respects while removing high-risk patients in others. If pneumonitis or other irAEs occur at rates exceeding class norms, the risk-benefit calculus weakens, and treatment-related AE counts are an explicit secondary endpoint. The sponsor's aggressive exclusions indicate safety was a recognized concern.
- LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

**RISK 4: Enrollment and biomarker-screening burden**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The trial requires fresh tumor tissue (or ≥8 unstained slides) received by a central lab prior to randomization, plus measurable disease per RECIST 1.1, plus prior platinum doublet failure, plus PD-L1 testing to assign cohorts. Requiring fresh biopsies in pretreated advanced NSCLC is a well-known bottleneck — many patients are unfit for re-biopsy, decline it, or have insufficient tissue. Stratifying into four PD-L1 cohorts further fragments enrollment. The sponsor already doubled enrollment (146→292), which increases the operational burden. Slow accrual can force protocol amendments, extend timelines, or produce underpowered cohorts.
- LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

**RISK 5: Competitive and regulatory landscape**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: By the time this trial was running, pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and atezolizumab were already approved or in late-stage development for pretreated NSCLC globally, and China had multiple domestic PD-1 programs (including Hengrui's own and competitors such as BeiGene's tislelizumab, Innovent's sintilimab). A Phase 2 single-arm study in this space faces a crowded field for both regulatory differentiation and clinical adoption. If the drug does not show a differentiated profile — in efficacy, safety, biomarker enrichment, or dosing convenience — it risks being a "me-too" result that does not support a competitive registration path, particularly for the biomarker-negative population where competitors have a stronger evidence base.
- LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: Rectal Cancer, Adenocarcinoma, Locally Advanced Malignant Neoplasm, Chemoradiation
Lead sponsor: Instituto Nacional de Cancer, Brazil
Enrollment: 50
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=75 Years

Brief summary:
The benefit of aspirin in cancer of the colon and rectum is already known. Recently, it was described its potential activity during chemoradiotherapy, with higher rate of tumor downstaging. Furthermore, induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation represents an attractive approach, with more favorable compliance and toxicity profiles. The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of total neoadjuvant treatment and assess the efficacy and feasibility of aspirin use during chemoradiotherapy for high-risk rectal cancer. Based on interim power analysis, enrollment was expanded from 25 to 50 subjects to ensure adequate statistical power for the primary endpoint.

Detailed description:
Methods: This is a randomized trial to evaluate induction treatment with XELOX and Capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy with or without aspirin in a high-risk population selected by MRI. High-risk will be defined by presence of at least one of the following criteria on high-resolution thin-slice MRI (3 mm): tumors extending to within 1 mm of, or beyond the mesorectal fascia; tumor extending 5 mm or more into perirectal fat; resectable cT4 tumors; lower third; nodal involvement; extramural vascular invasion. Random assignment of treatment will be stratified by MRI tumour regression grade. All the patients enrolled in the study will receive XELOX every 21 days for four cycles, unless unacceptable toxicity or progression is detected. After this treatment, patients will be randomized to receive Capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy with aspirin or placebo (Capecitabine 850 mg/m² 5 days per week combined with radiotherapy with total dose of 50.4 Gy in 28 days). After 8-10 weeks, they will be evaluate by MRI. Patients with incomplete clinical response will be referred to immediate surgery and patients with complete clinical response will be managed with "watch and wait" approach. Patients with progression disease during the treatment phase will be withdrawn from the study and will receive their treatment according to the investigator's judgment.

# Independent Knowledge About NCT03170115 and Aspirin in Rectal Cancer

## Trial Identification & Context

**What I can reasonably infer/recall:**

- **NCT03170115** is a Brazilian Phase 2 randomized trial conducted by the Instituto Nacional de Câncer (INCA) in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. INCA is Brazil's national cancer institute and has a track record of conducting investigator-initiated trials in gastrointestinal malignancies, though it is not a major multinational sponsor like NRG Oncology or EORTC. Its publication record is respectable within Latin America but limited in global phase 3 trials.

- The concept of **total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT)** — induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation — was an active area of investigation around 2017–2020, with trials like RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23 reporting results. This trial appears to follow that paradigm using XELOX (capecitabine + oxaliplatin) as induction.

## Aspirin: Mechanism of Action Relevant to Rectal Cancer

- **COX-1/COX-2 inhibition:** Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase enzymes, reducing prostaglandin synthesis. In colorectal cancer, COX-2 overexpression is common and associated with worse prognosis.
- **Proposed anti-tumor mechanisms:** Reduction of PGE2-mediated proliferation, angiogenesis (VEGF), and immunosuppression; possible enhancement of radiation sensitivity via inhibition of prosurvival signaling (NF-κB, Akt); antiplatelet effects may reduce tumor cell shielding by platelets.
- **Evidence in colorectal cancer:** The ASPREE and other observational/meta-analytic data suggest aspirin may reduce colorectal cancer incidence and mortality, particularly in COX-2-positive or PIK3CA-mutant tumors. However, **randomized evidence for aspirin as an adjunct to chemoradiation in rectal cancer is very limited.**

## Earlier Studies of Aspirin + Chemoradiation in Rectal Cancer

- **Preclinical data:** Several mouse xenograft studies (circa 2010–2016) suggested aspirin enhances radiosensitivity in colorectal cancer cell lines, often COX-2-dependent.
- **Clinical data before this trial:** I am aware of a small Phase 2 trial from Brazil (same group, possibly related) that tested aspirin with capecitabine-based chemoradiation in rectal cancer and reported higher downstaging rates. This likely formed the rationale for NCT03170115. **I cannot confirm the exact publication details or sample size — unknown.**
- **Larger trials:** No large randomized phase 3 trial of aspirin with chemoradiation in rectal cancer has been reported to my knowledge as of my last update.

# What Would Constitute a Successful Outcome for NCT03170115

## 1. Primary Endpoint and Measurement

**Primary endpoint (as stated):**
- **Tumor downstaging** after induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy with or without aspirin
- **Time frame:** 8–10 weeks after chemoradiotherapy

**How it would be measured:**
- Downstaging is typically assessed by comparing pre-treatment clinical stage (via MRI, sometimes supplemented by endoscopy/clinical exam) to post-treatment pathological stage (ypT/ypN) in patients who undergo surgery, and/or clinical downstaging in patients managed by "watch and wait."
- The trial's eligibility uses high-resolution thin-slice MRI (3 mm) with specific high-risk features, so MRI-based restaging (mrT/mrN, and possibly MRI tumor regression grade — mrTRG) is likely central to the response assessment.
- Given the "watch and wait" arm for complete clinical responders, the endpoint may combine pathological downstaging (for surgical patients) and clinical complete response (for non-surgical patients). **The exact operational definition of "downstaging" is unknown** — whether it means any T/N downstaging, downstaging to ypT0-2, or a specific TRG threshold.

## 2. Statistical Threshold

**From the registered design (Simon's optimal two-stage design):**
- **Stage 1:** 11 patients per group
- **Stage 2:** 20 additional patients per group
- **Total:** 31 evaluable patients per group (note: the enrollment total of 50 is less than 2 × 31 = 62, which suggests either the 31 refers to a pooled/combined analysis, or there is a discrepancy in the registration — **unknown**)
- **Success threshold:** "A treatment regimen will be considered effective if more than 18 patients of the total 31 show downstaging"
  - This translates to **≥19 of 31 patients (≈61%)** showing downstaging in the relevant arm
- **Power:** 80%
- **Alpha:** 0.05 (one-sided, as is standard for Simon's design)

**Important caveat:** The registration describes this as a Simon's two-stage design, which is classically a **single-arm** phase 2 design. However, the trial is also described as **randomized with a placebo comparator**. This is unusual — it suggests either:
- The Simon's design applies to one arm (likely the aspirin arm) against a historical benchmark, with the placebo arm providing contemporaneous control, **or**
- The statistical framework is a hybrid not fully captured in the registration text. **Unknown which interpretation is correct.**

If a formal between-arm comparison is intended, a p-value threshold (likely p<0.05) or a difference in downstaging proportions would be used, but the registration does not specify this explicitly.

## 3. Superiority, Non-Inferiority, or Equivalence

- **Likely superiority trial.** The phrasing ("considered effective if more than 18 patients show downstaging") and the use of a Simon's optimal design are consistent with testing whether the aspirin arm exceeds a predefined activity threshold.
- **Non-inferiority is unlikely** — the trial is testing whether adding aspirin *improves* downstaging, not whether it is *no worse* than placebo.
- **Equivalence is very unlikely** — no equivalence margin is mentioned.

| **Allocation** | Randomized |
| **Intervention model** | Parallel assignment |
| **Masking** | Quadruple (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor) |
| **Control arm** | Placebo oral tablet, daily during chemoradiotherapy |
| **Experimental arm** | Aspirin 100 mg daily during chemoradiotherapy |
| **Backbone treatment (both arms)** | XELOX every 21 days × 4 cycles (induction) → capecitabine 850 mg/m² 5 days/week + radiotherapy 50.4 Gy/28 fractions (chemoradiation) |
| **Stratification** | By MRI tumor regression grade |
| **Post-treatment management** | Incomplete clinical response → immediate surgery; complete clinical response → "watch and wait" |
| **Progression during treatment** | Withdrawn; treated at investigator's discretion |

A successful outcome for NCT03170115 would require **at least 19 of 31 evaluable patients in the aspirin arm (or in the relevant analysis population) to show tumor downstaging**, meeting the Simon's optimal two-stage threshold with 80% power at a one-sided alpha of 0.05, and ideally demonstrating a clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement over the placebo arm in the randomized comparison.

- Whether "31" refers to one arm or the total across both arms — **unknown**
- The exact definition of "downstaging" (pathological vs. clinical vs. combined) — **unknown**
- Whether a formal between-arm statistical test is prespecified — **unknown**
- Handling of the "watch and wait" patients in the primary analysis — **unknown**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The central hypothesis — that low-dose aspirin (100 mg) enhances downstaging when added to capecitabine-based chemoradiation — rests on limited clinical evidence. The largest randomized tests of aspirin in colorectal cancer (ASPREE, Add-Aspirin) have been largely null or equivocal for anti-tumor benefit. The 100 mg dose is a cardioprotective dose, lower than some oncology trials, and may be insufficient for a meaningful radiosensitizing effect. If the true effect size is small, the trial will likely fail its ≥19/31 threshold.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

## RISK 3: Confounded or Diluted Primary Endpoint Due to "Watch and Wait" Strategy

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Patients achieving a complete clinical response are managed with a "watch and wait" approach rather than surgery, meaning they may never contribute pathological downstaging data. Since the primary endpoint is tumor downstaging measured 8–10 weeks after chemoradiotherapy, the analysis must either rely on clinical/MRI assessment for these patients or exclude them — both of which introduce heterogeneity. If the aspirin arm produces more complete clinical responders (the desired effect), those patients may paradoxically be the hardest to classify for "downstaging," potentially biasing the endpoint against showing benefit or making the endpoint non-comparable between arms.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM-HIGH

---

## RISK 4: Enrollment Challenges in a Narrow High-Risk Population

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The trial requires a highly specific population: histologically confirmed mid/low rectal adenocarcinoma, locally advanced, with at least one of six MRI-defined high-risk features (mesorectal fascia involvement, ≥5 mm perirectal fat invasion, resectable cT4, lower third, nodal involvement, or extramural vascular invasion), ECOG 0–2, age 18–75, and no prior malignancy or recent thromboembolic/haemorrhagic events. This is a narrow window. The enrollment target was already expanded from 25 to 50, suggesting slower-than-expected accrual. Single-institution trials (INCA, Brazil) in a narrow population frequently fail to reach target enrollment within the planned timeframe, leading to underpowering or premature termination.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

## RISK 5: Safety Signal — Bleeding Risk from Aspirin During Chemoradiation

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Aspirin 100 mg daily is generally safe, but the trial population has specific vulnerabilities: patients with locally advanced rectal cancer receiving capecitabine-based chemoradiation may develop mucositis, thrombocytopenia, or GI mucosal injury, all of which could be exacerbated by aspirin's antiplatelet and GI-irritant effects. The exclusion criteria already screen out patients with recent thromboembolic/haemorrhagic events (within 6 months) or active GI bleeding, but de novo bleeding during treatment could still occur and lead to dose reductions, treatment interruptions, or early discontinuation — potentially compromising both safety and efficacy assessments. If bleeding events are imbalanced between arms, the trial could be halted or the aspirin arm could be compromised.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

| 2 | Weak/null efficacy signal for aspirin | HIGH |

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
Lead sponsor: Institut de Recherches Internationales Servier
Enrollment: 422
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=7 Years; maximum age=17 Years

Brief summary:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and the safety of bumetanide/S95008 in the improvement of Autism Spectrum Disorder core symptoms. Based on interim power analysis, enrollment was expanded from 211 to 422 subjects to ensure adequate statistical power for the primary endpoint.

Detailed description:
The present study (CL3-95008-001) was performed in children and adolescents from 7 to less than 18 years old presenting with ASD. A 6-month double-blind treatment period was performed in which efficacy and safety of bumetanide 0.5mg BID were assessed versus placebo. This double-blind period was followed by a 6-month open label treatment period of bumetanide 0.5mg BID in which long term safety was evaluated.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Bumetanide/S95008: 
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: 

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Bumetanide Oral Solution: Oral Solution dosed at 0.5mg/mL Taken twice daily
  - [DRUG] Placebo: Oral Solution Taken twice daily

Primary outcomes:
  - Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2) total raw score [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition (SRS-2) total raw score [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]
  - Clinical Global Impression - Global Improvement (CGI-I) score [time frame: At 6 months]
  - Vineland Adaptative Behaviour Sales, Second Edition (VABS II) subscores [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]
  - Adverse events and Paediatric Adverse Event Rating Scale (PAERS) [time frame: On average of 52 weeks]
  - Abnormalities in 12-leads electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters [time frame: selection visit/Week004/Week008/Week012/Week 026/Week030/Week034/Week038/Week052]
  - Renal ultrasound [time frame: selection visit/Week026/Week052]
  - the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale Children's version (C-SSRS-C) [time frame: Week000/Week012/Week026/Week038/Week052]
  - Tanner stage [time frame: Week000/Week026/Week052]
  - Acceptability and palatability questionnaire [time frame: Week026]
  - Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) questionnaire [time frame: Week000/Week004/Week012/Week026/Week030/Week038/Week052]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Male and female patients from 7 to less than 18 years
* Out patients
* Primary diagnosis of ASD as per Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders - Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria
* Criteria met for ASD on Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2) and Autism Diagnosis Interview Revised (ADI-R)
* CGI (Clinical Global Impression) - Severity rating Score ≥ 4
* Childhood Autism Rating Scale second edition (CARS2-ST or HF) total raw score ≥ 34
* Social responsiveness Scale second edition total score (SRS-2 T-Score) ≥ 66
* Absence of known monogenic syndrome (Fragile X, Rett syndrome ...)
* Absence of any clinically significant abnormality likely to interfere with the conduct of the study according to the judgment of the investigator

Exclusion Criteria:

* Patients not able to follow the study assessments defined by the protocol, with the exception of self-rating questionnaires which will be assessed by parent/legal representative/caregiver for those patients unable to complete them
* Patients having a high suicidal risk according to the investigator judgement
* Chronic renal dysfunction
* Chronic cardiac dysfunction
* Patient with unstable psychotherapy, behavioural, cognitive or cognitive-behavioural therapy
* Severe electrolyte imbalance that is likely to interfere with the study conduct or evaluation

# Independent Knowledge: Bumetanide for Autism Spectrum Disorder (NCT03715166)

## Drug Mechanism of Action

Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC1). In the context of autism, the proposed mechanism relates to the GABAergic excitation/inhibition imbalance hypothesis: NKCC1 is upregulated in some ASD models, leading to elevated intracellular chloride and paradoxical excitatory effects of GABA. Bumetanide, by blocking NKCC1, is hypothesized to shift GABA toward its inhibitory function. This mechanism remains investigational and is not an approved indication for bumetanide.

## Sponsor Track Record

- **Institut de Recherches Internationales Servier (Servier)** is a French pharmaceutical company. It is not a traditional CNS/psychiatry-focused sponsor relative to companies like Roche or Janssen, though it has a broad portfolio.
- Servier has conducted multiple trials in the ASD/bumetanide program (including earlier-phase studies).
- **Unknown:** Specific prior regulatory approvals for neurodevelopmental indications by Servier.

## Results of Earlier Studies

- **Lemonnier et al. (2012, Translational Psychiatry):** Small open-label/randomized pilot study (n≈60) suggesting improvement in CARS scores with bumetanide in children with ASD. This generated significant interest.
- **Lemonnier et al. (2017, Molecular Psychiatry):** A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n≈88) reported positive effects on CARS and SRS. However, the study had methodological criticisms (e.g., small size, potential unblinding due to diuretic effects).
- Larger, more rigorous trials have been mixed. A **pre-registered, well-powered European trial** (sometimes referred to as the "Bumetanide in Autism Medication and Biomarker" study or similar) did not clearly replicate the large effect sizes seen in earlier single-center studies.
- **Unknown:** Exact published results of NCT03715166 itself in peer-reviewed literature (I cannot confirm whether final results were published as of my knowledge cutoff).

## Key Dates

- **Unknown:** Exact study start date, primary completion date, and final completion date. The registration lists a 6-month double-blind phase followed by a 6-month open-label extension (52 weeks total per-patient participation), but I cannot state confirmed calendar dates.
- **Unknown:** Whether the trial has been completed, terminated, or results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov.

## Other Notes

- The expansion from 211 to 422 subjects based on interim power analysis suggests the initial effect size assumption was optimistic—this is a notable signal that the primary endpoint may have been underpowered at the original enrollment.
- Bumetanide is a generic, inexpensive diuretic; the commercial rationale for Servier would depend on a proprietary formulation (oral solution) and/or a new indication with market exclusivity.
- **Unknown:** Regulatory submission status or any approval decisions stemming from this program.
- The trial's use of QUADRUPLE masking is notable and attempts to address the unblinding concern (diuresis/urination changes could reveal active drug), though whether this was fully successful is **unknown** to me.

# What Would Constitute a Successful Outcome for NCT03715166

## 1. Likely Primary Endpoint and Measurement

- **Primary endpoint:** Change from baseline to Month 6 in the **Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2) total raw score** (explicitly listed in the registration).
- **Measurement:** CARS2 is a clinician-rated instrument (typically 15 items scored 1–4, with total raw scores ranging from 15 to 60). Higher scores indicate more severe autistic symptomatology. The endpoint is the **change score** (baseline minus Month 6, or Month 6 minus baseline depending on direction convention), compared between bumetanide and placebo arms.
- The registration lists both CARS2-ST (Standard) and CARS2-HF (High Functioning) forms as eligibility instruments; whether the primary analysis pooled or stratified by form is **unknown** from the information given.

## 2. Statistical Threshold

- **Unknown** exactly, but the standard convention for a superiority Phase 3 trial of this type would be a **two-sided p < 0.05** on the primary comparison (bumetanide vs. placebo) in the primary analysis population (likely ITT or mITT).
- Given the enrollment expansion from 211 to 422 based on interim power analysis, the trial was presumably powered for a **smaller effect size** than originally assumed. The exact assumed effect size (e.g., a specific point difference on CARS2) is **unknown**.
- Secondary endpoints (SRS-2, CGI-I, VABS-II) would typically be tested hierarchically or with multiplicity control; failure to control type I error across secondaries is a common criticism, but the specific strategy here is **unknown**.
- Whether a **minimal clinically important difference (MCID)** on CARS2 was pre-specified is **unknown**.

## 3. Trial Type

- This is clearly a **superiority trial**, not non-inferiority or equivalence. The stated purpose is to "evaluate the efficacy and safety of bumetanide/S95008 in the improvement of ASD core symptoms" vs. placebo—i.e., to demonstrate that bumetanide is **better than** placebo on CARS2.
- Non-inferiority would make no sense here because there is no active comparator; the control is placebo.

## 4. Key Design Features

- **Allocation:** Randomized ✔
- **Intervention model:** Parallel-group ✔
- **Masking:** Quadruple (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor) ✔ — notable because bumetanide's diuretic effect could otherwise unblind participants; quadruple masking attempts to mitigate this, though whether it fully succeeded is **unknown**.
- **Control arm:** Placebo comparator (oral solution, twice daily) ✔
- **Experimental arm:** Bumetanide oral solution 0.5 mg/mL, 0.5 mg BID ✔
- **Duration:** 6-month double-blind period, followed by 6-month open-label extension (total 52 weeks) ✔
- **Enrollment:** 422 (expanded from 211) ✔
- **Population:** Children/adolescents 7 to <18 years, outpatient, DSM-5 ASD diagnosis confirmed by ADOS-2 and ADI-R, CGI-S ≥ 4, CARS2 ≥ 34, SRS-2 T-score ≥ 66 ✔

## Summary: What Success Would Look Like

A successful trial would show a **statistically significant (p < 0.05, two-sided) greater improvement from baseline to Month 6 in CARS2 total raw score** in the bumetanide arm compared to placebo, in the primary analysis population, with acceptable safety/tolerability (no clinically meaningful excess in AEs, ECG abnormalities, renal findings, or suicidal ideation). Supportive secondary endpoints (SRS-2, CGI-I, VABS-II) trending in the same direction would strengthen the claim.

**Unspecified/unclear:** exact effect size assumed for powering, multiplicity strategy, handling of CARS2-ST vs. HF forms, and whether a responder analysis or MCID threshold was pre-specified.

## RISK 2: Unblinding Due to Bumetanide's Diuretic Effect (Design/Measurement Validity)

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Bumetanide is a potent loop diuretic causing increased urination, electrolyte changes, and possible dehydration symptoms. Even with QUADRUPLE masking, participants, caregivers, and raters may infer treatment assignment. Because the primary endpoint (CARS2) is a clinician-rated instrument that can be influenced by expectancy effects, unblinding could inflate or distort the treatment signal in either direction—typically biasing toward false positive in open-label-prone designs, but also potentially undermining the trial's credibility regardless of outcome.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

## RISK 3: High Placebo Response in Pediatric ASD Trials (Endpoint Sensitivity)

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** ASD behavioral trials are notorious for large placebo responses due to regression to the mean, caregiver expectation, increased clinical attention, and the fluctuating nature of core symptoms. With a 6-month endpoint and a clinician-rated primary measure (CARS2), a substantial placebo response could shrink the between-group difference below detectability, even if bumetanide has a real but modest effect.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

## RISK 4: Safety/Tolerability Signals (Renal, Electrolyte, Cardiac)

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The protocol specifically monitors renal ultrasound, 12-lead ECG, electrolyte imbalance, and Tanner stage—suggesting pre-specified concerns about bumetanide's known class effects (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, renal function changes, possible cardiac conduction effects). In a pediatric population treated for 6–12 months, even modest rates of these AEs could lead to dropouts, dose reductions, and a null or uninterpretable ITT result.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

## RISK 5: Enrollment/Retention Challenges and Generalizability

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The trial requires a narrowly defined population (age 7–<18, ADOS-2 + ADI-R confirmation, CGI-S ≥ 4, CARS2 ≥ 34, SRS-2 T ≥ 66, exclusion of monogenic syndromes and unstable psychotherapy). This restricts recruitment and may enrich for a more severely affected, treatment-resistant sample—reducing the likelihood of detecting a modest effect. The 12-month total participation (6-month double-blind + 6-month open-label) also risks attrition, especially in the placebo arm during the open-label phase.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

## Notes

- Regulatory risk is **unknown** to me in terms of specific FDA/EMA feedback on this program.
- Competitive landscape risk (e.g., other ASD programs) is **unknown** but likely low-impact on the trial's own success definition.
- The most concerning combination is **Risk 1 + Risk 2 + Risk 3**: a modest true effect, a design vulnerable to unblinding, and a high placebo response—any two of which could produce a null result even if bumetanide is genuinely effective.

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Constipation Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Lead sponsor: Ardelyx
Enrollment: 1212
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=75 Years

Brief summary:
This phase 3, 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center study will evaluate the safety and efficacy of tenapanor in subjects with constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-C) as defined by the ROME III criteria and who have active disease as determined after a two-week screening period. Subjects who qualify and are randomized into the study will either receive 50mg BID of tenapanor or placebo BID for 12 week treatment period and then undergo a 4 week placebo controlled randomized withdrawal. Based on interim power analysis, enrollment was expanded from 606 to 1212 subjects to ensure adequate statistical power for the primary endpoint.

Detailed description:
During the 12-week treatment period, subjects will record daily assessments including: frequency and timing of bowel movements; sensation and complete bowel emptying; consistency of bowel movements; degree of straining, worst abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, abdominal bloating, abdominal fullness and abdominal cramping. Subjects will also record weekly assessments including: adequate relief of IBS severity, and constipation severity.

At the end of the 12-week treatment period, there will be a 4-week randomized withdrawal period in which subjects who complete the study in Tenapanor group will be randomized to either Tenapanor 50mg BID or placebo BID (1:1) and subjects who complete the study in the placebo group will be assigned to receive Tenapanor 50mg BID.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] 50mg BID: Tenapanor
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Placebo

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Tenapanor: 
  - [DRUG] Placebo: 

Primary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Secondary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Complete Spontaneous Bowel Movement (CSBM)Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall CSBM Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* 18 to 75 years old
* Females must be of non-childbearing potential; If of child-bearing potential, must have negative pregnancy test and confirm the use of one of the appropriate means of contraception.
* Males must agree to use an appropriate method of barrier contraception or have documented surgical sterilization
* Subject meets definition of IBS-C using Rome III Criteria for the Diagnosis of IBS
* A colonoscopy based on AGA guidelines; every 10 years at ≥ 50 years old, or the occurrence of any warning signs

Exclusion Criteria:

* Functional diarrhea as defined by Rome III criteria
* IBS with diarrhea (IBS-D), mixed IBS (IBS-M), or unsubtyped IBS as defined by Rome III criteria
* Diagnosis or treatment of any clinically symptomatic biochemical or structural abnormality of the GI tract within 6 months prior to screening, or active disease within 6 months prior to screening; including but not limited to cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis, duodenal ulcer, erosive esophagitis, gastric ulcer, pancreatitis (within 12 months of screening), cholelithiasis, amyloidosis, ileus, non-controlled GERD, gastrointestinal obstruction, ischemic colitis or carcinoid syndrome.
* Subject has a history or current evidence of laxative abuse (in the clinical judgment of the physician)
* Hepatic dysfunction (ALT \[SGPT\] or AST \[SGOT\] \>2.5 times the upper limit of normal) or renal impairment (serum creatinine \> 2mg/dL)
* Any evidence of or treatment of malignancy (other than localized basal cell, squamous cell skin cancer or cancer in situ that has been resected) within the previous year
* Any surgery on the stomach, small intestine or colon, excluding appendectomy or cholecystectomy (unless within 60 days of screening visit)

Here is what I independently know about tenapanor and this trial, based on my training data. I've marked uncertain items as "unknown."

**Drug: Tenapanor (AZD1722 / RDX5791)**

- **Mechanism of action:** Tenapanor is an orally administered, minimally absorbed small-molecule inhibitor of the sodium–hydrogen exchanger NHE3 (SLC9A3), which is expressed on the apical surface of enterocytes in the small intestine and colon. By inhibiting NHE3, it reduces sodium absorption and, indirectly, phosphate absorption; it also increases intracellular proton retention and tight-junction permeability. The net effect in the gut is increased water and sodium secretion into the lumen, which accelerates transit and softens stool — the basis for its use in IBS-C and constipation. Separately, NHE3 inhibition in the gut reduces paracellular phosphate absorption, which is the basis for its approved use in hyperphosphatemia in chronic kidney disease (marketed as Xphozah/Ibsrela).
- **Formulation/administration:** Oral tablet; in this trial dosed 50 mg twice daily. For IBS-C the approved dose (Ibsrela, FDA-approved September 2019) is 50 mg BID. For hyperphosphatemia (Xphozah, FDA-approved October 2023) the dose is titrated, typically 30 mg BID with food.
- **Common adverse effects:** Diarrhea is the most frequent adverse event (reflecting the mechanism), along with abdominal distension, flatulence, and nausea. Diarrhea-related discontinuation was a notable issue in the IBS-C program. Because it is minimally absorbed, systemic exposure and systemic adverse effects are limited. A boxed warning for serious dehydration risk in pediatric patients (under 12 years) was added later, based on reports in the hyperphosphatemia/pediatric context — I believe this was added around 2022–2023; exact timing is **unknown** to me with certainty.

**Sponsor: Ardelyx**

- Ardelyx is a biopharmaceutical company (Fremont, California) focused on GI and cardiorenal therapies. Its lead assets are tenapanor (Ibsrela/Xphozah) and tenapanor-related programs. The company had a notable regulatory setback when the FDA initially declined to approve tenapanor for hyperphosphatemia (2021), before later approving it. Ardelyx also markets Ibsrela for IBS-C. I do not have reliable independent information on Ardelyx's full pipeline history beyond these; specifics of earlier-phase tenapanor trials (e.g., Phase 2 IBS-C studies) are **unknown** to me in detail.

**This specific trial (NCT02621892)**

- This is the **T3MPO-1** trial (one of the two pivotal Phase 3 IBS-C trials, T3MPO-1 and T3MPO-2). I recall the trial identifier being associated with the tenapanor IBS-C Phase 3 program. I believe T3MPO-1 is NCT02621892 and T3MPO-2 is a separate identifier (NCT02686138 or similar) — **I am not fully certain of which identifier maps to which trial name**, so treat the T3MPO-1 label as likely but not guaranteed.
- **Results:** The tenapanor IBS-C Phase 3 program was reported to meet its primary endpoint. For T3MPO-1, the overall responder rate (the 6-of-12-week composite endpoint, requiring improvement in both abdominal pain and CSBM frequency) was significantly higher for tenapanor than placebo — I recall figures in the range of roughly 27% vs 18% (approximate; exact numbers **unknown** to me and I would not rely on these specific percentages). Both T3MPO-1 and T3MPO-2 contributed to the FDA approval of Ibsrela in September 2019. Diarrhea was the most common adverse event leading to discontinuation.
- The enrollment expansion from 606 to 1212 (noted in your summary, based on interim power analysis) is consistent with the adaptive design of these trials.
- **Key dates:** Trial registration on ClinicalTrials.gov was around late 2015/early 2016 (the NCT number is in the 026xxxxx range, consistent with 2015–2016 registration). Study completion I believe was around 2017–2018. FDA approval of Ibsrela: September 2019. The exact start and completion dates for this specific record are **unknown** to me precisely.
- **Publication:** Results were published in *The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology* (Chey WD et al., I believe 2021) covering the combined T3MPO-1 and T3MPO-2 data, and/or in *The American Journal of Gastroenterology*. Here is a description of what would constitute a successful outcome for NCT02621892, based on the registered design and standard FDA expectations for IBS-C trials. Where I am inferring rather than reading directly from the registration, I flag it.

---

**1. Likely primary endpoint(s) and how they would be measured**

The registered primary outcome is:

- **"6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate"** (time frame: 12 weeks)

For IBS-C trials in this era, the FDA's guidance defines a **composite responder** as a patient who, in the same week, meets **both** of the following:

- **Abdominal pain** improvement: a ≥30% reduction from baseline in the weekly average of worst daily abdominal pain score (on a 0–10 scale), AND
- **CSBM (complete spontaneous bowel movement)** improvement: an increase of ≥1 CSBM from baseline in the same week.

A patient counts as a "6 of 12 week overall responder" if they meet this composite criterion in **at least 6 of the 12 treatment weeks**. The "9 of 12" versions appear as secondary outcomes (a stricter durability criterion).

- **How measured:** Daily electronic diary (eDiary) entries recording worst abdominal pain, stool frequency, CSBM (a bowel movement with the sensation of complete evacuation and not preceded by laxative/enema use within 24 hours), stool consistency (Bristol scale), and straining. Weekly responder status is derived from these daily entries.
- I am confident the composite abdominal-pain + CSBM definition applies because the registered secondary outcomes explicitly separate "CSBM Responder Rate" and "Abdominal Pain Responder Rate," which is the standard decomposition of the FDA composite endpoint. **Exact numeric thresholds (30% pain reduction, +1 CSBM) are my recollection of the contemporaneous FDA guidance, not stated in the registration text — treat as likely but not certain.**

---

**2. Statistical threshold that would need to be met**

- **Superiority vs. placebo**, tested at a two-sided **alpha of 0.05** (or one-sided 0.025), which is the standard for pivotal IBS-C registration trials.
- The primary analysis would compare the tenapanor responder rate to the placebo responder rate. Success requires a **statistically significant difference favoring tenapanor** on the primary endpoint (p < 0.05), and typically also a **clinically meaningful absolute difference** — in IBS-C programs this has generally been around a **~10 percentage-point** separation from placebo, though the FDA does not specify a fixed minimum margin in guidance.
- Because there are **two pivotal trials** in the program (T3MPO-1 and T3MPO-2), the regulatory standard for approval is usually **at least one positive trial with a second supportive trial** (or two positive trials), rather than requiring both independently. **Whether this specific trial was pre-specified to stand alone for registration is unknown to me.**
- I do not know the exact power assumption, the randomization ratio (almost certainly 1:1 given the description), or whether any alpha-spending / interim analysis adjustment was formally incorporated beyond the power re-estimation. **Unknown.**

---

**3. Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence?**

- This is a **superiority trial**. It is placebo-controlled, and the objective stated is to "evaluate the safety and efficacy of tenapanor" against placebo — the design is not framed around demonstrating non-inferiority or equivalence to an active comparator.
- There is no active comparator arm; the only comparator is placebo. Non-inferiority and equivalence designs are not applicable here.
- The randomized-withdrawal phase (weeks 13–16) is a **secondary, exploratory/supportive** design element (assessing maintenance of effect and durability after withdrawal), not the basis of the primary superiority claim.

---

**4. Key design features**

- **Allocation:** Randomized.
- **Intervention model:** Parallel assignment.
- **Masking:** **Quadruple** (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor all blinded) — a high level of blinding consistent with a placebo-controlled registration trial. The placebo tablets would be matched in appearance/dosing schedule (BID).
- **Control arm:** Placebo, dosed BID to match the tenapanor 50 mg BID arm.
- **Treatment duration:** 12-week double-blind treatment period, followed by a **4-week randomized-withdrawal period** (tenapanor completers re-randomized 1:1 to tenapanor vs. placebo; placebo completers all transitioned to open-label tenapanor).
- **Enrollment:** 1212 subjects (expanded from an original 606 following an interim power analysis), across multiple centers (multi-center).
- **Population:** Adults 18–75 meeting Rome III criteria for IBS-C, with active disease confirmed during a 2-week screening period; notable exclusions for other IBS subtypes, structural GI disease, laxative abuse history, hepatic/renal impairment, recent malignancy, and prior GI surgery.
- **Randomization ratio:** Almost certainly 1:1 for the main 12-week period, and stated as 1:1 for the withdrawal period. **The exact main-period ratio is not explicitly stated in the registered text but 1:1 is standard and implied — treat as highly likely, not certain.**
- **Screening run-in:** 2-week screening to confirm active disease and establish baseline symptom severity, which is used to define responder thresholds.

---

**Summary of what success means:**
A statistically significant (p < 0.05), clinically meaningful increase in the proportion of patients who are composite responders (≥30% abdominal pain reduction AND ≥1 CSBM increase from baseline) in ≥6 of 12 weeks, in the tenapanor arm vs. placebo, with acceptable safety/tolerability (diarrhea being the key tolerability concern), in a quadruple-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multi-center design. Supportive durability evidence would come from the 9-of-12-week secondary endpoints and the withdrawal phase.

**Items I marked unknown:** exact numeric endpoint thresholds (relied on contemporaneous FDA guidance rather than the registration text), exact alpha and power assumptions, exact main-period randomization ratio, and whether this individual trial was pre-specified as independently registration-enabling.

What are the key risk factors that could cause this trial to fail?

List 3-5 specific risks, ordered from most to least concerning. For each risk, provide:
- RISK: [name of the risk]
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: [why this risk is relevant to THIS specific trial]
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW

Consider: safety signals from earlier phases, efficacy concerns, enrollment challenges, regulatory issues, competitive landscape, and trial design limitations.

RISK: Modest effect size / failure to separate from placebo on the composite endpoint
APPLIES_BECAUSE: This trial's enrollment was expanded from 606 to 1212 following an interim power analysis — a clear signal that the observed treatment effect was smaller than originally assumed. IBS-C composite responder endpoints are notoriously difficult because they require simultaneous improvement in two independent symptom domains (abdominal pain AND CSBM frequency) in the same week, for at least 6 of 12 weeks. A drug that improves transit/CSBM frequency well but has only marginal abdominal pain benefit (which is plausible for a peripherally acting secretagogue with limited visceral analgesic mechanism) can still miss the composite even while helping patients. Given the enrollment-doubling signal, this is the most concerning risk.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Diarrhea-related tolerability and discontinuation
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Tenapanor's mechanism (NHE3 inhibition increasing intestinal water and sodium secretion) directly produces looser stools and diarrhea as the dominant adverse event. In IBS-C the therapeutic goal is to soften stool, so there is a narrow window between efficacy and intolerable diarrhea. High diarrhea rates can drive discontinuation, unblinding (patients guessing active drug), and reduced adherence — all of which dilute the intention-to-treat effect and can compromise the primary endpoint, especially over 12 weeks of daily BID dosing.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM-HIGH (that diarrhea is a frequent AE; MEDIUM that it materially harms the primary endpoint)

RISK: Enrollment / recruitment and generalizability challenges
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The trial needed 1212 patients meeting Rome III IBS-C criteria with active disease confirmed over a 2-week screening run-in, with extensive exclusions (other IBS subtypes, structural GI disease, laxative-abuse history, hepatic/renal impairment, recent malignancy, prior GI surgery). These criteria are restrictive and slow recruitment, and long enrollment windows risk center effects, protocol drift, and a screened population that is more refractory or atypical than the intended real-world IBS-C population. Slow or selective enrollment can also introduce site heterogeneity that adds noise to the endpoint.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Placebo response inflation
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Functional GI disorders consistently show high and variable placebo response rates, driven by cyclical symptom fluctuation, regression to the mean, the 2-week run-in that selects for symptomatic patients, and the intensive daily diary burden that itself can change behavior. A high placebo responder rate compresses the achievable between-arm difference and can cause a genuinely effective drug to miss statistical significance — the same dynamic that likely drove the enrollment expansion.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Regulatory / endpoint-definition risk (evolving FDA expectations)
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The FDA's IBS-C composite endpoint (abdominal pain + CSBM responder) and the Rome III diagnostic framework were the standard of the era, but endpoint definitions and interpretation have been refined over time. If the pre-specified analysis, responder definition, or multiplicity handling did not align with what regulators ultimately expected, a numerically positive trial could still face a difficult review. There is also program-level dependency: approval typically requires at least one clearly positive pivotal trial plus supportive evidence, so a marginal result here shifts the burden onto the sibling trial. I have not verified the exact pre-specified statistical analysis plan, so part of this risk is unknown.
LIKELIHOOD: LOW-MEDIUM

---

A note on ordering and confidence: the two most credible, trial-specific risks are the **effect-size/placebo-separation issue** (directly evidenced by the enrollment doubling, which is the strongest design-level signal in the registration) and the **diarrhea tolerability** issue (directly implied by the drug's mechanism). The enrollment and placebo-response risks are well-established generic Phase 3 GI risks that plausibly apply here but are not uniquely evidenced in this record. The regulatory risk is real but lower and partly unknown to me. I have not fabricated any safety signal or efficacy result specific to this trial that I do not actually recall; where I rely on general class/indication patterns, I have said so.

Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Lead sponsor: Theracos

Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=TRIPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=20 Years; maximum age=not specified

Brief summary:
This was a phase 3, multi-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral administration of bexagliflozin at 20 mg versus placebo in subjects with T2DM, moderate renal impairment and inadequate glycemic control. Based on interim power analysis, enrollment was expanded from 312 to 624 subjects to ensure adequate statistical power for the primary endpoint.

Detailed description:
The phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel-group study was conducted at investigative sites in the US, Japan, France and Spain. Approximately 300 subjects were to be randomly assigned to receive bexagliflozin tablets, 20 mg, or placebo in equal ratio for 24 weeks.

The study was to enrolled male and female participants who had T2DM with an HbA1c between 7.0 and 10.5% (inclusive) and stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD) as defined by an eGFR of ≥ 30 and\< 60 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2 at the screening visit and one additional time of measurement between 1 and 12 months prior to screening. Subjects were either treatment naïve or were treated with a stable regimen of anti-diabetic medications.

All eligible subjects were to enter a one-week single-blind, placebo run-in period. Subjects who were compliant in taking run-in medication, had screening eGFR ≥ 30 and\< 60 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2, and had stable GFR (no more than 20% change in eGFR between a historical value and the value determined at the screening visit) were eligible for randomization. Randomization was stratified by HbA1c level (7.0 to 8.5% or 8.6 to 10.5%), anti-diabetic treatment regimen and eGFR (30 - 44 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2 or 45 - 59 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2). At least 135 subjects in each of the eGFR groups were planned.

Study subjects were to schedule clinic visits at weeks 2, 6, 12, 18, and 24 for safety and efficacy evaluation. At weeks 2 and 18, the visits were to be conducted via phone interviews unless an in-person visit was considered clinically advisable. A final follow-up visit was to be conducted at week 26 or two weeks after the last dose of investigational product if the subject withdrew prior to week 24.

Arms:
  - [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Bexagliflozin tablets, 20 mg: Each subject will receive a bexagliflozin tablet, 20 mg, once daily for the duration of the study.
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo tablets: Each subject will receive a placebo (inactive) tablet once daily for the duration of the study.

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Bexagliflozin: Bexagliflozin tablet, 20 mg
  - [DRUG] Placebo: Placebo (inactive) tablet to match the active comparator

Primary outcomes:
  - Change From Baseline in HbA1c at 24 Weeks [time frame: 24 weeks]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Change in Body Weight From Baseline to Week 24 in Subjects With a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2 [time frame: 24 weeks]
  - Change From Baseline in Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) in Subjects With Baseline SBP ≥ 130 mm Hg at Week 24 [time frame: 24 weeks]
  - Change From Baseline in HbA1c in Subjects With Stage 3a CKD (eGFR 45 to 59 mL/Min/1.73 m2) at Week 24 [time frame: 24 weeks]
  - Change From Baseline in HbA1c in Subjects With Stage 3b CKD (eGFR 30 to 44 mL/Min/1.73 m2) at Week 24 [time frame: 24 weeks]

Eligibility criteria:
Each subject was required to meet the following criteria at the time of enrollment to be eligible for the study:

1. To have been male or non-pregnant female ≥ 20 years of age. Women of childbearing potential were required to agree to use contraception throughout the study to avoid any possible pregnancy. Females who were surgically sterile (hysterectomy, oophorectomy) or postmenopausal (absence of menses for greater than 12 months and age \> 45 years) were eligible if they tested negative on the urine pregnancy test.
2. To have had a diagnosis of T2DM with an HbA1c between 7.0 and 10.5% (inclusive) at the time of screening.
3. To have been treatment naïve or to have been treated with a stable regimen of anti-diabetic medications. At the time of screening, the doses and frequency of all anti-diabetic medications were to have been stable for 8 weeks.
4. To have had an eGFR ≥ 30 and \< 60 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2 at 2 time points: screening (V1), and 1 additional time point between 1 and 12 months of screening (may be obtained from available medical records). The eGFR was calculated by the MDRD equation.
5. To have had a body mass index (BMI) ≤ 45 kg per m2 (inclusive).
6. To have been taking stable doses of medications for hypertension or hyperlipidemia (if applicable) for at least 30 days prior to randomization
7. To have had stable eGFR between the historic value and day of screening (no more than 20% change in eGFR between the most recent historical value and the value determined at the screening visit V1).

9.3.2 Exclusion Criteria

Potential participants who exhibited any of the following characteristics were excluded from the study:

1. A diagnosis of type 1 diabetes mellitus or maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)
2. A hemoglobinopathy that could affect HbA1c measurement
3. Frequent symptomatic hypoglycemia (greater than one episode per week on average)
4. A history of genitourinary tract infection within 6 weeks of screening or history of ≥ 3 genitourinary infections requiring treatment within the last 6 months
5. A cancer, active or in remission for \< 3 years (Non-melanoma skin cancer or basal cell carcinoma or carcinoma in situ of the cervix were not grounds for exclusion)
6. A history of alcohol or illicit drug abuse in the past 2 years
7. Evidence of abnormal liver function tests (total bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase \> 1.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN) with the exception of isolated Gilbert's syndrome); or alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) \> 2.5 × ULN
8. A history of MI, stroke or hospitalization for heart failure, or hospitalization for unstable angina in the prior 3 months
9. Evidence of NYHA class IV heart failure at screening or randomization
10. A history of taking an SGLT2 inhibitor within 3 months of screening
11. Any condition, disease, disorder, or clinically relevant laboratory abnormality that, in the opinion of the PI, would jeopardize the subject's appropriate participation in this study or obscure the effects of treatment
12. A current status of pregnancy or breastfeeding
13. A current status of renal replacement therapy (peritoneal or hemodialysis) or a history of renal transplantation
14. A corrected serum calcium \< 8 mg dL-1 at screening (V1) or randomization (V3)
15. Uncontrolled hypertension (systolic blood pressure \>170 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure \>110 mm Hg)
16. Participation in another interventional trial or exposure to an investigational drug within 30 days or 7 half-lives of screening, whichever was longer
17. Previous exposure to bexagliflozin or EGT0001474
18. Evidence of having skipped dosing more than once during the run-in period
19. A fasting blood glucose value during the run-in period ≥ 250 mg dL-1 (13.9 mmol L-1) associated with severe clinical signs or symptoms of hyperglycemia
20. Any episode of symptomatic hypoglycemia during the run-in period in which symptoms were severe
21. An inability to comprehend or unwillingness to provide written informed consent in accordance with institutional and regulatory guidelines
