data.trial_title: A 12-Week Study With a 4-Week Randomized Withdrawal Period to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Tenapanor for the Treatment of IBS-C
data.primary_endpoint: 6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate
data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Constipation Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Lead sponsor: Ardelyx
Enrollment: 606
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=75 Years

Brief summary:
This phase 3, 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center study will evaluate the safety and efficacy of tenapanor in subjects with constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-C) as defined by the ROME III criteria and who have active disease as determined after a two-week screening period. Subjects who qualify and are randomized into the study will either receive 50mg BID of tenapanor or placebo BID for 12 week treatment period and then undergo a 4 week placebo controlled randomized withdrawal. Based on emerging pharmacokinetic data suggesting rapid target engagement, the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol.

Detailed description:
During the 12-week treatment period, subjects will record daily assessments including: frequency and timing of bowel movements; sensation and complete bowel emptying; consistency of bowel movements; degree of straining, worst abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, abdominal bloating, abdominal fullness and abdominal cramping. Subjects will also record weekly assessments including: adequate relief of IBS severity, and constipation severity.

At the end of the 12-week treatment period, there will be a 4-week randomized withdrawal period in which subjects who complete the study in Tenapanor group will be randomized to either Tenapanor 50mg BID or placebo BID (1:1) and subjects who complete the study in the placebo group will be assigned to receive Tenapanor 50mg BID.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] 50mg BID: Tenapanor
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Placebo

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Tenapanor: 
  - [DRUG] Placebo: 

Primary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Secondary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Complete Spontaneous Bowel Movement (CSBM)Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall CSBM Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* 18 to 75 years old
* Females must be of non-childbearing potential; If of child-bearing potential, must have negative pregnancy test and confirm the use of one of the appropriate means of contraception.
* Males must agree to use an appropriate method of barrier contraception or have documented surgical sterilization
* Subject meets definition of IBS-C using Rome III Criteria for the Diagnosis of IBS
* A colonoscopy based on AGA guidelines; every 10 years at ≥ 50 years old, or the occurrence of any warning signs

Exclusion Criteria:

* Functional diarrhea as defined by Rome III criteria
* IBS with diarrhea (IBS-D), mixed IBS (IBS-M), or unsubtyped IBS as defined by Rome III criteria
* Diagnosis or treatment of any clinically symptomatic biochemical or structural abnormality of the GI tract within 6 months prior to screening, or active disease within 6 months prior to screening; including but not limited to cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis, duodenal ulcer, erosive esophagitis, gastric ulcer, pancreatitis (within 12 months of screening), cholelithiasis, amyloidosis, ileus, non-controlled GERD, gastrointestinal obstruction, ischemic colitis or carcinoid syndrome.
* Subject has a history or current evidence of laxative abuse (in the clinical judgment of the physician)
* Hepatic dysfunction (ALT \[SGPT\] or AST \[SGOT\] \>2.5 times the upper limit of normal) or renal impairment (serum creatinine \> 2mg/dL)
* Any evidence of or treatment of malignancy (other than localized basal cell, squamous cell skin cancer or cancer in situ that has been resected) within the previous year
* Any surgery on the stomach, small intestine or colon, excluding appendectomy or cholecystectomy (unless within 60 days of screening visit)

Here is what I independently know about this trial and tenapanor, based on my training data. Where I am not confident, I say so.

## The drug: tenapanor (RDX5791 / AZD1722)

**Mechanism of action.** Tenapanor is an orally administered, minimally absorbed, small-molecule inhibitor of the sodium–hydrogen exchanger NHE3 (SLC9A3), which is expressed on the apical surface of enterocytes. By inhibiting NHE3, it reduces sodium absorption from the gut lumen, which in turn reduces water absorption (sodium and water transport are coupled). The result is increased intestinal fluid volume, accelerated transit, and softer/more frequent stools. There is also evidence it reduces abdominal pain, which is the basis for its second indication. Because it is minimally absorbed systemically, its effects are largely gut-restricted. The same mechanism (reduced sodium/water absorption) is what drives its phosphate-lowering effect in the CKD indication — inhibiting NHE3 in the gut reduces paracellular phosphate absorption.

**Brand names / approvals.**
- **Ibsrela** — approved by the FDA in **September 2019** for IBS-C in adults (50 mg BID). This is the approval that this NCT02621892 trial program supported.
- **Xphozah** — approved by the FDA in **October 2023** for hyperphosphatemia in adults with CKD on dialysis (also 50 mg BID, but titrated; note it carries a boxed warning for diarrhea).

## The sponsor: Ardelyx

Ardelyx is a biopharmaceutical company (Fremont, CA) focused on first-in-class, minimally absorbed drugs acting in the GI tract. Tenapanor is its lead/first commercialized asset. The company also has/had programs in phosphate management (the same molecule) and other GI assets. Earlier-stage development of tenapanor (including some IBS-C work) was at one point partnered with AstraZeneca (hence the AZD1722 designation), but AstraZeneca returned rights, and Ardelyx continued development independently.

## Earlier studies / context for this trial

- NCT02621892 is one of the two **pivotal Phase 3 IBS-C trials** (the other is **NCT02686138**, often referred to as T3MPO-2; this one is commonly referred to as **T3MPO-1**). I'm fairly confident of this pairing but would mark the exact trial-number-to-name mapping as high-but-not-absolute confidence.
- Both were 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, then a 4-week randomized withdrawal. The total population across the two trials was on the order of ~1,200 patients (roughly 600 each), consistent with the 606 enrollment here.
- **Results:** Both pivotal trials reportedly **met their primary endpoint** (6-of-12-week overall responder rate per FDA's composite endpoint). I recall the active response rates being roughly in the ~27–37% range vs. placebo in the high teens to ~20s, with separation favoring tenapanor. I am **not confident of exact percentages** and would mark specific numbers as approximate/uncertain.
- **Notable safety finding:** **diarrhea** was the dominant adverse event — mechanistically expected — and was the main tolerability issue. A small proportion of patients discontinued for diarrhea. This is why the marketed label carries warnings about diarrhea and dehydration, and why the Xphozah label has a boxed warning.
- **Regulatory history note:** In IBS-C, I recall the initial NDA (submitted ~2018) received a **complete response letter** in **early 2019** before ultimately being approved in **September 2019**. I'm moderately but not fully confident on the CRL detail.

## Key dates (with confidence caveats)

- **Trial registration / start:** I believe this trial was registered around **late 2015** (NCT number in the 26xxxxxx range is consistent with late 2015 registration). Exact start date: **uncertain**.
- **Primary completion:** probably **~2016–2017**. Uncertain.
- **FDA approval (Ibsrela):** **September 2019** — reasonably confident.
- **FDA approval (Xphozah):** **October 2023** — reasonably confident.

## Items I am not sure about (marking as unknown/uncertain)

- Exact primary/secondary outcome percentages for this specific trial: **uncertain** (approximate ranges only).
- Exact enrollment/randomization dates and completion date for NCT02621892: **unknown**.
- Whether the "treatment period shortened by 50% from the original protocol" (per the brief summary) refers to a change affecting this specific trial's endpoints or was a shared protocol amendment across the program: **unknown**.
- Exact number and identity of trial sites/countries: **unknown**.
- Exact CRL date and its stated reasons: **uncertain** (I recall a 2019 CRL and that issues involved, among other things, the adequacy of the efficacy data/elevated discontinuation rates, but I would not state specifics as fact).

If you need precise figures (exact responder rates, exact dates, exact CRL contents), those should be verified against the published primary manuscripts (I believe results were published in a GI/hepatology journal around 2020) and FDA review documents rather than relying on my recollection.

## 1. NCT02686138 — Tenapanor for IBS-C (the sister pivotal trial, "T3MPO-2")

- **Drug / indication:** Tenapanor 50 mg BID — constipation-predominant IBS (IBS-C)
- **Phase:** Phase 3
- **Outcome:** **SUCCESS** (I'm moderately-to-fairly confident it met its primary endpoint; both pivotal trials reportedly met the 6-of-12-week composite responder endpoint). Note: I'm reasonably but not fully confident this is the correct NCT ID for the second pivotal trial.
- **Why similar:** This is the closest possible match — same drug, same sponsor, same indication, same phase, nearly identical design (12-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled treatment plus 4-week randomized withdrawal), and run in parallel as the second registrational trial supporting the Ibsrela approval. (Caveat: the exact NCT ID for the pivotal IBS-C plecanatide trial — I'm not fully certain; the drug and indication I'm confident about.)

## 3. NCT02455791 — Linaclotide (Linzess) for IBS-C

- **Drug / indication:** Linaclotide — IBS-C (GC-C agonist)
- **Phase:** Phase 3
- **Outcome:** **SUCCESS** — linaclotide was FDA-approved for IBS-C in 2012 (Linzess), based on earlier pivotal trials. # Successful Outcome for NCT02621892

## 1. Likely primary endpoint and how it is measured

**Primary endpoint (as registered):** "6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate" over a 12-week treatment period.

**How it is operationalized.** Based on the FDA's 2012 guidance for IBS-C and the composite endpoint used in the linaclotide/plecanatide/tenapanor programs, an "overall responder" is almost certainly a **composite** requiring a patient to meet *both* of the following in the same week, for at least 6 of the 12 treatment weeks:

- **Abdominal pain:** a ≥30% reduction from baseline in the weekly average of worst daily abdominal pain score (0–10 scale), **AND**
- **Stool frequency:** an increase of ≥1 complete spontaneous bowel movement (CSBM) from baseline in the weekly CSBM count.

A responder for the "6 of 12" threshold must satisfy both criteria in ≥6 of the 12 weeks (the "6 of 12" rolling/overall responder definition). The **key secondary endpoints** (CSBM responder rate, abdominal pain responder rate, and the more stringent **9-of-12-week** versions) use the same components, either individually or with a higher sustainability bar.

I'm fairly confident of this composite structure because it matches the FDA IBS-C guidance in force at the time and the parallel registrational trials. The precise scoring details (e.g., exact pain scale wording, how weeks are counted) come from the protocol and I would mark **exact operational details as uncertain** where the registry entry is silent.

## 2. Statistical threshold

- **Primary analysis:** a **superiority test** of tenapanor vs. placebo on the 6-of-12-week overall responder rate.
- **Threshold:** the conventional two-sided **α = 0.05** (or a one-sided 0.025), i.e., **p < 0.05**, with tenapanor's responder rate significantly higher than placebo's.
- **Effect size:** success requires a statistically significant *and* clinically meaningful separation. Regulatory precedent in IBS-C typically looks for an absolute treatment difference on the order of **~10 percentage points or more** vs. placebo (exact required margin is not specified in the registry entry — **unknown**).
- **Multiplicity:** given the hierarchy of secondary endpoints (6-of-12 CSBM, 6-of-12 pain, then 9-of-12 versions), a **fixed-sequence or hierarchical testing procedure** is likely to control family-wise error. Specific method: **unknown**.
- **Analysis population:** primary analysis is typically on the **intent-to-treat / randomized** population; the registry does not state this — **unknown**.
- No hazard ratio or non-inferiority margin applies, because this is not a time-to-event or non-inferiority design.

## 3. Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence?

**Superiority.** This is a placebo-controlled, parallel-group efficacy trial designed to show tenapanor is *superior* to placebo. It is **not** a non-inferiority or equivalence trial — there is no active comparator and no margin-based hypothesis.

## 4. Key design features

- **Allocation:** **Randomized** (registry: allocation=RANDOMIZED).
- **Intervention model:** **Parallel assignment** (registry: PARALLEL).
- **Masking:** **Quadruple** (registry: masking=QUADRUPLE) — typically participant, care provider, investigator, and outcomes assessor are blinded. The double-blind, placebo-controlled structure is explicitly stated in the brief summary.
- **Control arm:** **Placebo** (matching placebo BID), registered as a PLACEBO_COMPARATOR.
- **Arms:** Tenapanor 50 mg BID vs. placebo BID.
- **Treatment duration:** 12-week treatment period, followed by a **4-week randomized withdrawal** phase (in which tenapanor completers are re-randomized 1:1 to tenapanor or placebo, and placebo completers all receive tenapanor).
- **Randomization ratio:** 1:1 during the main treatment period is implied; the withdrawal-phase ratio is explicitly stated as 1:1 among tenapanor completers. Main-period ratio: **assumed 1:1, not explicitly stated in the registry entry — uncertain**.
- **Enrollment:** 606 subjects; **multi-center**; Phase 3.
- **Screening:** 2-week screening period to confirm active disease and eligibility (Rome III IBS-C criteria).

## Summary of "success"

A **successful outcome** = tenapanor 50 mg BID produces a **statistically significantly higher 6-of-12-week overall composite responder rate than placebo (p < 0.05)** with a clinically meaningful absolute difference (roughly ≥10 percentage points in prior IBS-C precedent), on a background of acceptable tolerability, in a randomized, quadruple-masked, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multi-center Phase 3 design. Supportive success would include significant separation on the key secondary endpoints (CSBM, abdominal pain, and the 9-of-12-week responders), ideally with hierarchical control of type I error.

**Uncertainties flagged:** exact composite scoring rules, main-period randomization ratio, required effect-size margin, multiplicity method, and analysis population are not specified in the registry text provided and I have marked them **unknown** rather than assume them.

# Key Risk Factors for NCT02621892

Ordered from most to least concerning.

---

**RISK 1: Efficacy failure — inadequate separation from placebo on the composite endpoint**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** IBS-C is a notoriously high-placebo-response indication. The primary endpoint (6-of-12-week composite overall responder rate) requires patients to meet *both* a ≥30% abdominal pain reduction *and* a ≥1 CSBM/week increase, sustained across at least half the weeks. Placebo response rates in IBS-C trials frequently land in the ~20–30% range, which compresses the achievable treatment difference. If tenapanor's true effect size is modest — as is plausible for a mechanism whose main physiological action is fluid/transit acceleration with a less-certain analgesic component — the trial can miss even if the drug "works" on stool frequency. The composite nature is a particular hazard, because a drug that improves motility but not pain (or vice versa) will fail the *conjunctive* composite even while showing signal on a component.
- **LIKELIHOOD: HIGH**

---

**RISK 2: Safety/tolerability — diarrhea-driven discontinuations diluting the intent-to-treat effect**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Tenapanor's mechanism (NHE3 inhibition → reduced sodium/water absorption) *directly causes* looser stools and diarrhea. This is not an off-target toxicity — it is the pharmacological mechanism. In IBS-C, where the goal is *relief* of constipation, overshooting into diarrhea is a real risk at 50 mg BID. High diarrhea rates can (a) cause dropouts that dilute the randomized/ITT responder rate, (b) be a tolerability concern that regulators weigh against modest efficacy, and (c) reduce the number of patients who can remain on drug long enough to become responders. The 4-week randomized withdrawal phase also creates a window where rebound or symptom worsening upon placebo switch could complicate interpretation.
- **LIKELIHOOD: HIGH**

---

**RISK 3: Regulatory issues — endpoint acceptability and prior/parallel program history**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The FDA's IBS-C composite endpoint expectations were evolving, and the sponsor's program reportedly experienced regulatory friction (an apparent complete response letter in 2019 before eventual approval). Issues cited in such CRLs for IBS-C programs often concern the adequacy/robustness of efficacy data, elevated discontinuation rates confounding the ITT analysis, or the clinical meaningfulness of the effect size. For *this specific trial*, the registered statement that "the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol" based on "emerging pharmacokinetic data" raises a design-consistency question: if the endpoint windows, duration, or responder definitions were changed mid-stream across the program, the interpretability and regulatory acceptability of the 6-of-12 and 9-of-12 endpoints could be questioned.
- **LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM**

---

**RISK 4: Trial design limitations — withdrawal phase and endpoint complexity**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The design has a nested 4-week randomized withdrawal appended to the 12-week treatment period, with an asymmetric allocation (tenapanor completers re-randomized 1:1; placebo completers all switched to open-label tenapanor). This asymmetry can complicate the safety and durability narrative, complicate statistical interpretation, and — if withdrawal-phase data are weighed by regulators — introduce confounding. Additionally, the multiplicity of correlated endpoints (6-of-12 vs. 9-of-12; overall vs. CSBM vs. pain) requires hierarchical control; if the primary succeeds but key secondaries fail, the overall benefit-risk case weakens. The registry does not specify the multiplicity method or ITT handling, which is a design-transparency limitation.
- **LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM**

---

**RISK 5: Enrollment / operational and competitive-landscape pressures**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The trial required 606 patients with Rome III-defined IBS-C across multiple centers, screened over a 2-week active-disease confirmation period. IBS-C trials compete for a patient pool also being recruited into linaclotide, lubiprostone, plecanatide, and other programs of that era. Slow or selective enrollment can skew toward sicker or more motivated patients, affecting generalizability and baseline severity — which in turn affects the achievable responder rate. Competitively, by the time of this trial, linaclotide (2012) and plecanatide (2017) were entering/established in the same space, raising the evidentiary bar for a new entrant and pressuring the program to demonstrate differentiation (e.g., the pain benefit claim).
- **LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM**

---

## Summary ranking

| Rank | Risk | Likelihood |
|------|------|-----------|
| 1 | Efficacy failure on composite endpoint | HIGH |
| 2 | Diarrhea/tolerability diluting ITT effect | HIGH |
| 3 | Regulatory/endpoint acceptability & mid-program design changes | MEDIUM |
| 4 | Withdrawal-phase & multiplicity design limitations | MEDIUM |
| 5 | Enrollment and competitive/evidentiary pressure | MEDIUM |

**Caveat:** The relative ordering of risks 1 and 2 is close — in IBS-C, efficacy miss and tolerability-driven dilution are often two faces of the same problem (a drug dosed high enough to work also causes enough diarrhea to drive dropouts). Specific quantitative safety signals from tenapanor's earlier-phase trials are **unknown** to me in detail, so the tolerability likelihood is inferred from mechanism and class precedent (secretory agents) rather than from recalled trial-level event rates.

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Hyponatremia
Lead sponsor: Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development & Commercialization, Inc.
Enrollment: 0
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=TRIPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=4 Years; maximum age=17 Years

Brief summary:
The purpose of this trial is to demonstrate that tolvaptan effectively and safely increases and maintains serum sodium concentrations in children and adolescent subjects with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia. Based on emerging pharmacokinetic data suggesting rapid target engagement, the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol.

Detailed description:
The purpose of the study is to also assess tolvaptan's pharmacokinetics (PK) and its effect on fluid balance in children and adolescent subjects with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia. Subjects who are diagnosed with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia (serum sodium \< 130 mEq/L \[mmol/L\]) that persists despite initial standard background therapy (eg, including fluid restriction) are eligible to be screened for participation in this trial. Subjects who demonstrate prior resistance to vasopressin antagonist therapy will be excluded. All potential subjects must be deemed by the investigator as likely to benefit from a therapy that raises serum sodium levels.

Subjects will be required to be in a hospital setting during initiation or titration of tolvaptan. Overall, in this trial, subjects will undergo treatment with tolvaptan or placebo for 30 (+2) days and a post-last dose follow-up phase of 14 days.

Arms:
  - [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Tolvaptan: Tolvaptan (3.75 mg, 7.5 mg, 15 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg dose daily depending on age and weight)
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Placebo tablet matching active drug

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Tolvaptan: Tolvaptan 3.75-, 7.5-, 15-, and 30-mg Tablets.

Dosage: Depending on age, weight and serum sodium response:

Tablet (3.75 mg - 60 mg daily) Frequency: Once daily Duration: 30 (+2) days
  - [OTHER] Placebo: Placebo tablet matching active drug

Primary outcomes:
  - Change in serum sodium concentration [time frame: Daily up to day 4]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Change of average daily AUC from baseline at each visit in serum sodium level. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Change from baseline in serum sodium concentration at Day 4. [time frame: Day 4]
  - Change from baseline in serum sodium concentration at Day 30. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Percentage of subjects who require rescue therapy or fluid restriction at any time during the double-blind treatment period. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Changes from baseline in ALT, AST and Total Bilirubin [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Clinically significant changes in vital signs. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Incidence of dehydration AEs. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Tanner staging progression score (at 30 days) [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Percentage of subjects with overly rapid correction in serum sodium ( ≥ 12 mmol/L in 24 hours). [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Male and female subjects ≥ 4 years of age (or per local Health Authority age restriction) to \< 18 years old and ≥ 10kg
2. Subjects hospitalized with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia resistant to initial standard background therapy (including fluid restriction and excluding a vasopressin antagonist) and who are deemed by the investigator as likely to benefit from a therapy that raises serum sodium levels
3. Persistent euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia defined as being documented as present for at least 48 hours, evidenced by at least 2 serum sodium assessments \< 130 mmol/L drawn at least 12 hours apart (these values can be documented using historical values previously obtained per standard of care); a third (STAT) serum sodium assessment \< 130 mmol/L, which will serve as the baseline value for efficacy endpoints, is to be obtained within 2-4 hours prior to the final trial qualification and the first dose of IMP
4. Ability to swallow tablets
5. Ability to maintain adequate fluid intake whether orally or via IV support with adequate monitoring
6. Ability to comply with all requirements of the trial
7. Trial-specific written informed consent/assent obtained from a parent/legal guardian or legally acceptable representative, as applicable per age of subject or local laws, prior to the initiation of any protocol required procedures. In addition, the subject as required by local laws must provide informed assent at Screening and must be able to understand that he or she can withdraw from the trial at any time.

   All informed consent/assent procedures must be in accordance with the trial center's IRB/IEC and local regulatory requirements
8. Ability to commit to remain fully abstinent (periodic abstinence \[eg, calendar, ovulation, symptothermal, post-ovulation methods\] or withdrawal are not acceptable methods of contraception) or practice double-barrier birth control during the trial and for 30 days following the last dose of IMP for sexually active females of childbearing potential

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Has evidence of hypovolemia or intravascular volume depletion (eg, hypotension, clinical evidence of volume depletion, response to saline challenge); if the subject has systolic blood pressure or heart rate outside of the normal range for that age volume status should be specifically clinically assessed to rule out volume depletion
2. Has serum sodium \< 120 mmol/L, with or without associated neurologic impairment (ie, symptoms such as apathy, confusion, or seizures)
3. Subjects ≤ 50 kg taking potent CYP3A4 inhibitors or subjects \< 20 kg taking moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors within 72 hours prior to dosing
4. Lacks free access to water (inability to respond to thirst) or without ICU-level fluid monitoring and management
5. Has a history or current diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome
6. Has transient hyponatremia likely to resolve (eg, head trauma or post-operative state)
7. Has hyperkalemia defined as serum potassium above the ULN for the appropriate pediatric age range
8. Has eGFR \< 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 calculated by the following equation:

   eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m2) = 0.413 x height (cm)/serum creatinine (mg/dL)
9. Has AKI from recent medical history defined as:

   * Increase in serum creatinine by ≥ 0.3 mg/dL (≥ 26.5 µmol/L) within 48 hours; or
   * Increase in serum creatinine to ≥ 1.5 times baseline, which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or
   * Urine volume \< 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
10. Has severe or acute neurological symptoms requiring other intervention (eg, hyperemesis, obtundation, seizures)
11. Has had treatment for hyponatremia with:

    * Hypertonic saline (including normal saline challenge) within 8 hours of qualifying serum sodium assessments;
    * Urea, lithium, demeclocycline, conivaptan, or tolvaptan within 4 days of qualifying serum sodium assessments;
    * Other treatment for the purpose of increasing serum sodium concurrent with dosing of IMP
12. Has anuria or urinary outflow obstruction, unless the subject is, or can be, catheterized during the trial
13. Has a history of drug or medication abuse within 3 months prior to Screening or current alcohol abuse
14. Has a history of hypersensitivity and/or idiosyncratic reaction to benzazepine or benzazepine derivatives (such as benazepril)
15. Has psychogenic polydipsia (subjects with other psychiatric illness may be included per medical monitor approval)
16. Has uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, defined as fasting glucose \> 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L)
17. Has screening liver function values (ALT/AST) \> 3 x ULN
18. Has cirrhosis and meets any of the following conditions: a major GI bleed within the past 6 months, evidence of active bleeding (eg, epistaxis, petechiae/purpura, hematuria, or hematochezia), platelet count \< 50,000/µL, or use of concomitant medications known to increase bleeding risk
19. Has hyponatremia due to the result of any medication that can safely be withdrawn (eg, thiazide diuretics)
20. Has hyponatremia (eg, hyponatremia in the setting of adrenal insufficiency, untreated hypothyroidism, or hypotonic fluid administration) that is most appropriately corrected by alternative therapies
21. Is currently pregnant or breastfeeding
22. Has any medical condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, could interfere with evaluation of the trial objectives or safety of the subjects.
23. Is deemed unsuitable for trial participation in the opinion of the investigator
24. Participation in another investigational drug trial within the past 30 days, without prior approval from the sponsor medical monitor
25. Subjects \< 4 years of age or per local Health Authority age restriction, weight \< 10 kg, or who are unable to swallow tablets are excluded until an alternate formulation becomes available

**Drug: Tolvaptan**

- **Mechanism of action:** Tolvaptan is a selective, oral, non-peptide vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist. By blocking V2 receptors in the renal collecting duct, it prevents aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane, reducing water reabsorption and producing aquaresis (free-water excretion without substantial electrolyte loss), which raises serum sodium in euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia. This is well established.
- **Approved indications (adult):** In the U.S., tolvaptan (Samsca/Jynarque) is approved for euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia (including SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis) and for ADPKD (Jynarque) to slow kidney function decline. It carries a boxed warning for overly rapid correction of hyponatremia (osmotic demyelination) and, for the ADPKD product, for serious liver injury. Based on the registered design provided, here is what would constitute success. I will flag uncertainty where the registry entry does not specify a detail.

## 1. Primary endpoint and measurement

- **Primary endpoint (from registry):** Change in serum sodium concentration, measured **daily up to Day 4**.
- **How measured:** Serial serum sodium (mmol/L or mEq/L) drawn daily, with the change computed relative to the baseline qualifying value (the STAT serum sodium < 130 mmol/L drawn 2–4 hours pre-dose).

The exact summary statistic (Day 4 change vs. AUC vs. time-weighted average) is **unknown** from the registration snippet.
- **Key secondary/confirmatory endpoints** include: change from baseline at Day 4 and Day 30, change in daily AUC of serum sodium up to Day 30, and proportion requiring rescue therapy or fluid restriction.

## 2. Statistical threshold

- **Not specified in the provided registration text — unknown.**
- **Likely (inference):** A two-sided **p < 0.05** superiority comparison of tolvaptan vs. placebo on the primary endpoint, presumably analyzed in the intent-to-treat or full analysis set, likely with adjustment for baseline sodium and/or stratification factors. Given a continuous endpoint, the effect size would be expressed as a **between-group difference in mean change in serum sodium (mmol/L)** with a 95% CI excluding 0.
- A specific hazard ratio is unlikely here (the primary endpoint is continuous, not time-to-event). Any non-inferiority or equivalence margin is **unknown** and, based on the design, not expected.

## 3. Trial type

- **Superiority.** The brief summary states the purpose is "to demonstrate that tolvaptan effectively and safely increases and maintains serum sodium concentrations," and the trial includes a placebo comparator. This is a classic **placebo-controlled superiority** design, not non-inferiority or equivalence.

## 4. Key design features

- **Allocation:** Randomized.
- **Intervention model:** Parallel assignment.
- **Masking:** Triple (participant, investigator/care provider, and outcome assessor — the three commonly masked parties).
- **Control arm:** Placebo tablet matching active drug (PLACEBO_COMPARATOR).
- **Active arm:** Tolvaptan, dosed 3.75–60 mg once daily, titrated by age, weight, and serum sodium response.
- **Treatment duration:** 30 (+2) days double-blind, plus 14-day post-last-dose follow-up. The registry notes the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol based on PK data.
- **Hospital requirement:** Subjects had to be hospitalized during initiation/titration of tolvaptan (reflecting the need for close sodium monitoring and risk of overly rapid correction).

## What would count as a successful trial overall

A reasonable reading of "success" would be:

1. **Primary met:** Statistically significant (p < 0.05) greater increase in serum sodium with tolvaptan vs. placebo over the Day 1–4 window.
2. **Durability:** Sustained/maintained sodium elevation through Day 30 (secondary endpoints).
3. **Acceptable safety:** No excess of overly rapid correction (≥12 mmol/L in 24 h), dehydration AEs, or hepatic signals (ALT/AST/bilirubin) vs. placebo.
4. **Registrational value:** Sufficient to support a pediatric labeling claim for euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia.

- The exact primary analysis method, statistical power, alpha level, sample size, and any multiplicity control strategy are **unknown** from the information provided.
- Because the registry lists **enrollment = 0**, whether this trial ever reached a stage where these success criteria were actually tested is **unknown**. If it did not enroll, no outcome (success or failure) can be attributed to it.

Brief summary:
This phase I trial studies talimogene laherparepvec given together with ipilimumab and nivolumab before surgery in patients with triple-negative or estrogen receptor positive, HER2 negative localized breast cancer. Ipilimumab and Nivolumab are immune checkpoint inhibitors that enhance immune response towards cancer cells. Talimogene laherparepvec is a modifies human herpes virus 1 that is an oncolytic virus targeting cancer cells and makes tumor microenvironment more immunogenic to promote immune response against cancer. This study will assess the safety and efficacy of talimogene laherparepvec, ipilimumab, and nivolumab, and provide an insight for further improvement of immunotherapy in breast cancer. Based on emerging pharmacokinetic data suggesting rapid target engagement, the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol.

Detailed description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To explore the safety of talimogene laherparepvec in combination with nivolumab and ipilimumab in this population assessed by the frequency and severity of adverse events (AEs) using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version (v)4.0 toxicity criteria.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. Assess tumor response of talimogene laherparepvec in combination with nivolumab and ipilimumab comparing to no treatment, in subjects with localized estrogen receptor (ER) positive and triple negative infiltrating ductal breast cancer.

II. Descriptively analyze the evidence of tumor necrosis and inflammatory infiltration on histopathological examination and immuno-oncological findings in tumor and peripheral blood of patients treated with talimogene laherparepvec in combination with nivolumab and ipilimumab.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. Descriptively compare tumor response in patients whose tumors are PD-L1 positive (+) and PD-L1 negative (-) at baseline.

II. Determine the baseline mutational load of patients at the start of treatment and relate it to the response to treatment.

III. Determine if hormone receptor status correlates with tumor responses. IV. Determine the number of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes in patient samples at the start and at the end of treatment and relate them to tumor response.

V. Analyze T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire in tumor infiltrating lymphocytes and peripheral blood mononuclear cells.

Participants receive talimogene laherparepvec intratumorally on days 1, 22, and 36, nivolumab intravenously (IV) over 60 minutes on days 1, 15, 29, and 43, and ipilimumab IV over 90 minutes on days 1 and 43 in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

Here is what I independently know about this trial and the agents involved, based on my training knowledge. Where I am uncertain, I say so explicitly.

## Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC, brand name Imlygic)

- **Mechanism of action**: T-VEC is an oncolytic immunotherapy derived from a modified herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). It is attenuated by deletion of the HSV-1 ICP34.5 gene (which confers tumor-selective replication) and the ICP47 gene (which normally blocks antigen presentation). It also expresses human granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), which recruits and activates dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells. - **Regulatory status**: T-VEC was approved by the FDA in October 2015 for the treatment of unresectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, and nodal lesions in patients with melanoma recurrent after initial surgery. - **Key earlier studies**: The pivotal study was a phase III randomized trial in unresectable stage IIIB–IV melanoma (Andtbacka et al., J Clin Oncol 2015), which showed a durable response rate of ~16% vs ~2% for GM-CSF, though it did not meet its primary endpoint of overall survival benefit in the overall population. **RISK: Safety / toxicity from the triple combination (T-VEC + nivolumab + ipilimumab)**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE**: This is a first-in-class-style combination of three immunostimulatory agents, including ipilimumab, which carries well-documented immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, hypophysitis, rash, etc.), and T-VEC, a live replicating HSV-1 with its own risks (herpetic lesions, systemic viral spread concerns, contraindications in immunosuppressed patients). Stacking an oncolytic virus with dual checkpoint blockade plausibly increases both the frequency and severity of immune-related toxicities. In a 6-patient sample, even 1–2 serious AEs could halt the study or prevent dose escalation/recommended-phase-2-dose determination. This is the registered **primary** endpoint, so toxicity is the central determinant of the trial's stated success.
- **LIKELIHOOD**: HIGH

---

**RISK: Efficacy / lack of measurable signal (futility)**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE**: The trial is a tiny, non-randomized, single-arm pilot in **localized, resectable** disease — the least favorable setting in which to detect an efficacy signal, since patients will go on to surgery regardless. The secondary "tumor response compared to no treatment" comparison has no randomized control, so any observed change is hard to attribute to the intervention. T-VEC is **not approved in breast cancer**, and while T-VEC + checkpoint inhibition has shown signal in melanoma, that does not reliably translate to breast cancer. Beyond safety, there is a real possibility the immunologic/pathologic changes are too modest or too variable (n=6) to support further development.
- **LIKELIHOOD**: MEDIUM

---

**RISK: Regulatory / manufacturing / logistics burden of the oncolytic virus**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE**: T-VEC is a live, replicating biologic requiring specialized handling, storage, intratumoral administration, and infection-control precautions for staff and patients; the protocol imposes extensive herpetic-infection and live-vaccine exclusions reflecting these constraints. Additionally, any future registrational path for a T-VEC–based regimen in breast cancer would face substantial regulatory and manufacturing hurdles, since the agent is not approved in this indication.

**RISK: Competitive landscape / changing standard of care in early TNBC**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE**: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has already moved into standard practice for high-risk early TNBC — most notably pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy (KEYNOTE-522), which is FDA-approved in this setting. That means the clinical question this trial poses (can an immunotherapy regimen help in localized TNBC?) is being answered by larger, randomized, chemo-backbone trials, potentially making this chemo-free, triple-agent approach less relevant or harder to position. Conversely, the trial deliberately **excludes** patients for whom neoadjuvant chemotherapy is indicated, which limits its population to a lower-risk subset where a novel intensive immunotherapy regimen may be harder to justify.

Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
Lead sponsor: Institut de Recherches Internationales Servier
Enrollment: 211
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=7 Years; maximum age=17 Years

Brief summary:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and the safety of bumetanide/S95008 in the improvement of Autism Spectrum Disorder core symptoms. Based on emerging pharmacokinetic data suggesting rapid target engagement, the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol.

Detailed description:
The present study (CL3-95008-001) was performed in children and adolescents from 7 to less than 18 years old presenting with ASD. A 6-month double-blind treatment period was performed in which efficacy and safety of bumetanide 0.5mg BID were assessed versus placebo. This double-blind period was followed by a 6-month open label treatment period of bumetanide 0.5mg BID in which long term safety was evaluated.

  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: 

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Bumetanide Oral Solution: Oral Solution dosed at 0.5mg/mL Taken twice daily
  - [DRUG] Placebo: Oral Solution Taken twice daily

Primary outcomes:
  - Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2) total raw score [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition (SRS-2) total raw score [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]
  - Clinical Global Impression - Global Improvement (CGI-I) score [time frame: At 6 months]
  - Vineland Adaptative Behaviour Sales, Second Edition (VABS II) subscores [time frame: Change from baseline to 6 month]
  - Adverse events and Paediatric Adverse Event Rating Scale (PAERS) [time frame: On average of 52 weeks]

  - the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale Children's version (C-SSRS-C) [time frame: Week000/Week012/Week026/Week038/Week052]
  - Tanner stage [time frame: Week000/Week026/Week052]
  - Acceptability and palatability questionnaire [time frame: Week026]
  - Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) questionnaire [time frame: Week000/Week004/Week012/Week026/Week030/Week038/Week052]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Male and female patients from 7 to less than 18 years
* Out patients
* Primary diagnosis of ASD as per Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders - Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria
* Criteria met for ASD on Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2) and Autism Diagnosis Interview Revised (ADI-R)
* CGI (Clinical Global Impression) - Severity rating Score ≥ 4
* Childhood Autism Rating Scale second edition (CARS2-ST or HF) total raw score ≥ 34
* Social responsiveness Scale second edition total score (SRS-2 T-Score) ≥ 66
* Absence of known monogenic syndrome (Fragile X, Rett syndrome ...)
* Absence of any clinically significant abnormality likely to interfere with the conduct of the study according to the judgment of the investigator

Exclusion Criteria:

* Patients not able to follow the study assessments defined by the protocol, with the exception of self-rating questionnaires which will be assessed by parent/legal representative/caregiver for those patients unable to complete them
* Patients having a high suicidal risk according to the investigator judgement
* Chronic renal dysfunction
* Chronic cardiac dysfunction
* Patient with unstable psychotherapy, behavioural, cognitive or cognitive-behavioural therapy
* Severe electrolyte imbalance that is likely to interfere with the study conduct or evaluation

**1. Likely primary endpoint and how it would be measured**

- **Primary endpoint:** Change in **Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2) total raw score** from baseline to the primary time point (registered as 6 months; note the brief summary says the treatment period was shortened by 50%, so the actual primary time point may be shorter — **unknown** which one was used in the final analysis).
- **Measurement:** CARS2 is a clinician-rated instrument. Total raw score is a sum across items, with higher scores indicating more severe autism symptomatology. The endpoint is the **change from baseline** (i.e., baseline minus post-baseline, or the modeled difference in change between arms).
- **Direction of benefit:** A **greater reduction** in CARS2 total raw score in the bumetanide arm versus placebo would indicate benefit.
- **Note:** CARS2 has no universally agreed minimal clinically important difference; what counts as a clinically meaningful change is a matter of interpretation and would typically be pre-specified. **Unknown** whether a specific MCID was pre-specified.

**2. Statistical threshold**

- **Conventional threshold:** Almost certainly a two-sided **p < 0.05** for the primary comparison, which is standard for a Phase 3 superiority trial. I cannot confirm this from the registration — **unknown** as a certainty, but p < 0.05 is the near-universal default.
- **Effect estimate:** The reportable result would be a between-group difference in mean change in CARS2 total raw score with a 95% confidence interval. Statistical significance requires the CI to exclude 0 (for a difference) in the favorable direction, corresponding to the p-value threshold.
- **Multiplicity / hierarchical testing:** The trial lists several secondary endpoints (SRS-2, CGI-I, VABS-II, etc.). A rigorous design would use a hierarchical or alpha-controlled testing procedure to protect the type I error rate. **Unknown** whether such a procedure was pre-specified.
- **No hazard ratio or non-inferiority margin** applies here, because this is not a time-to-event or non-inferiority design (see below).

**3. Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence**

- This is a **superiority trial**. The stated purpose is to evaluate **efficacy** of bumetanide versus placebo in improving ASD core symptoms — i.e., to show bumetanide is **better** than placebo, not merely equivalent or non-inferior.
- The presence of a placebo comparator and the framing around "improvement" confirm a superiority hypothesis.

**4. Key design features**

- **Allocation:** **Randomized** (registered as allocation=RANDOMIZED).
- **Intervention model:** **Parallel group** (registered as PARALLEL) — participants receive either bumetanide or placebo, not both.
- **Masking:** **Quadruple** (registered as QUADRUPLE) — this generally means participant, care provider, investigator, and outcomes assessor are all blinded. For a pediatric ASD trial this is important because of the risk of unblinding from diuretic side effects.
- **Control arm:** **Placebo comparator** (oral solution, twice daily), matching the active arm's dosing schedule and formulation appearance.
- **Active arm:** Bumetanide oral solution 0.5 mg/mL, 0.5 mg BID.

A successful outcome would be a **statistically significant (p < 0.05, two-sided), favorable between-group difference in change from baseline in CARS2 total raw score** at the primary time point, with bumetanide showing greater reduction than placebo, ideally corroborated by consistent direction of effect on key secondary measures (SRS-2, CGI-I) under a multiplicity-controlled testing strategy, in a randomized, quadruple-blinded, placebo-controlled, parallel-group design.

RISK: Weak and non-independent efficacy evidence base, with a subjective primary endpoint prone to placebo response
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The bumetanide-in-ASD rationale rests mainly on small, largely single-group trials (notably Lemonnier 2012, n≈60), and no drug has ever been approved for ASD core symptoms. The primary endpoint here — change in CARS2 total raw score — is a clinician/parent-influenced subjective measure with a well-documented, high placebo response in pediatric ASD trials. Large, better-controlled Phase 3 trials in this space (e.g., arbaclofen) have repeatedly failed to replicate small positive Phase 2 signals. This is the single most likely reason a well-powered Phase 3 would miss its primary endpoint.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Functional unblinding due to diuretic side effects
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that reliably causes increased urination, and possibly dehydration or electrolyte effects, that are perceptible to families and possibly to raters. Even though the trial is quadruple-masked with a matching placebo oral solution, participants and caregivers may infer assignment, which can inflate apparent efficacy on subjective outcomes (CARS2, SRS-2, CGI-I). This is a specific, drug-class-driven threat to this trial's internal validity, not a generic one.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Safety and tolerability signal (diuresis, electrolyte/renal effects) in a pediatric population, prompting dropout or regulatory concern
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Bumetanide's known pharmacology includes hypokalemia, hyponatremia, dehydration, and renal effects. The protocol explicitly excludes chronic renal dysfunction, chronic cardiac dysfunction, and severe electrolyte imbalance — signaling the sponsor's awareness of these concerns. In children, tolerability problems can drive differential dropout, and any imbalance in serious adverse events could undermine a favorable benefit-risk assessment with regulators even if efficacy is shown. The registered secondary outcomes (renal ultrasound, ECG, Tanner stage, C-SSRS) reflect this safety scrutiny.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Design/protocol changes undermining statistical power or interpretability
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The brief summary states the treatment period was "shortened by 50% from the original protocol," while the detailed description still describes a 6-month double-blind period — an internal inconsistency in the public record. Sample size was fixed at 211 with no publicly stated re-estimation.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Enrollment/retention and competitive/regulatory landscape challenges

Retention can also be affected by diuretic inconvenience. Additionally, the competitive and regulatory environment for ASD is unfavorable for sponsors: no approved core-symptom therapies, high regulatory hurdle for a repurposed generic-class drug, and multiple prior failures, which raises the bar for what regulators will accept.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

Detailed description:
Background and Rationale:

Epacadostat (INCB024360) is an Inhibitor of Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) is a 403 amino acid cytosolic haem enzyme encoded by the INDO gene on human chromosome 8p22. IDO1 is responsible for the catabolism of the essential amino acid tryptophan (trp) to kynurenine (kyn) within immune cells and a subset of tumor cells resulting in inhibition of antitumor cell-mediated immune responses. Increased IDO activity correlates with lower CR rates and shorter OS in AML.

Objective:

The primary objective is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive Treatment.

Study Duration:

Phase I part will last from 3 to 18 months (permitting the enrolment of minimum of 3 and a maximum of 18 patients).

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Dosis finding: Epacadostat is given for 2 cycles of 28 days at a dose according to the titration design together with Standard chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Epacadostat: Epacadostat orally two times daily (BID) for two cycles (28 days each) in combination with standard induction chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)
  - [DRUG] Idarubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-d3 cycle 1
  - [DRUG] Cytarabine: Standard chemotherapy d1-d7 cycle 1 and 2
  - [DRUG] Daunorubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-3 cycle 2

Primary outcomes:
  - Phase 1: Dose finding [time frame: 30 days]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Rate of morphologic complete remission (CR) [time frame: 60 days]
  - Adverse events [time frame: 90 days]
  - Overall survival [time frame: 12 months]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* AML (according to the 2016 World Health Organization (WHO) classification definition of ≥ 20% blasts; Arber et al, 2016) suitable for intensive treatment (including stem cell transplantation) with a curative intent.
* Patients must be aged \> 18 years, and must have given voluntary written informed consent.
* Women of childbearing potential having a negative serum pregnancy test at screening or at least within 48 hours before start with epacadostat, and willing to use an effective contraceptive method (intrauterine devices, hormonal contraceptives, contraceptive pill, implants, transdermal patches, hormonal vaginal devices, infusions with prolonged release) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration
* Men willing to use an effective contraceptive method (eg, condom, vasectomy) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Prior or concurrent malignancy, except for the following: adequately treated basal cell or squamous cell skin cancer, or any other cancer from which the subject has been disease-free for more than 6 months.
* Any previous AML or MDS chemotherapy (with the exception of hydroxyurea/Litalir® for leukocyte control which should be discontinued by the first day of induction chemotherapy
* Treatment with any investigational product within 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)
* Abnormal organ function if not caused by the underlying disease as considered by the treating physician
* Use of immune-suppressive agents for the past 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360). For regular use of systemic corticosteroids, subjects may only be included after stepwise discontinuation to be free of steroids for a minimum of 5 days before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE1
Conditions: AML
Lead sponsor: Insel Gruppe AG, University Hospital Bern
Enrollment: 0
Design: allocation=NA; intervention model=SINGLE_GROUP; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=not specified

Brief summary:
This trial assess the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive treatment Based on emerging pharmacokinetic data suggesting rapid target engagement, the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol.

Detailed description:
Background and Rationale:

Epacadostat (INCB024360) is an Inhibitor of Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) is a 403 amino acid cytosolic haem enzyme encoded by the INDO gene on human chromosome 8p22. IDO1 is responsible for the catabolism of the essential amino acid tryptophan (trp) to kynurenine (kyn) within immune cells and a subset of tumor cells resulting in inhibition of antitumor cell-mediated immune responses. Increased IDO activity correlates with lower CR rates and shorter OS in AML.

Objective:

The primary objective is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive Treatment.

Study Duration:

Phase I part will last from 3 to 18 months (permitting the enrolment of minimum of 3 and a maximum of 18 patients).

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Dosis finding: Epacadostat is given for 2 cycles of 28 days at a dose according to the titration design together with Standard chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Epacadostat: Epacadostat orally two times daily (BID) for two cycles (28 days each) in combination with standard induction chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)
  - [DRUG] Idarubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-d3 cycle 1
  - [DRUG] Cytarabine: Standard chemotherapy d1-d7 cycle 1 and 2
  - [DRUG] Daunorubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-3 cycle 2

Primary outcomes:
  - Phase 1: Dose finding [time frame: 30 days]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Rate of morphologic complete remission (CR) [time frame: 60 days]
  - Adverse events [time frame: 90 days]
  - Overall survival [time frame: 12 months]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* AML (according to the 2016 World Health Organization (WHO) classification definition of ≥ 20% blasts; Arber et al, 2016) suitable for intensive treatment (including stem cell transplantation) with a curative intent.
* Patients must be aged \> 18 years, and must have given voluntary written informed consent.
* Women of childbearing potential having a negative serum pregnancy test at screening or at least within 48 hours before start with epacadostat, and willing to use an effective contraceptive method (intrauterine devices, hormonal contraceptives, contraceptive pill, implants, transdermal patches, hormonal vaginal devices, infusions with prolonged release) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration
* Men willing to use an effective contraceptive method (eg, condom, vasectomy) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Prior or concurrent malignancy, except for the following: adequately treated basal cell or squamous cell skin cancer, or any other cancer from which the subject has been disease-free for more than 6 months.
* Any previous AML or MDS chemotherapy (with the exception of hydroxyurea/Litalir® for leukocyte control which should be discontinued by the first day of induction chemotherapy
* Treatment with any investigational product within 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)
* Abnormal organ function if not caused by the underlying disease as considered by the treating physician
* Use of immune-suppressive agents for the past 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360). For regular use of systemic corticosteroids, subjects may only be included after stepwise discontinuation to be free of steroids for a minimum of 5 days before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)

Here is what I independently know about this trial and drug, with uncertainties marked:

**Epacadostat (INCB024360) — mechanism of action**
Epacadostat is an oral, potent, and selective inhibitor of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1), a heme-containing enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting step in tryptophan catabolism along the kynurenine pathway. IDO1 is expressed by tumor cells, dendritic cells, and other immune cells; its activity depletes tryptophan and produces kynurenine metabolites that suppress effector T-cell function and promote regulatory T-cell (Treg) differentiation, thereby contributing to tumor immune evasion. Epacadostat was developed by Incyte Corporation as an immune checkpoint–modulating agent intended to be combined with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (notably pembrolizumab). The mechanism described in your trial summary is consistent with this.

**Sponsor track record**
- **Insel Gruppe AG / University Hospital Bern** is a Swiss academic medical center and a legitimate clinical trial sponsor, particularly for investigator-initiated hematology/oncology trials. Their specific track record in AML trials is **unknown** to me in detail.
- **Incyte Corporation** is the originator/manufacturer of epacadostat. Incyte has a substantial oncology portfolio (e.g., ruxolitinib/Jakafi, pemigatinib). Epacadostat specifically became a high-profile failure after the Phase 3 ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252 trial.

**Earlier studies and key results**
- **Phase 1/2 (ECHO-202/KEYNOTE-037):** Epacadostat plus pembrolizumab showed promising early response rates in melanoma and other solid tumors, which drove enthusiasm.
- **Phase 3 ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252 (melanoma, 2018):** Epacadostat + pembrolizumab vs. pembrolizumab + placebo failed to improve progression-free survival; this was the pivotal negative result that halted most of the epacadostat development program.
- **In AML specifically:** I recall that epacadostat was investigated in AML/myelodysplastic syndromes in early-phase studies, including a Phase 1 study of epacadostat + azacitidine in MDS/AML (study results modest). The specific NCT03444649 combination with idarubicin/cytarabine as first-line induction is something I know of mainly from the registry entry you provided; independent published results from this exact trial are **unknown** to me.
- Overall, epacadostat's clinical development was largely discontinued after the melanoma failure; many combination trials were terminated or stopped enrolling.

**Key dates**
- NCT03444649 registration and start date: **unknown** to me precisely (the registry number suggests registration around early 2018).
- Epacadostat's development timeline: INCB024360 entered clinical trials around 2010–2011; ECHO-301 results reported in 2018.
- Current status of this specific Bern trial (completed/terminated, results posted): **unknown**.

**Important caveats**
- The trial summary you provided states **Enrollment: 0**, which suggests the trial may never have enrolled participants or was withdrawn before starting. This is a notable signal.
- The summary also mentions the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol based on emerging PK data — this is a protocol amendment detail I cannot independently verify.
- Whether epacadostat has any established role in AML induction therapy: **not established** to my knowledge; the field's interest in IDO1 inhibition in AML remains investigational, and the broader epacadostat program did not yield positive confirmatory results.

Based on your knowledge of clinical trials, what is the historical base rate of success for trials like this one?

Consider:
- Phase: PHASE1
- Indication: AML
- Drug class and mechanism (from what you recalled earlier)

BASE_RATE: [a number between 0.0 and 1.0]
REASONING: [one paragraph explaining how you arrived at this estimate]

BASE_RATE: 0.03

REASONING: I am interpreting "success" here as the trial leading to a drug eventually reaching marketing approval for this indication, which is the conventional meaning of a phase-transition success rate. The base rate of approval for a Phase 1 oncology drug is roughly 5–7%. However, several factors push this specific trial below that. First, AML is a particularly difficult indication for novel agents added to intensive induction chemotherapy — the standard of care (anthracycline/cytarabine ± transplant) is already curative in a substantial fraction of fit patients, making incremental benefit hard to demonstrate, and many immune-modulating agents have failed in this space. Second, the drug class is IDO1 inhibition, which has a poor historical record: the flagship epacadostat program suffered a definitive Phase 3 failure (ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252 in melanoma, 2018), and the broader IDO-pathway inhibitor field has not produced an approved agent despite extensive testing. Third, this is an investigator-initiated academic Phase 1 with a registry enrollment of 0, suggesting it may never have meaningfully progressed. Combining the low Phase 1 oncology base rate, the especially failure-prone drug mechanism, and the difficult indication, I estimate the probability of eventual success at roughly 3%. This is a judgment estimate; the precise empirical base rate for this exact drug/indication/phase combination is unknown.

Based on the trial design of NCT03444649, describe what would constitute a successful outcome.

Include:
1. The likely primary endpoint(s) and how they would be measured
2. The statistical threshold that would need to be met (e.g., p<0.05, hazard ratio, non-inferiority margin)
3. Whether this is likely a superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence trial
4. Key design features (randomization, blinding, control arm)

If you are unsure about any detail, say 'unknown'. Do not fabricate.

1. **Likely primary endpoint(s) and measurement**

   The stated primary outcome is **"Phase 1: Dose finding"** with a **30-day time frame**. In a Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of this type, "success" on the primary endpoint is conventionally defined as **identifying the maximum tolerated dose (MTD)** and **characterizing dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs)**. Operationally:
   - DLTs would be graded using **CTCAE** criteria (specific grade thresholds defined in the protocol, which I do not have).
   - The MTD is typically defined as the highest dose level at which **≤ 1 of 6 (or a predefined fraction of) evaluable patients** experience a DLT during the DLT observation window (here 30 days).
   - "Success" is therefore not a comparative efficacy claim but the **feasibility/safety determination of a recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D)**.

2. **Statistical threshold**

   This is a **dose-finding/titration design**, not a hypothesis test. There is typically **no p-value, hazard ratio, or formal statistical significance threshold** for the primary endpoint. The "threshold" is a **decision rule** (e.g., stop escalation if ≥ 2 of 6 patients at a dose level have a DLT; declare MTD otherwise). Formal statistical inference may be applied only to secondary endpoints (e.g., CR rate), but the specific alpha, power, or confidence intervals are **unknown** to me from the provided information.

3. **Superiority / non-inferiority / equivalence**

   This is **none of these** in the classic sense. It is a **single-arm, dose-finding (toxicity-driven) trial** with no comparative hypothesis for the primary endpoint. Any efficacy comparison would be exploratory/descriptive against historical benchmarks (e.g., historical CR rates for intensive induction in AML), not a formal superiority or non-inferiority test. I classify it as **exploratory/descriptive**, not a confirmatory superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence design.

4. **Key design features**

   - **Allocation:** NA (non-randomized)
   - **Intervention model:** SINGLE_GROUP (single-arm)
   - **Masking:** NONE (open-label)
   - **Control arm:** None; all patients receive epacadostat + standard induction chemotherapy (idarubicin/cytarabine in cycle 1; cytarabine/daunorubicin in cycle 2, per the listed interventions)
   - **Dose titration:** Epacadostat given BID for two 28-day cycles at doses determined by a titration/escalation design
   - **Eligibility:** Intensive-treatment-fit AML patients ≥18 years; exclusion of prior AML/MDS chemotherapy (except hydroxyurea), recent investigational products, immunosuppressants, and prior/concurrent malignancy
   - **Secondary endpoints:** morphologic CR rate (60 days), adverse events (90 days), overall survival (12 months)

   **Caveats:** The exact DLT definitions, dose levels, titration algorithm, evaluable-patient rules, and any interim stopping rules are **unknown** to me — these would be in the full protocol. Whether any formal statistical analysis is planned for secondary endpoints is also **unknown**. Given the registry **Enrollment: 0**, it is unclear whether this design was ever actually executed.

What are the key risk factors that could cause this trial to fail?

List 3-5 specific risks, ordered from most to least concerning. For each risk, provide:
- RISK: [name of the risk]
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: [why this risk is relevant to THIS specific trial]
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW

Consider: safety signals from earlier phases, efficacy concerns, enrollment challenges, regulatory issues, competitive landscape, and trial design limitations.

RISK: Efficacy failure of the IDO1-inhibitor mechanism in AML
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Epacadostat's development was effectively ended by the negative Phase 3 ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252 result in melanoma (2018), and no IDO1 inhibitor has since achieved approval in any indication. The rationale for adding IDO1 inhibition to intensive AML induction rests on correlative data (IDO activity associates with lower CR rates and shorter OS) rather than demonstrated clinical benefit. Adding epacadostat to an already effective, potentially curative anthracycline/cytarabine backbone in fit patients leaves little room to show incremental benefit, and immune-modulating agents have repeatedly failed in this exact setting.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Enrollment failure / trial non-viability
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The registry lists Enrollment: 0, which strongly suggests the trial never actually accrued patients (or was withdrawn before starting). This is consistent with the broader collapse of epacadostat development after the melanoma failure, which caused many combination trials to stop enrolling. A single-arm Phase 1 in a narrow population of intensive-treatment-fit AML patients (excluding prior chemotherapy, prior malignancy, recent investigational products, and immunosuppressants) is difficult to fill even under favorable circumstances. If enrollment is 0, the trial cannot generate any usable data.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Safety / tolerability signal from combining epacadostat with intensive chemotherapy
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The trial assesses MTD and DLTs of epacadostat added to idarubicin/cytarabine (and cytarabine/daunorubicin in cycle 2). Intensive AML induction is already highly myelosuppressive and toxic, with substantial rates of febrile neutropenia, mucositis, and organ toxicity. Adding an immune-modulating agent could compound these effects (e.g., immune-related adverse events, infection risk), potentially preventing escalation to a biologically relevant dose. If the MTD turns out to be below the dose needed for target engagement, the combination cannot be taken forward.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Trial design limitations (single-arm, no control, open-label)
APPLIES_BECAUSE: This is a single-group, non-randomized, unmasked dose-finding trial with no comparator. It can determine an MTD/DLT profile but cannot establish efficacy or distinguish drug effect from the standard chemotherapy backbone and from patient selection. Any CR or OS signal is confounded and will not support a regulatory claim; optimism bias and lack of blinding further weaken interpretation. Even if completed successfully, the design limits what conclusions — and what level of investment — can follow.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Regulatory / competitive landscape shifts
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The regulatory and commercial environment for IDO1 inhibitors deteriorated sharply after 2018, with sponsors deprioritizing the class. Simultaneously, the AML therapeutic landscape has been evolving (e.g., approval of venetoclax-based regimens, targeted agents, and refined transplant strategies), changing the standard of care and raising the evidentiary bar for adding a novel agent to intensive induction. A Phase 1 academic trial in a class with a failed flagship program is unlikely to attract the follow-on funding or regulatory interest needed to progress, even if it generates a clean safety dataset.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

**Caveats:** I do not have access to the full protocol, DLT definitions, dose levels, interim rules, or actual accrual/safety data for this specific trial, so likelihoods are judgment estimates based on the trial summary provided and general knowledge of the epacadostat program. The exact reasons for the Enrollment: 0 status are **unknown**.

Based on the trial specification shown at the start, your own knowledge, and the similar trials you listed, make your final prediction:

Format your answer EXACTLY as:
PREDICTION: SUCCESS or FAILURE
CONFIDENCE: a number between 0.0 and 1.0
KEY_REASON: one sentence explaining the most important factor

PREDICTION: FAILURE
CONFIDENCE: 0.97
KEY_REASON: The trial is almost certainly non-viable, as the registry shows Enrollment: 0 and the IDO1-inhibitor class (epacadostat) had already collapsed after the definitive Phase 3 ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252 failure, leaving neither a plausible efficacy rationale nor an executed study to succeed.

data.label: SUCCESS
data.trial_title: Safety and Efficacy of Bexagliflozin in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients With Moderate Renal Impairment
data.primary_endpoint: Change From Baseline in HbA1c at 24 Weeks
data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Lead sponsor: Theracos
Enrollment: 312
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=TRIPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=20 Years; maximum age=not specified

Brief summary:
This was a phase 3, multi-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral administration of bexagliflozin at 20 mg versus placebo in subjects with T2DM, moderate renal impairment and inadequate glycemic control. Based on emerging pharmacokinetic data suggesting rapid target engagement, the treatment period was shortened by 50% from the original protocol.

Detailed description:
The phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel-group study was conducted at investigative sites in the US, Japan, France and Spain. Approximately 300 subjects were to be randomly assigned to receive bexagliflozin tablets, 20 mg, or placebo in equal ratio for 24 weeks.

The study was to enrolled male and female participants who had T2DM with an HbA1c between 7.0 and 10.5% (inclusive) and stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD) as defined by an eGFR of ≥ 30 and\< 60 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2 at the screening visit and one additional time of measurement between 1 and 12 months prior to screening. Subjects were either treatment naïve or were treated with a stable regimen of anti-diabetic medications.

All eligible subjects were to enter a one-week single-blind, placebo run-in period. Subjects who were compliant in taking run-in medication, had screening eGFR ≥ 30 and\< 60 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2, and had stable GFR (no more than 20% change in eGFR between a historical value and the value determined at the screening visit) were eligible for randomization. Randomization was stratified by HbA1c level (7.0 to 8.5% or 8.6 to 10.5%), anti-diabetic treatment regimen and eGFR (30 - 44 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2 or 45 - 59 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2). At least 135 subjects in each of the eGFR groups were planned.

Study subjects were to schedule clinic visits at weeks 2, 6, 12, 18, and 24 for safety and efficacy evaluation. At weeks 2 and 18, the visits were to be conducted via phone interviews unless an in-person visit was considered clinically advisable. A final follow-up visit was to be conducted at week 26 or two weeks after the last dose of investigational product if the subject withdrew prior to week 24.

Arms:
  - [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Bexagliflozin tablets, 20 mg: Each subject will receive a bexagliflozin tablet, 20 mg, once daily for the duration of the study.
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo tablets: Each subject will receive a placebo (inactive) tablet once daily for the duration of the study.

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Bexagliflozin: Bexagliflozin tablet, 20 mg
  - [DRUG] Placebo: Placebo (inactive) tablet to match the active comparator

Primary outcomes:
  - Change From Baseline in HbA1c at 24 Weeks [time frame: 24 weeks]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Change in Body Weight From Baseline to Week 24 in Subjects With a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2 [time frame: 24 weeks]
  - Change From Baseline in Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) in Subjects With Baseline SBP ≥ 130 mm Hg at Week 24 [time frame: 24 weeks]
  - Change From Baseline in HbA1c in Subjects With Stage 3a CKD (eGFR 45 to 59 mL/Min/1.73 m2) at Week 24 [time frame: 24 weeks]
  - Change From Baseline in HbA1c in Subjects With Stage 3b CKD (eGFR 30 to 44 mL/Min/1.73 m2) at Week 24 [time frame: 24 weeks]

Eligibility criteria:
Each subject was required to meet the following criteria at the time of enrollment to be eligible for the study:

1. To have been male or non-pregnant female ≥ 20 years of age. Women of childbearing potential were required to agree to use contraception throughout the study to avoid any possible pregnancy. Females who were surgically sterile (hysterectomy, oophorectomy) or postmenopausal (absence of menses for greater than 12 months and age \> 45 years) were eligible if they tested negative on the urine pregnancy test.
2. To have had a diagnosis of T2DM with an HbA1c between 7.0 and 10.5% (inclusive) at the time of screening.
3. To have been treatment naïve or to have been treated with a stable regimen of anti-diabetic medications. At the time of screening, the doses and frequency of all anti-diabetic medications were to have been stable for 8 weeks.
4. To have had an eGFR ≥ 30 and \< 60 mL min-1 per 1.73 m2 at 2 time points: screening (V1), and 1 additional time point between 1 and 12 months of screening (may be obtained from available medical records). The eGFR was calculated by the MDRD equation.
5. To have had a body mass index (BMI) ≤ 45 kg per m2 (inclusive).
