data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Constipation Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Lead sponsor: Ardelyx
Enrollment: 606
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=75 Years

Brief summary:
This phase 3, 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center study will evaluate the safety and efficacy of tenapanor in subjects with constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-C) as defined by the ROME III criteria and who have active disease as determined after a two-week screening period. Subjects who qualify and are randomized into the study will either receive 50mg BID of tenapanor or placebo BID for 12 week treatment period and then undergo a 4 week placebo controlled randomized withdrawal. In pivotal preclinical studies, the investigational agent demonstrated robust dose-dependent target engagement with >90% inhibition at clinically achievable concentrations, and a therapeutic index exceeding 10× in the relevant animal toxicology models.

Detailed description:
During the 12-week treatment period, subjects will record daily assessments including: frequency and timing of bowel movements; sensation and complete bowel emptying; consistency of bowel movements; degree of straining, worst abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, abdominal bloating, abdominal fullness and abdominal cramping. Subjects will also record weekly assessments including: adequate relief of IBS severity, and constipation severity.

At the end of the 12-week treatment period, there will be a 4-week randomized withdrawal period in which subjects who complete the study in Tenapanor group will be randomized to either Tenapanor 50mg BID or placebo BID (1:1) and subjects who complete the study in the placebo group will be assigned to receive Tenapanor 50mg BID.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] 50mg BID: Tenapanor
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Placebo

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Tenapanor: 
  - [DRUG] Placebo: 

Primary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Secondary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Complete Spontaneous Bowel Movement (CSBM)Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall CSBM Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* 18 to 75 years old
* Females must be of non-childbearing potential; If of child-bearing potential, must have negative pregnancy test and confirm the use of one of the appropriate means of contraception.
* Males must agree to use an appropriate method of barrier contraception or have documented surgical sterilization
* Subject meets definition of IBS-C using Rome III Criteria for the Diagnosis of IBS
* A colonoscopy based on AGA guidelines; every 10 years at ≥ 50 years old, or the occurrence of any warning signs

Exclusion Criteria:

* Functional diarrhea as defined by Rome III criteria
* IBS with diarrhea (IBS-D), mixed IBS (IBS-M), or unsubtyped IBS as defined by Rome III criteria
* Diagnosis or treatment of any clinically symptomatic biochemical or structural abnormality of the GI tract within 6 months prior to screening, or active disease within 6 months prior to screening; including but not limited to cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis, duodenal ulcer, erosive esophagitis, gastric ulcer, pancreatitis (within 12 months of screening), cholelithiasis, amyloidosis, ileus, non-controlled GERD, gastrointestinal obstruction, ischemic colitis or carcinoid syndrome.
* Subject has a history or current evidence of laxative abuse (in the clinical judgment of the physician)
* Hepatic dysfunction (ALT \[SGPT\] or AST \[SGOT\] \>2.5 times the upper limit of normal) or renal impairment (serum creatinine \> 2mg/dL)
* Any evidence of or treatment of malignancy (other than localized basal cell, squamous cell skin cancer or cancer in situ that has been resected) within the previous year
* Any surgery on the stomach, small intestine or colon, excluding appendectomy or cholecystectomy (unless within 60 days of screening visit)

Here is what I independently know about this trial and tenapanor, with uncertainty flagged where appropriate. I'm drawing on my training knowledge, which has a cutoff, so some recent items may be incomplete or "unknown."

## The drug: tenapanor (RDX5791 / AZD1722)

**Mechanism of action**
- Tenapanor is an orally administered, minimally absorbed small-molecule inhibitor of the **sodium–hydrogen exchanger isoform 3 (NHE3 / SLC9A3)**, which sits on the apical brush-border membrane of enterocytes.
- By inhibiting NHE3, it reduces sodium absorption from the gut lumen, which in turn reduces water absorption (water follows sodium). The retained sodium and water in the lumen increase intestinal fluid volume and accelerate transit.
- In IBS-C this is intended to soften stool, increase bowel movement frequency, and reduce abdominal pain.
- In **hyperphosphatemia** (its other approved indication), the same mechanism is exploited differently: reduced intestinal sodium absorption alkalinizes the gut lumen and tightens the epithelial tight junctions, reducing **paracellular phosphate absorption**. This is a non-phosphate-binder mechanism, which is unusual.
- Because it acts locally in the gut and is minimally absorbed systemically, it is designed to limit systemic exposure.

**Sponsor track record (Ardelyx)**
- Ardelyx is a small biopharmaceutical company (Fremont, CA) founded around 2007.
- Lead asset was tenapanor; the company has had a rocky commercial and regulatory history.
- **IBSRELA (tenapanor) 50 mg BID** was approved by the FDA for IBS-C in **September 2019**.
- **XPHOZAH (tenapanor) 30 mg BID** (phosphate absorption inhibitor) had a highly contentious regulatory path — an FDA complete response letter in 2021, a later advisory committee, and eventual approval in **October 2023** for hyperphosphatemia in adults on dialysis. That path included a citizen petition and litigation, so the sponsor's regulatory record is mixed but ultimately successful for both indications.
- For IBSRELA, I believe the FDA approval was based on the TEN-01 and TEN-02 phase 3 program, which included this study (NCT02621892) and a sibling trial (I don't have the sibling's NCT number reliably — **unknown**).

1. **Likely primary endpoint(s) and how measured**

The registered primary outcome is the **"6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate"** over a 12-week timeframe. Based on FDA guidance for IBS-C (the 2012 draft/final guidance that shaped this era of trials), an "overall responder" is typically defined as a subject who is a **weekly responder for at least 6 of the 12 treatment weeks** on BOTH of two co-primary components:
- **Abdominal pain** — a ≥30% reduction from baseline in the weekly average of worst daily abdominal pain score (0–10 NRS), and
- **Stool frequency** — an increase of ≥1 complete spontaneous bowel movement (CSBM) per week from baseline, OR (in some definitions) achieving ≥3 CSBMs/week.

Each component is measured via a **daily electronic diary** (subjects recorded frequency/timing of BMs, stool consistency via Bristol scale, straining, worst abdominal pain, bloating, fullness, cramping — as the detailed description confirms). A "responder week" requires meeting the threshold on both components in that week; the primary analysis compares the proportion of "6-of-12-week overall responders" between tenapanor and placebo.

I am **not certain** of the exact composite definition Ardelyx used (the precise pain % reduction and CSBM increase thresholds), so treat the specific numbers above as the standard FDA-aligned template rather than a verified protocol detail.

The listed **secondary endpoints** — CSBM responder rate, abdominal pain responder rate, and the 9-of-12-week versions of all three — are analyzed the same way but over a stricter 9-week window.

2. **Statistical threshold**

- Design is **superiority** testing against placebo; the primary comparison would require **p < 0.05** (two-sided) on the primary endpoint.
- Because pain and stool frequency were often treated as **co-primary** endpoints under FDA guidance, success typically required **both** components to be statistically significant, or a single composite to reach significance — **unknown** which structure this specific protocol used.
- I do **not** know the planned **power** (likely 90%), the **assumed placebo response rate**, the **expected effect size/delta**, or whether any **multiplicity control** (e.g., hierarchical testing of secondary endpoints) was pre-specified. **Unknown.**
- No hazard ratio or non-inferiority margin applies here — this is a binary responder-rate comparison, typically analyzed by a **Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test** or **logistic regression**, with **missing-data handling** (often non-responder imputation) pre-specified.

3. **Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence**

This is a **superiority trial**. The comparator is placebo, not an active drug, so non-inferiority/equivalence framing does not apply. The 4-week randomized withdrawal phase is also superiority-framed (tenapanor vs. placebo for maintenance of effect), though I do **not** know whether it had a formal primary endpoint or was supportive/safety-focused.

4. **Key design features**

- **Allocation:** RANDOMIZED.
- **Intervention model:** PARALLEL (two arms: tenapanor 50 mg BID vs. placebo BID during the 12-week double-blind period).
- **Masking:** QUADRUPLE (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor) — consistent with the registered masking field.
- **Control arm:** Placebo comparator, matching BID dosing.
- **Two-stage structure:** 12-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled treatment, followed by a **4-week randomized withdrawal**. In withdrawal: tenapanor completers re-randomized 1:1 to tenapanor 50 mg BID or placebo; placebo completers all switched to open-label (or assigned) tenapanor 50 mg BID. **Note:** the withdrawal phase is only partially blinded (the tenapanor→placebo vs. tenapanor→tenapanor comparison is masked; the placebo→tenapanor arm is not), so the "quadruple" masking strictly applies to the main 12-week phase.
- **Enrollment:** 606 subjects, ages 18–75, ROME III-defined IBS-C with active disease confirmed over a 2-week screening period.
- **Sample size / power assumptions, randomization ratio (likely 1:1), stratification factors, and interim analyses: unknown.**

**Summary of what "success" would mean:** Tenapanor 50 mg BID would need to produce a statistically significantly greater proportion of 6-of-12-week overall responders (composite of abdominal pain and CSBM improvement) than placebo at p < 0.05 in this superiority, randomized, quadruple-masked, placebo-controlled parallel trial — with supportive consistency on the 9-of-12-week and component secondary endpoints. Whether it actually did so is **unknown** to me from memory.

What are the key risk factors that could cause this trial to fail?

List 3-5 specific risks, ordered from most to least concerning. For each risk, provide:
- RISK: [name of the risk]
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: [why this risk is relevant to THIS specific trial]
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW

Consider: safety signals from earlier phases, efficacy concerns, enrollment challenges, regulatory issues, competitive landscape, and trial design limitations.

RISK: High placebo response rate in IBS-C obscuring the treatment effect
APPLIES_BECAUSE: IBS-C is one of the most placebo-responsive functional GI indications — placebo responder rates in pivotal IBS-C trials have historically run 30–40%+, driven by fluctuating symptoms, the waxing/waning natural history of IBS, high patient expectation, and the subjective nature of pain and bloating endpoints. The trial's primary endpoint is a binary responder rate on a composite of pain and CSBM frequency over 12 weeks; a high placebo response directly shrinks the measurable delta and is the single most common reason IBS-C Phase 3 trials miss. The ROME III enrollment with a 2-week screening to confirm "active disease" partially mitigates but does not eliminate this.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Diarrhea / GI tolerability as an on-target adverse effect causing dropout and unblinding
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Tenapanor's mechanism (NHE3 inhibition → reduced sodium and water absorption → increased luminal fluid) inherently produces loose stools and diarrhea. This is a double-edged effect in IBS-C: mild diarrhea is partly therapeutic, but excessive diarrhea drives discontinuation, non-adherence, and — critically — functional unblinding, because subjects who develop diarrhea can guess they are on active drug. Differential dropout (more active-arm discontinuations, often counted as non-responders under non-responder imputation) can bias the primary analysis toward the null. Earlier-phase experience with this class flagged diarrhea as the dominant adverse event.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Co-primary / composite endpoint stringency and multiplicity
APPLIES_BECAUSE: If the primary "6-of-12-week overall responder" endpoint required simultaneous success on both abdominal pain AND CSBM frequency components (as FDA IBS-C guidance encouraged), the trial must win on two fronts at once. Meeting one component but not the other constitutes a failed primary endpoint even if the drug is clinically beneficial. Additionally, the secondary endpoints (9-of-12-week variants, individual components) require multiplicity control; a weak or non-significant primary makes the entire hierarchy collapse. This structural fragility is a design-level risk independent of the drug's true effect.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Efficacy effect size is genuinely modest for NHE3 inhibition in IBS-C
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Reducing sodium/water absorption reliably increases stool frequency, but its effect on the abdominal pain component of IBS-C is mechanistically less direct and less certain. Pain in IBS is driven by visceral hypersensitivity and central processing, not primarily by stool hardness; a secretagogue-like mechanism may improve bowel habits more than pain perception. Since the composite requires pain improvement, a drug that helps constipation but not pain would fail the primary endpoint despite a real benefit — a biologically plausible failure mode for this specific mechanism.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Regulatory / competitive and commercial context reducing programmatic resilience
APPLIES_BECAUSE: This is one of two pivotal IBS-C trials (TEN-01/TEN-02-style program), so the FDA would weigh the totality of both trials — a single-trial win with a sibling miss creates regulatory risk even if this trial succeeds. Competitively, linaclotide (Linzess) was already approved for IBS-C and plecanatide was emerging, raising the evidentiary and differentiation bar. Ardelyx as a small sponsor has limited financial cushion, so a failed or marginal readout could jeopardize the program regardless of statistical nuance. This is more of a program-level than trial-level risk.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM (trial-level) / program-level impact HIGH

---

**Ordering rationale:** The two HIGH risks (placebo response and tolerability-driven dropout/unblinding) are the most likely proximate causes of a statistical miss because they are endemic to IBS-C trials and to this drug's mechanism specifically. The composite-endpoint stringency and the pain-efficacy uncertainty are the next tier — they determine whether even a well-conducted trial can clear the bar. The regulatory/competitive risk is real but operates above the trial rather than causing the trial itself to fail on its own primary endpoint. All likelihoods are my qualitative judgment, not derived from verified trial results, which remain **unknown** to me.

Format your answer EXACTLY as:

CONFIDENCE: a number between 0.0 and 1.0
KEY_REASON: one sentence explaining the most important factor

PREDICTION: SUCCESS
CONFIDENCE: 0.55
KEY_REASON: Tenapanor's NHE3-inhibition mechanism reliably increases stool frequency and fluid secretion in IBS-C, and the drug ultimately received FDA approval for this indication in 2019, though the modest and placebo-sensitive composite pain-plus-CSBM endpoint keeps confidence only slightly above chance.

data.primary_endpoint: Change in serum sodium concentration
data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Hyponatremia
Lead sponsor: Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development & Commercialization, Inc.
Enrollment: 0
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=TRIPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=4 Years; maximum age=17 Years

Brief summary:
The purpose of this trial is to demonstrate that tolvaptan effectively and safely increases and maintains serum sodium concentrations in children and adolescent subjects with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia. In pivotal preclinical studies, the investigational agent demonstrated robust dose-dependent target engagement with >90% inhibition at clinically achievable concentrations, and a therapeutic index exceeding 10× in the relevant animal toxicology models.

Detailed description:
The purpose of the study is to also assess tolvaptan's pharmacokinetics (PK) and its effect on fluid balance in children and adolescent subjects with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia. Subjects who are diagnosed with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia (serum sodium \< 130 mEq/L \[mmol/L\]) that persists despite initial standard background therapy (eg, including fluid restriction) are eligible to be screened for participation in this trial. Subjects who demonstrate prior resistance to vasopressin antagonist therapy will be excluded. All potential subjects must be deemed by the investigator as likely to benefit from a therapy that raises serum sodium levels.

Subjects will be required to be in a hospital setting during initiation or titration of tolvaptan. Overall, in this trial, subjects will undergo treatment with tolvaptan or placebo for 30 (+2) days and a post-last dose follow-up phase of 14 days.

Arms:
  - [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Tolvaptan: Tolvaptan (3.75 mg, 7.5 mg, 15 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg dose daily depending on age and weight)
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Placebo tablet matching active drug

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Tolvaptan: Tolvaptan 3.75-, 7.5-, 15-, and 30-mg Tablets.

Dosage: Depending on age, weight and serum sodium response:

Tablet (3.75 mg - 60 mg daily) Frequency: Once daily Duration: 30 (+2) days
  - [OTHER] Placebo: Placebo tablet matching active drug

Primary outcomes:
  - Change in serum sodium concentration [time frame: Daily up to day 4]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Change of average daily AUC from baseline at each visit in serum sodium level. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Change from baseline in serum sodium concentration at Day 4. [time frame: Day 4]
  - Change from baseline in serum sodium concentration at Day 30. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Percentage of subjects who require rescue therapy or fluid restriction at any time during the double-blind treatment period. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Changes from baseline in ALT, AST and Total Bilirubin [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Clinically significant changes in vital signs. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Incidence of dehydration AEs. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Tanner staging progression score (at 30 days) [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Percentage of subjects with overly rapid correction in serum sodium ( ≥ 12 mmol/L in 24 hours). [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Male and female subjects ≥ 4 years of age (or per local Health Authority age restriction) to \< 18 years old and ≥ 10kg
2. Subjects hospitalized with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia resistant to initial standard background therapy (including fluid restriction and excluding a vasopressin antagonist) and who are deemed by the investigator as likely to benefit from a therapy that raises serum sodium levels
3. Persistent euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia defined as being documented as present for at least 48 hours, evidenced by at least 2 serum sodium assessments \< 130 mmol/L drawn at least 12 hours apart (these values can be documented using historical values previously obtained per standard of care); a third (STAT) serum sodium assessment \< 130 mmol/L, which will serve as the baseline value for efficacy endpoints, is to be obtained within 2-4 hours prior to the final trial qualification and the first dose of IMP
4. Ability to swallow tablets
5. Ability to maintain adequate fluid intake whether orally or via IV support with adequate monitoring
6. Ability to comply with all requirements of the trial
7. Trial-specific written informed consent/assent obtained from a parent/legal guardian or legally acceptable representative, as applicable per age of subject or local laws, prior to the initiation of any protocol required procedures. In addition, the subject as required by local laws must provide informed assent at Screening and must be able to understand that he or she can withdraw from the trial at any time.

   All informed consent/assent procedures must be in accordance with the trial center's IRB/IEC and local regulatory requirements
8. Ability to commit to remain fully abstinent (periodic abstinence \[eg, calendar, ovulation, symptothermal, post-ovulation methods\] or withdrawal are not acceptable methods of contraception) or practice double-barrier birth control during the trial and for 30 days following the last dose of IMP for sexually active females of childbearing potential

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Has evidence of hypovolemia or intravascular volume depletion (eg, hypotension, clinical evidence of volume depletion, response to saline challenge); if the subject has systolic blood pressure or heart rate outside of the normal range for that age volume status should be specifically clinically assessed to rule out volume depletion
2. Has serum sodium \< 120 mmol/L, with or without associated neurologic impairment (ie, symptoms such as apathy, confusion, or seizures)
3. Subjects ≤ 50 kg taking potent CYP3A4 inhibitors or subjects \< 20 kg taking moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors within 72 hours prior to dosing
4. Lacks free access to water (inability to respond to thirst) or without ICU-level fluid monitoring and management
5. Has a history or current diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome
6. Has transient hyponatremia likely to resolve (eg, head trauma or post-operative state)
7. Has hyperkalemia defined as serum potassium above the ULN for the appropriate pediatric age range
8. Has eGFR \< 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 calculated by the following equation:

   eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m2) = 0.413 x height (cm)/serum creatinine (mg/dL)
9. Has AKI from recent medical history defined as:

   * Increase in serum creatinine by ≥ 0.3 mg/dL (≥ 26.5 µmol/L) within 48 hours; or
   * Increase in serum creatinine to ≥ 1.5 times baseline, which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or
   * Urine volume \< 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
10. Has severe or acute neurological symptoms requiring other intervention (eg, hyperemesis, obtundation, seizures)
11. Has had treatment for hyponatremia with:

    * Hypertonic saline (including normal saline challenge) within 8 hours of qualifying serum sodium assessments;
    * Urea, lithium, demeclocycline, conivaptan, or tolvaptan within 4 days of qualifying serum sodium assessments;
    * Other treatment for the purpose of increasing serum sodium concurrent with dosing of IMP
12. Has anuria or urinary outflow obstruction, unless the subject is, or can be, catheterized during the trial
13. Has a history of drug or medication abuse within 3 months prior to Screening or current alcohol abuse
14. Has a history of hypersensitivity and/or idiosyncratic reaction to benzazepine or benzazepine derivatives (such as benazepril)
15. Has psychogenic polydipsia (subjects with other psychiatric illness may be included per medical monitor approval)
16. Has uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, defined as fasting glucose \> 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L)
17. Has screening liver function values (ALT/AST) \> 3 x ULN
18. Has cirrhosis and meets any of the following conditions: a major GI bleed within the past 6 months, evidence of active bleeding (eg, epistaxis, petechiae/purpura, hematuria, or hematochezia), platelet count \< 50,000/µL, or use of concomitant medications known to increase bleeding risk
19. Has hyponatremia due to the result of any medication that can safely be withdrawn (eg, thiazide diuretics)
20. Has hyponatremia (eg, hyponatremia in the setting of adrenal insufficiency, untreated hypothyroidism, or hypotonic fluid administration) that is most appropriately corrected by alternative therapies
21. Is currently pregnant or breastfeeding
22. Has any medical condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, could interfere with evaluation of the trial objectives or safety of the subjects.
23. Is deemed unsuitable for trial participation in the opinion of the investigator
24. Participation in another investigational drug trial within the past 30 days, without prior approval from the sponsor medical monitor
25. Subjects \< 4 years of age or per local Health Authority age restriction, weight \< 10 kg, or who are unable to swallow tablets are excluded until an alternate formulation becomes available

  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo:

  - Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) questionnaire [time frame: Week000/Week004/Week012/Week026/Week030/Week038/Week052]

* Male and female patients from 7 to less than 18 years
* Out patients
* Primary diagnosis of ASD as per Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders - Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria

* CGI (Clinical Global Impression) - Severity rating Score ≥ 4
* Childhood Autism Rating Scale second edition (CARS2-ST or HF) total raw score ≥ 34
* Social responsiveness Scale second edition total score (SRS-2 T-Score) ≥ 66

* Chronic cardiac dysfunction

Here's what I can independently tell you, with uncertainty flagged where it applies.

**The drug and mechanism**

Bumetanide is a well-established loop diuretic (a marketed, off-patent drug used for edema, heart failure, hypertension) that acts by inhibiting the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC1) in the kidney. The rationale for autism is based on the excitatory/inhibitory imbalance hypothesis: NKCC1 and KCC2 regulate intracellular chloride, and in some models the immature/atypical pattern (high NKCC1, low KCC2) shifts GABA from inhibitory to excitatory. The idea is that bumetanide, by blocking NKCC1, restores more inhibitory GABAergic signaling. This is a repurposing hypothesis associated prominently with Ben-Ari and colleagues, and with Yehezkel Ben-Ari's work and the French biotech Neurochlore.

**The sponsor situation (important and directly relevant)**

Servier licensed/partnered this program — the compound code S95008 corresponds to bumetanide as developed for ASD. This is not an oncology or rare-disease first-in-class asset; it's a repurposed generic, which shapes the whole story.

**Earlier studies**

- A notable earlier randomized controlled trial (Lemonnier et al., 2012, *Translational Psychiatry*) reported improvement on CARS and other measures with bumetanide in children with ASD. This was a small, single-center French study and was influential but has been viewed cautiously.
- A subsequent, larger, better-controlled trial (Lemonnier et al., 2017, *Translational Psychiatry*) again reported positive results, though still with methodological criticisms.
- There were also smaller trials and mechanistic studies; overall the earlier literature was mixed-to-positive but not uniformly replicated, and effect sizes have been debated.

**Results of THIS trial (NCT03715166, CL3-95008-001)**

My recollection is that this Phase 3 trial **failed to meet its primary endpoint** — bumetanide did not separate from placebo on the CARS2 total raw score at 6 months. I believe this was reported around 2021–2022 and was a significant disappointment for the program. I'm fairly confident of the negative outcome but not certain of every secondary-endpoint detail, so treat specifics as **partially uncertain**. Given the trial is registered by Servier, top-line disclosure would have come via Servier and/or conference/publication.

**Consequences**

I recall that after the negative Phase 3 results, the program was discontinued or deprioritized. Neurochlore (Ben-Ari's company) had its own parallel bumetanide ASD program that also ran into difficulty; I believe French authorities (ANSM) and/or an ethics body raised concerns and some ongoing trials were halted. I am **not fully certain** of the exact regulatory timeline here.

**Key dates**

- Study start: I believe enrollment began around **2018**.
- Primary completion: around **2020–2021**.
- Results posting/disclosure: around **2021–2022**. Exact dates: **unknown**.

**Sponsor track record**

Servier is a large French independent pharmaceutical company with a broad portfolio (cardiology, diabetes, CNS, oncology). Its CNS track record is mixed; it has had both successes and notable failures in psychiatric/neurological indications. For this specific ASD program, the outcome appears to have been negative.

Here's how I'd characterize a successful outcome for NCT03715166 based on its registered design.

**1. Primary endpoint and measurement**

- Primary endpoint: **Change from baseline to 6 months in the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2) total raw score.**
- Measurement: CARS2 is a clinician-rated instrument. The protocol specifies CARS2-ST (Standard Version) or CARS2-HF (High Functioning), and eligibility required a baseline total raw score ≥ 34. The endpoint is the **change score** (baseline minus Month 6, or Month 6 minus baseline depending on convention), analyzed across the double-blind period.
- A "successful" primary result means the bumetanide arm shows **significantly greater improvement** (greater reduction in CARS2 total raw score) than the placebo arm at Month 6.

**2. Statistical threshold**

- The specific alpha and power assumptions are **unknown** to me (they would be in the statistical analysis plan, which I don't have).
- Standard convention for a Phase 3 superiority trial of this type would be a **two-sided p < 0.05** (or a one-sided 0.025) on the primary comparison, typically analyzed on the intention-to-treat (ITT) population, often with a mixed-effects model for repeated measures (MMRM) or ANCOVA adjusting for baseline.
- Whether there was a pre-specified multiple-testing hierarchy across secondary endpoints (SRS-2, CGI-I, VABS-II) and whether alpha was controlled — **unknown**.
- No hazard ratio or non-inferiority margin applies, since the primary endpoint is a continuous change score, not a time-to-event or non-inferiority comparison.

**3. Superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence**

- This is clearly a **superiority trial**. The stated purpose is to demonstrate that bumetanide improves ASD core symptoms versus placebo. There is no active comparator and no non-inferiority framing in the registered design.

**4. Key design features**

- **Allocation:** Randomized.
- **Intervention model:** Parallel-group (two arms).
- **Masking:** Quadruple — typically meaning participant, care provider, investigator, and outcomes assessor are all blinded. This is appropriate for a subjective clinician-rated primary endpoint like CARS2.
- **Arms:** Experimental (bumetanide 0.5 mg BID, oral solution 0.5 mg/mL) vs. Placebo comparator (oral solution, twice daily). Both taken BID for 6 months double-blind.
- **Follow-on:** After the 6-month double-blind period, a **6-month open-label** bumetanide period (all participants on active drug) for long-term safety — this phase is not part of the primary efficacy comparison.
- **Population:** Children/adolescents 7 to <18 years, outpatient, DSM-5 ASD confirmed by ADOS-2 and ADI-R, CGI-S ≥ 4, CARS2 ≥ 34, SRS-2 T-score ≥ 66. Enrollment target 211.
- **Enrollment:** 211 randomized — modest for a Phase 3 in a heterogeneous indication, which affects power.

**Summary of a "successful" outcome**

A success would be: bumetanide 0.5 mg BID produces a statistically significant, clinically meaningful greater reduction in CARS2 total raw score versus placebo at Month 6 (p < 0.05, superiority, on the ITT population), with supportive directional consistency on key secondary measures (SRS-2, CGI-I, VABS-II) and an acceptable safety/tolerability profile. The exact pre-specified alpha, power, and any multiplicity strategy are **unknown** to me.

Here are the key risks I'd flag for NCT03715166, ordered from most to least concerning.

**RISK 1: Insufficient efficacy / target engagement translation failure**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: This is the dominant risk and the one that apparently materialized. The entire rationale rests on the NKCC1/GABA excitatory-inhibitory imbalance hypothesis, which has been poorly replicated across multiple mechanistically related ASD trials (bumetanide, arbaclofen, balovaptan, oxytocin). A repurposed loop diuretic achieving meaningful CNS target engagement at a tolerable 0.5 mg BID dose in children is uncertain, and the earlier positive bumetanide trials were small and methodologically criticized. Given the near-uniform failure record in ASD core-symptom Phase 3 trials, the prior probability of a true treatment effect large enough to detect is low.
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

**RISK 2: Outcome-measure insensitivity and high placebo response**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The primary endpoint is change in CARS2 total raw score, a clinician-rated scale that is the same instrument family used in the earlier positive trials — raising the risk of expectation bias, score drift, and inflated placebo response, especially in pediatric ASD where rater subjectivity and caregiver hope are strong. A 6-month double-blind period with a single primary timepoint is vulnerable to regression to the mean and to placebo-arm improvement that washes out any drug signal. This design vulnerability is well documented in the ASD literature and would have been flagged by regulators and statisticians.
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

**RISK 3: Safety and tolerability signals — diuretic and electrolyte effects in children**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: Bumetanide is a potent loop diuretic. In a pediatric neurodevelopmental population on a chronic 6-month dosing schedule, the concerns are electrolyte imbalance (hyponatremia, hypokalemia), renal effects (hence the mandated renal ultrasound), dehydration, cardiac effects (hence serial 12-lead ECGs), and growth/developmental effects (hence Tanner staging). The protocol's extensive safety monitoring (renal ultrasound, ECG at seven timepoints, PAERS, C-SSRS-C, Tanner stage) strongly implies the sponsor itself considered these risks material. Any emergent signal could undermine the benefit-risk assessment even if efficacy trended positive, and tolerability problems could drive dropout and dilute the ITT analysis.
- LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM–HIGH

**RISK 4: Enrollment and population heterogeneity challenges**
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: The trial targeted only 211 randomized patients across a narrow pediatric window (7 to <18 years) with strict entry criteria (ADOS-2 + ADI-R confirmed ASD, CGI-S ≥ 4, CARS2 ≥ 34, SRS-2 ≥ 66, exclusion of monogenic syndromes and unstable psychotherapy). ASD is highly heterogeneous, so even a real average effect can be masked by responder/non-responder mixing, and strict eligibility plus slow recruitment in a niche pediatric indication risks underpowering, site variability, and rater inconsistency across sites. The modest sample size (211 for a Phase 3 in a heterogeneous CNS indication) leaves little margin for dilution or dropout.

Phase: PHASE1
Conditions: AML

Enrollment: 0
Design: allocation=NA; intervention model=SINGLE_GROUP; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=not specified

Brief summary:
This trial assess the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive treatment In pivotal preclinical studies, the investigational agent demonstrated robust dose-dependent target engagement with >90% inhibition at clinically achievable concentrations, and a therapeutic index exceeding 10× in the relevant animal toxicology models.

Detailed description:
Background and Rationale:

Epacadostat (INCB024360) is an Inhibitor of Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) is a 403 amino acid cytosolic haem enzyme encoded by the INDO gene on human chromosome 8p22. IDO1 is responsible for the catabolism of the essential amino acid tryptophan (trp) to kynurenine (kyn) within immune cells and a subset of tumor cells resulting in inhibition of antitumor cell-mediated immune responses. Increased IDO activity correlates with lower CR rates and shorter OS in AML.

Objective:

The primary objective is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive Treatment.

Study Duration:

Phase I part will last from 3 to 18 months (permitting the enrolment of minimum of 3 and a maximum of 18 patients).

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Dosis finding: Epacadostat is given for 2 cycles of 28 days at a dose according to the titration design together with Standard chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Epacadostat: Epacadostat orally two times daily (BID) for two cycles (28 days each) in combination with standard induction chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)
  - [DRUG] Idarubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-d3 cycle 1
  - [DRUG] Cytarabine: Standard chemotherapy d1-d7 cycle 1 and 2
  - [DRUG] Daunorubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-3 cycle 2

Primary outcomes:
  - Phase 1: Dose finding [time frame: 30 days]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Rate of morphologic complete remission (CR) [time frame: 60 days]
  - Adverse events [time frame: 90 days]
  - Overall survival [time frame: 12 months]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* AML (according to the 2016 World Health Organization (WHO) classification definition of ≥ 20% blasts; Arber et al, 2016) suitable for intensive treatment (including stem cell transplantation) with a curative intent.
* Patients must be aged \> 18 years, and must have given voluntary written informed consent.
* Women of childbearing potential having a negative serum pregnancy test at screening or at least within 48 hours before start with epacadostat, and willing to use an effective contraceptive method (intrauterine devices, hormonal contraceptives, contraceptive pill, implants, transdermal patches, hormonal vaginal devices, infusions with prolonged release) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration
* Men willing to use an effective contraceptive method (eg, condom, vasectomy) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Prior or concurrent malignancy, except for the following: adequately treated basal cell or squamous cell skin cancer, or any other cancer from which the subject has been disease-free for more than 6 months.
* Any previous AML or MDS chemotherapy (with the exception of hydroxyurea/Litalir® for leukocyte control which should be discontinued by the first day of induction chemotherapy
* Treatment with any investigational product within 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)
* Abnormal organ function if not caused by the underlying disease as considered by the treating physician
* Use of immune-suppressive agents for the past 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360). For regular use of systemic corticosteroids, subjects may only be included after stepwise discontinuation to be free of steroids for a minimum of 5 days before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)

# Independent Knowledge: NCT03444649 / Epacadostat

## Drug: Epacadostat (INCB024360)

**Mechanism of action:** Epacadostat is an oral, potent, selective inhibitor of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). IDO1 catalyzes the rate-limiting step in tryptophan catabolism along the kynurenine pathway. By inhibiting IDO1, epacadostat aims to restore tryptophan levels and reduce kynurenine-mediated immunosuppression, thereby re-enabling T-cell–mediated antitumor immunity. It was developed by Incyte Corporation.

**Development history:** Epacadostat was studied most extensively in solid tumors, particularly in combination with pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1). The pivotal Phase 3 ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252 trial in unresectable/metastatic melanoma (epacadostat + pembrolizumab vs. placebo + pembrolizumab) **failed to meet its primary endpoint** of progression-free survival, which was reported in 2018. This was a major setback for the IDO1 inhibitor class. Subsequently, many epacadostat development programs were discontinued, including in AML. Incyte discontinued further development of epacadostat in 2019.

**Primary endpoint:** Determination of the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and characterization of dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to anthracycline/cytarabine induction.

- **MTD:** The highest dose level at which no more than a pre-specified fraction of patients (commonly 0/3 or ≤1/6, depending on the titration/accrual design) experience a DLT.
- The "titration design" mentioned in the arm description suggests a dose-escalation schema (likely a 3+3 or similar algorithm, given the planned 3–18 patients).

**Success (primary endpoint met) would mean:**

- No hazard ratio, non-inferiority margin, or equivalence margin is applicable to the primary endpoint as described.

# Key Risk Factors for NCT03444649

---

## RISK 1: Class-level efficacy failure of IDO1 inhibitors (epacadostat specifically)

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Epacadostat is the exact drug in this trial. Its most prominent test — the Phase 3 ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252 trial in melanoma (epacadostat + pembrolizumab) — **failed to meet its primary endpoint** in 2018. This was a decisive, well-publicized class-level setback that led Incyte to discontinue epacadostat development. Any trial of epacadostat after this point faces the fundamental question of whether the mechanism works at all in humans. If the mechanism is invalid, adding epacadostat to chemotherapy in AML is unlikely to succeed regardless of how well the Phase 1 is conducted.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

## RISK 2: Enrollment failure / trial non-initiation

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The registry lists **enrollment = 0**, and the sponsor is an academic hospital (Insel Gruppe AG) rather than a large pharmaceutical company with extensive site networks. AML is a relatively rare disease, and the eligibility criteria are restrictive (fit for intensive treatment, no prior AML/MDS chemotherapy, no recent investigational product, no recent immunosuppressants). The planned sample is small (3–18 patients), but even that may be difficult to accrue — especially once the epacadostat class fell out of favor. A trial that never enrolls cannot succeed.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

## RISK 3: Safety / toxicity of combining epacadostat with intensive chemotherapy

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The trial adds epacadostat to an already highly toxic backbone (idarubicin/cytarabine, then daunorubicin/cytarabine). Standard "7+3" induction in AML carries substantial myelosuppression, infection risk, and organ toxicity. Adding an immune-modulating agent could compound or introduce new toxicities (e.g., immune-related adverse events, hepatotoxicity, or exacerbation of cytopenias). If DLTs occur at low dose levels, the MTD may not be reachable, and the combination may be declared infeasible.

Brief summary:
This phase I trial studies talimogene laherparepvec given together with ipilimumab and nivolumab before surgery in patients with triple-negative or estrogen receptor positive, HER2 negative localized breast cancer. Ipilimumab and Nivolumab are immune checkpoint inhibitors that enhance immune response towards cancer cells. Talimogene laherparepvec is a modifies human herpes virus 1 that is an oncolytic virus targeting cancer cells and makes tumor microenvironment more immunogenic to promote immune response against cancer. This study will assess the safety and efficacy of talimogene laherparepvec, ipilimumab, and nivolumab, and provide an insight for further improvement of immunotherapy in breast cancer. In pivotal preclinical studies, the investigational agent demonstrated robust dose-dependent target engagement with >90% inhibition at clinically achievable concentrations, and a therapeutic index exceeding 10× in the relevant animal toxicology models.

Detailed description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To explore the safety of talimogene laherparepvec in combination with nivolumab and ipilimumab in this population assessed by the frequency and severity of adverse events (AEs) using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version (v)4.0 toxicity criteria.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. Assess tumor response of talimogene laherparepvec in combination with nivolumab and ipilimumab comparing to no treatment, in subjects with localized estrogen receptor (ER) positive and triple negative infiltrating ductal breast cancer.

II. Descriptively analyze the evidence of tumor necrosis and inflammatory infiltration on histopathological examination and immuno-oncological findings in tumor and peripheral blood of patients treated with talimogene laherparepvec in combination with nivolumab and ipilimumab.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. Descriptively compare tumor response in patients whose tumors are PD-L1 positive (+) and PD-L1 negative (-) at baseline.

II. Determine the baseline mutational load of patients at the start of treatment and relate it to the response to treatment.

III. Determine if hormone receptor status correlates with tumor responses. IV. Determine the number of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes in patient samples at the start and at the end of treatment and relate them to tumor response.

V. Analyze T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire in tumor infiltrating lymphocytes and peripheral blood mononuclear cells.

OUTLINE:

Participants receive talimogene laherparepvec intratumorally on days 1, 22, and 36, nivolumab intravenously (IV) over 60 minutes on days 1, 15, 29, and 43, and ipilimumab IV over 90 minutes on days 1 and 43 in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

After completion of study treatment, participants are followed up for 30 days.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Treatment (talimogene laherparepvec, nivolumab, ipilimumab): Participants receive talimogene laherparepvec intratumorally on days 1, 22, and 36, nivolumab IV over 60 minutes on days 1, 15, 29, and 43, and ipilimumab IV over 90 minutes on days 1 and 43 in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

Interventions:
  - [BIOLOGICAL] Ipilimumab: Given IV
  - [BIOLOGICAL] Nivolumab: Given IV
  - [BIOLOGICAL] Talimogene Laherparepvec: Given intratumorally

Primary outcomes:
  - Incidence and severity of adverse events (AEs) [time frame: Up to 100 days after last study drug]

Secondary outcomes:
  - histopathological evaluation of changes of tumor for inflammatory infiltration and tumor necrosis [time frame: Up to 2 years]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Written informed consent must be obtained from the subject/legal representative prior to performing any protocol-related procedures, including screening evaluations
* Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) 0-1
* Localized, palpable, biopsy proven triple negative or ER positive HER2 negative infiltrating ductal breast cancer with size \> 1.5 cm by palpation, excluding breast cancer where neoadjuvant chemotherapy is indicated by current guidelines (i.e. inflammatory subtype, etc.)
* Tumor that is palpable and injectable
* Hemoglobin \>= 9 g/dL
* Absolute neutrophil count \>= 1,500/mm\^3
* Platelet count \>= 100,000/mm\^3
* Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) =\< 2.5 x institutional upper limit of normal (ULN)
* Bilirubin =\< 1.5 x ULN; for subjects with documented/suspected Gilbert?s disease, bilirubin =\< 3 x ULN
* Albumin \>= 2.5 g/dl
* Prothrombin time (PT) / International normalized ratio (INR) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) =\< 1.5 x institutional upper limit of normal unless the patient is on anticoagulant therapy within 28 days prior to enrollment (if the patient is receiving anticoagulant therapy, PT, and a PTT must be within therapeutic range of intended use of anticoagulants)
* Patients must be willing to submit blood and tissue specimens for translational medicine studies
* Patients must be offered the opportunity to participate in specimen banking for future research
* Women of childbearing potential (WOCBP) must have a negative serum or urine pregnancy test (minimum sensitivity 25 IU/L or equivalent units of human chorionic gonadotropin \[HCG\]) within 24 hours prior to the start of study drug
* Women must not be breastfeeding
* Women of childbearing potential (WOCBP) must be willing to use either two adequate barrier methods or a barrier method plus a hormonal method of contraception to prevent pregnancy, or to abstain from heterosexual activity (complete abstinence) throughout the study, starting with visit 1 through 5 months after the last dose of study therapy. Approved contraceptive methods include, for example, intrauterine device, diaphragm with spermicide, cervical cap with spermicide, male condoms, female condoms with spermicide, or oral contraceptives. Spermicides alone are not an acceptable method of contraception. Should a woman become pregnant or suspect she is pregnant while she or her partner is participating in this study, she should inform her treating physician immediately
* Male patients must agree to use an adequate method of contraception, or to abstain from heterosexual activity (complete abstinence) starting with the first dose of study drug through 7 months after the last dose of study therapy

Exclusion Criteria:

* Contraindications to tumor biopsy and injections (coagulopathy, known history of keloid formation, etc.)
* Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding
* Sexually active subjects and their partners unwilling to use male or female latex condom to avoid potential viral transmission during sexual contact while on treatment and within 30 days after treatment with talimogene laherparepvec
* Inability to give informed consent
* History of malignancies except cured basal cell carcinoma, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma in situ, superficial bladder cancer or carcinoma in situ of the cervix; for other malignancies, must be documented to be free of cancer for \>= 2 years. All other cases can be considered on a case by case basis at the discretion of the principal investigator
* Any condition that might interfere with the subject?s participation in the study, safety, or in the evaluation of the study results
* Concurrent enrollment in another clinical study, unless it is an observational (non-interventional) clinical study or the follow-up period of an interventional study
* Prior exposure to any anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibody, or any anti-CTLA 4 antibodies
* Patients must not have received prior treatment with talimogene laherparepvec or other oncolytic virus agents
* Patients must not have received any live vaccine within 30 days prior to registration. Seasonal flu vaccines that do not contain live virus are permitted
* Patients must not have an active infection requiring systemic therapy nor a viral infection requiring intermittent treatment with an antiherpetic drug, other than intermittent topical use
* Patients must not have active herpetic skin lesions or prior complications of herpetic infection (e.g., herpetic keratitis or encephalitis) which requires intermittent or chronic treatment with an anti-herpetic drug other than intermittent topical use
* Any concurrent chemotherapy, immunotherapy, biologic or hormonal therapy for cancer treatment. Concurrent use of hormones for non-cancer-related conditions (e.g., insulin for diabetes and hormone replacement therapy) is acceptable
* Patient must not have evidence of any clinically significant immunosuppression such as the following: primary immunodeficiency state such as severe combined immunodeficiency disease; concurrent opportunistic infection; receiving systemic immunosuppressive therapy within 28 days before enrollment with the exceptions of intranasal, topical, and inhaled corticosteroids or oral corticosteroids at physiologic doses not to exceed 10 mg/day of prednisone or equivalent
* Patients must not have known history human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
* Clinical or laboratory evidence of an active herpetic infection and in patients who require daily antiviral therapy such as acyclovir
* Active or prior documented autoimmune disease within the past 3 years

  * NOTE: Subjects with active, known or suspected autoimmune disease such as vitiligo, type I diabetes mellitus, residual hypothyroidism due to autoimmune condition only requiring hormone replacement, psoriasis not requiring systemic treatment, or conditions not expected to recur in the absence of an external trigger are permitted to enroll
* Active or prior documented inflammatory bowel disease
* History of (non-infectious) interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis that required steroids or has current ILD/pneumonitis or where suspected ILD/pneumonitis cannot be ruled out by imaging at screening
* Exposure to any investigational drug within 7 days prior to screening visit or for which 5 half-lives have not elapsed
* Prisoners or subjects who are involuntarily incarcerated

  * Note: under certain specific circumstances a person who has been imprisoned may be included or permitted to continue as a subject
* Subjects who are compulsorily detained for treatment of either a psychiatric or physical (e.g., infectious disease) illness

## Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC, Imlygic)

- **Mechanism of action:** T-VEC is an attenuated herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) that has been genetically modified in two ways: (1) deletion of the ICP34.5 gene, which attenuates neurovirulence and confers tumor-selective replication; and (2) deletion of ICP47, which normally blocks antigen presentation, thereby enhancing MHC class I–mediated antigen presentation. It also expresses human GM-CSF, which recruits and activates dendritic cells and promotes a systemic antitumor immune response. It replicates preferentially in tumor cells, causing direct oncolysis, and can induce a systemic "abscopal" immune effect.
- **Approval status:** FDA-approved in October 2015 (Imlygic, Amgen) for the local treatment of unresectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, and nodal lesions in patients with melanoma recurrent after initial surgery. It is not approved for breast cancer.
- **Prior breast cancer studies:** I am aware that T-VEC has been investigated in early-phase breast cancer trials (e.g., a phase I study in advanced breast cancer combined with chemotherapy, and a window-of-opportunity study in early breast cancer). Specific results and citations are not something I can reliably reproduce in detail; **unknown** for exact figures.
- **Notable safety considerations:** Herpesvirus-based; contraindicated in immunocompromised patients, those with active herpetic infections, and it carries a risk of viral transmission. This aligns with the exclusion criteria in the registration.

## Ipilimumab

- **Mechanism:** Fully human anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody. Blocks CTLA-4-mediated inhibition of T-cell activation, thereby enhancing T-cell priming and antitumor immunity.
- **Approval:** FDA-approved for melanoma (2011) and in combination with nivolumab for certain cancers (e.g., renal cell carcinoma, colorectal cancer with MSI-H/dMMR, hepatocellular carcinoma, NSCLC, mesothelioma).
- **Track record:** Well-characterized; extensive clinical experience. Not approved as monotherapy for breast cancer.

## Nivolumab

- **Mechanism:** Fully human anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody. Blocks PD-1 interaction with PD-L1/PD-L2, restoring T-cell effector function.
- **Approval:** Approved across many tumor types (melanoma, NSCLC, renal cell carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, head and neck, urothelial, hepatocellular, colorectal MSI-H/dMMR, etc.). In breast cancer, pembrolizumab (a different anti-PD-1) is approved in triple-negative breast cancer; nivolumab is not approved for breast cancer as of my knowledge.
- **Track record:** Extensive; well-characterized safety profile including immune-related adverse events.

## Sponsor: Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center (JCCC)

- **Identity:** The Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center is the cancer center at UCLA. It is an NCI-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center.
- **Track record:** JCCC has a substantial history of conducting investigator-initiated early-phase trials, including immunotherapy trials in breast cancer. Specific prior experience with this exact combination is **unknown** to me.
- **Note:** This is an investigator-initiated, academic-sponsored trial, not an industry-sponsored registration trial. Enrollment of 6 is consistent with a small phase I safety/feasibility study.

## Trial Design Context

- **Phase I, single-group, open-label, window-of-opportunity design:** Participants receive intratumoral T-VEC plus systemic nivolumab and ipilimumab before surgery. This is a "window" trial where the investigational regimen is given in the neoadjuvant window prior to definitive surgery, allowing assessment of histopathological changes in the tumor.
- **Rationale:** Combining an oncolytic virus (which induces immunogenic cell death and local inflammation) with dual checkpoint blockade (anti-CTLA-4 + anti-PD-1) is a rational strategy to convert "cold" breast tumors (especially ER+/HER2− and triple-negative) into "hot" tumors and potentially induce systemic antitumor immunity.

# Key Risk Factors for NCT04185311

Ordered from most to least concerning.

---

**RISK 1: Safety — overlapping immune toxicity from triple combination (T-VEC + ipilimumab + nivolumab)**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** This trial combines an oncolytic herpesvirus that induces local inflammation and GM-CSF release with **dual checkpoint blockade** (anti-CTLA-4 + anti-PD-1). The ipilimumab + nivolumab combination is itself associated with substantially higher rates of grade 3–4 immune-related adverse events (hepatitis, colitis, pneumonitis, hypophysitis, rash) than either agent alone. Adding intratumoral T-VEC — which causes tumor lysis, cytokine release, and possible systemic viral exposure — could compound this. The primary endpoint is safety, so any excess toxicity directly causes trial failure. The 100-day post-treatment AE monitoring window suggests the investigators themselves anticipated delayed irAEs.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

**RISK 2: Futility — no efficacy signal in a disease setting where checkpoint monotherapy is already weak in ER+/HER2− disease**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The trial enrolls both triple-negative **and ER+/HER2−** localized breast cancer. ER+/HER2− tumors are generally immunologically "cold" — low tumor mutational burden, low PD-L1 expression, few tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes — and have shown poor responses to checkpoint monotherapy in prior studies. Even in TNBC, anti-PD-1 agents require chemotherapy backbone to show benefit (e.g., KEYNOTE-522). A 6-patient, chemotherapy-free, window-of-opportunity trial is unlikely to generate a convincing histopathological or immunological signal, especially in the ER+ subgroup. If the exploratory endpoints show no evidence of immune activation or tumor necrosis, the rationale for further development collapses.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

**RISK 3: Enrollment failure — extremely narrow eligibility plus n=6 target at a single academic site**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Eligibility requires: localized, **palpable**, biopsy-proven, injectable tumor >1.5 cm; no neoadjuvant chemotherapy indication; no prior checkpoint inhibitor; no autoimmune disease; no herpetic history; no active infection; female only; ECOG 0–1. This is a highly restricted population. The trial needs only 6 patients, but even that can be difficult when competing neoadjuvant trials (e.g., KEYNOTE-522-style regimens) offer standard-of-care chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab, which many patients and oncologists would prefer over an experimental intratumoral virus plus dual checkpoint blockade. Slow or failed accrual is a common cause of early-phase academic trial termination.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM-HIGH

---

**RISK 4: Trial design limitations — single-arm, open-label, no control, no formal efficacy endpoint**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** As registered, the trial has allocation=NA, single-group, no masking, and no randomized control. The primary endpoint is safety, and secondary/exploratory endpoints are descriptive. This design **cannot** establish efficacy, cannot distinguish drug effect from natural immune fluctuation or biopsy-related inflammation, and cannot support a regulatory path on its own. If the goal was to generate a signal sufficient to justify a larger trial, the absence of a control arm and the small n=6 make it vulnerable to ambiguous or uninterpretable results — a "failed" trial even if technically completed. The secondary objective of "comparing to no treatment" is methodologically weak without a control group.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

**RISK 5: Competitive and regulatory landscape — checkpoint inhibitors already standard in TNBC neoadjuvant setting**

- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy is now FDA-approved for high-risk early-stage TNBC (based on KEYNOTE-522), and multiple neoadjuvant immunotherapy trials are ongoing. For a patient with localized TNBC or ER+/HER2− breast cancer, the standard of care already includes effective options. This makes an experimental regimen with no established efficacy, a novel intratumoral virus, and dual checkpoint blockade a hard sell — both for accrual and for eventual regulatory acceptance. If the field moves further toward approved neoadjuvant immunotherapies, the window for this trial's rationale narrows. Additionally, T-VEC is not approved in breast cancer, and combining it with dual checkpoint blockade in this setting has no precedent positive registration trial.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

Beyond what is shown above, tell me what you independently know about this trial or this drug: mechanism of action, sponsor track record, results of earlier studies, key dates. For any item you are not sure about, write 'unknown'. Do not fabricate.

Here is what I independently know, with uncertainty flagged explicitly:

**Drug / mechanism of action**
- Bexagliflozin (also known by the development code EGT0001474 / EGT1442) is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor — the same class as canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, and ertugliflozin. It lowers blood glucose by inhibiting SGLT2 in the proximal tubule of the kidney, promoting urinary glucose excretion. This is consistent with the "target engagement" language in the summary you provided.
- It is an oral, once-daily agent. This much is strongly supported by the class mechanism and the protocol text.

**Sponsor track record**
- Theracos is a small clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company (based in Marlborough, Massachusetts, as I recall). It is not a large pharma; bexagliflozin was its lead (and essentially only late-stage) asset. I do not have detailed independent knowledge of its broader pipeline or financial history — **unknown** in detail.

**Regulatory / approval status**
- Bexagliflozin was approved by the FDA in **2023** (January) under the brand name **Brenzavvy**, for glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. This is my recollection and I'm fairly confident, but the exact approval date and current commercial status I would treat as approximate.
- I do **not** have reliable knowledge of whether it was approved in Japan, Europe, or elsewhere, or of its current marketing status — **unknown**.

**Results of earlier / other studies**
- There was a phase 2 program and at least one other phase 3 trial in T2DM (sometimes referred to in the literature as a 24-week study in patients with T2DM and stage 3 CKD — which is essentially the trial described here, NCT02836873).
- There was also a phase 3 program in **type 2 diabetes with hypertension** (sometimes called the "Bexagliflozin in T2DM and hypertension" studies) and I believe a cardiovascular outcome trial was planned or underway. Specific results, effect sizes, and safety findings I cannot cite reliably — **unknown** at the level of detail you'd want.
- I do **not** have reliable knowledge of the specific HbA1c reduction, weight, or blood pressure results of NCT02836873. **Unknown.**

**Key dates**
- Trial registration (NCT02836873) would have been around 2016, consistent with the NCT number range. Start and completion dates I cannot state precisely — **unknown.**
- FDA approval (Brenzavvy): my recollection is early 2023 — treat as approximate.

**Things I would caution about**
- I cannot verify enrollment numbers, stratification details, or outcome results from memory. Do not rely on my recollection for any quantitative result.
- I have no independent knowledge of the preclinical toxicology "therapeutic index >10×" claim beyond what the protocol text states — that is sponsor-provided text, not independent knowledge.

If you need verified specifics (approval date, trial results, publications), the reliable sources would be FDA labeling for Brenzavvy, ClinicalTrials.gov results postings, and PubMed-indexed publications — I'd be fabricating if I gave you numbers from memory.

Here are trials I believe are genuinely similar, with confidence flagged. I want to be upfront: I am **not confident about most NCT IDs from memory**, and I will mark those as unknown rather than guess, because a wrong NCT ID is worse than none.

---

**1. Canagliflozin — CANVAS / CANVAS-R (cardiovascular and renal outcomes program)**
- NCT ID: unknown (I believe CANVAS is NCT01032629 and CANVAS-R is NCT01989754, but treat both as low-confidence)
- Drug / indication: canagliflozin; T2DM with high cardiovascular risk
- Phase: 3
- Outcome: SUCCESS (met primary CV composite endpoint; subsequently had a boxed warning added for amputation risk, so "success" is nuanced)
- Why similar: same drug class (SGLT2 inhibitor), T2DM population, large phase 3 program, glycemic + CV/renal endpoints. Structurally analogous to what a bexagliflozin pivotal+outcomes program looks like.

---

**2. Dapagliflozin — DECLARE-TIMI 58**
- NCT ID: unknown (low confidence: possibly NCT01730534)
- Drug / indication: dapagliflozin; T2DM with or at risk of atherosclerotic CV disease
- Phase: 3
- Outcome: SUCCESS for the composite (non-inferiority / reduction in CV death or HF hospitalization), though it missed the MACE superiority endpoint — again nuanced
- Why similar: same class, T2DM, phase 3, CV-focused design. Relevant comparator class readout.

---

**3. Empagliflozin — EMPA-REG OUTCOME**
- NCT ID: unknown (low confidence: possibly NCT01131676)
- Drug / indication: empagliflozin; T2DM with established CV disease
- Phase: 3
- Outcome: SUCCESS (reduced CV death, a landmark positive result; drove class expansion)
- Why similar: same class, T2DM, phase 3, and this is the trial that essentially validated the SGLT2 class clinically — useful context for interpreting bexagliflozin's prospects.

---

**4. Ertugliflozin — VERTIS CV**
- NCT ID: unknown
- Drug / indication: ertugliflozin; T2DM with atherosclerotic CV disease
- Phase: 3
- Outcome: mixed / largely viewed as FAILURE on superiority (met non-inferiority for MACE but failed to show CV benefit; the "fourth-in-class" launch was weak)
- Why similar: same class, T2DM, phase 3 CV outcomes design. Directly analogous as a "late entrant SGLT2 inhibitor" — and bexagliflozin is also a late entrant, so VERTIS is arguably the most relevant cautionary comparator.

---

**5. Bexagliflozin — the companion phase 3 in T2DM with hypertension**
- NCT ID: unknown
- Drug / indication: bexagliflozin; T2DM with hypertension
- Phase: 3
- Outcome: unknown (I do not reliably know the result)

BASE_RATE: 0.75

REASONING: For a phase 3 SGLT2 inhibitor in type 2 diabetes, the historical success rate is high relative to most therapeutic areas, because this is a mature, well-validated drug class with a mechanistically reliable glucose-lowering effect and well-defined regulatory endpoints (HbA1c reduction). Published phase-transition analyses (e.g., from BIO/Informa/QLS and similar datasets) put phase 3 success rates for diabetes/metabolism drugs that have reached phase 3 at roughly 60–80%, and this particular trial has several favorable features that push it toward the upper end: it is a straightforward placebo-controlled glycemic-efficacy study with no CV outcomes superiority requirement, the active comparator class has repeatedly succeeded on this endpoint, and it uses a confirmed target (SGLT2) with a well-understood safety profile. The main caveats that keep it below ~0.85 are the difficult-to-treat population (moderate renal impairment, which blunts SGLT2 efficacy), the fact that being a late entrant raises commercial rather than statistical/regulatory risk, and the reality that some SGLT2 programs (notably ertugliflozin's VERTIS CV) failed to differentiate. On balance, for the narrow question of "does this phase 3 meet its primary glycemic endpoint and support approval," ~0.75 is a defensible central estimate — and I'd note the true base rate would be somewhat lower (~0.6–0.65) if you mean "commercial/overall success" rather than "trial success."

Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: Schizophrenia
Lead sponsor: Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development & Commercialization, Inc.
Enrollment: 157
Design: allocation=NA; intervention model=SINGLE_GROUP; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=40 Years

Brief summary:
An extension study of safety and tolerability of SEP-363856 in adult subjects with schizophrenia In pivotal preclinical studies, the investigational agent demonstrated robust dose-dependent target engagement with >90% inhibition at clinically achievable concentrations, and a therapeutic index exceeding 10× in the relevant animal toxicology models.

Detailed description:
This is a 26 week, multiregional, open-label extension study designed to evaluate the long-term safety and tolerability of SEP-363856 for the treatment of subjects with schizophrenia who have completed the 4 week double-blind treatment phase of Study SEP361-201 (NCT02969382) Subjects received open-label SEP-363856 50 mg/day from Day 1 through Day 3, and then received flexible dosing of SEP-363856 (25, 50, or 75 mg/day) for the rest of the trial.

No statistical hypothesis tests will be performed.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] SEP-363856: SEP-363856 capsule (25 mg, 50 mg, or 75 mg) once daily

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] SEP-363856: One SEP-363856 capsule (25 mg, 50 mg or 75 mg (flex)) daily for 26 weeks

Primary outcomes:
  - The Incidence of Overall Adverse Events (AEs), Serious Adverse Events (SAEs), and Adverse Events (AEs) Leading to Discontinuation [time frame: From first dose of study drug to last study visit (27 weeks)]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Frequency of Suicidal Ideation (SI) and Suicidal Behavior (SB) Using the Columbia - Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) [time frame: Overall post Open-label Baseline treatment period (26 weeks)]
  - Severity of Suicidal Ideation (SI) and Suicidal Behavior (SB) Using the Columbia - Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) [time frame: Overall post Open-label Baseline treatment period (26 weeks)]
  - Time to Relapse During the 26-week Open-label Treatment Period for Subjects Who Demonstrated a Clinical Response to 4 Weeks of Treatment With SEP-363856 [time frame: From the time of clinical response to relapse or censor (one day after the last study drug dose)]
  - Rate of Relapse During the 26-week Open-label Treatment Period for Subjects Who Demonstrated a Clinical Response to 4 Weeks of Treatment With SEP-363856 [time frame: From the time of clinical response to relapse or censor (one day after the last study drug dose)]
  - Changes From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 and Open-label Baseline of Study SEP361-202 in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) Total Score and Subscale Scores (Positive, Negative, and General Psychopathology) [time frame: Double-blind Baseline (DB BLN), Open-label Baseline (OL BLN), Week 26 (Wk 26)]
  - Change From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 and Open-label Baseline of Study SEP361-202 in Clinical Global Impression - Severity (CGI-S) Score [time frame: Double-blind (DB) Baseline, Open-label (OL) Baseline, Week 26]
  - Change From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 and Open-label Baseline of Study SEP361-202 in Brief Negative Symptom Scale (BNSS) Total Score [time frame: Double-blind (DB) Baseline, Open-label (OL) Baseline, Week 26]
  - Change From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 and Open-label Baseline of Study SEP361-202 in Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) Total Score [time frame: Double-blind (DB) Baseline, Open-label (OL) Baseline, Week 26]
  - Proportion of Subjects Who Achieved a Response, Defined as a 20% or Greater Improvement in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) Total Score From Double-blind Baseline of Study SEP361-201 [time frame: Week 26]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

Subject must give written informed consent and privacy authorization prior to participation in the study and able to comply with the protocol, in the opinion of the investigator.

* Subject has completed Study SEP361 201 through Week 4
* Subject has not taken any medication other than the study drug for the purpose of controlling schizophrenia symptoms during Study SEP361 201.
* Female subject must have a negative urine pregnancy test at Visit 7 of Study SEP361 201; females who are post-menopausal (defined as at least 12 months of spontaneous amenorrhea) and those who have undergone hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy will be exempted from the pregnancy test.
* Male subjects with female partner(s) of childbearing potential must agree to avoid fathering a child and use acceptable methods of birth control from screening until at least 30 days after the last study drug administration

Exclusion Criteria:

* Subject answers "yes" to "suicidal ideation" Item 4 (active suicidal ideation with some intent to act, without specific plan) or Item 5 (active suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent) on the C-SSRS assessment at Visit 7 of Study SEP361 201. Subjects who answer "yes" to this question must be referred to the Investigator for follow up evaluation.
* Subject has a clinically significant abnormality including physical examination, vital signs, ECG, or laboratory test at Visit 7 of Study SEP361 201 that the investigator in consultation with the medical monitor considers to be inappropriate to allow participation in the study.
* Subject has a positive urine drug screen (UDS) or breath alcohol test at Visit 7 of Study SEP361 201.
* Subject is pregnant or lactating.
* Subject is at high risk of non-compliance in the Investigator's opinion.
* Subject is in the opinion of the Investigator, unsuitable in any other way to participate in this study.

Here is what I independently know, with uncertainty flagged:

**Drug / mechanism of action**
- SEP-363856 (also known as ulotaront) is a **TAAR1 (trace amine-associated receptor 1) agonist** with additional **5-HT1A agonist** activity. This is notable because it is a **non-D2** mechanism — it does not rely primarily on dopamine D2 receptor blockade, which distinguishes it from essentially all approved antipsychotics. (Reasonably well established, though the precise contribution of each receptor to efficacy has been debated.)
- It was developed under a collaboration between **Otsuka** and **Sunovion** (Sunovion is a subsidiary of Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma).
- It received **FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation** for schizophrenia (I believe in 2019 — I'm not fully certain of the exact date, so treat the date as low confidence).

**Earlier / related studies**
- The antecedent trial referenced here, **SEP361-201 (NCT02969382)**, was a 4-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial in acutely exacerbated schizophrenia. It was published in the **New England Journal of Medicine in 2020** (Koblan et al.). That study reported statistically significant improvement in PANSS total score versus placebo, with relatively favorable tolerability (notably less weight gain and metabolic burden, and low EPS). This was a major reason for excitement around a non-D2 antipsychotic.
- SEP-363856 has also been studied in **Parkinson's disease psychosis** (a separate program).

**This specific trial (NCT02970929 / SEP361-202)**
- As the registered text indicates, it is the **open-label 26-week extension** to the 4-week double-blind trial — i.e., a long-term safety/tolerability study, not a controlled efficacy study.
- I do not independently have reliable knowledge of its specific **posted results numbers** (e.g., exact AE rates, relapse rates). **Unknown** to me in detail.
- **Key dates**: The registered record lists a start date around **2017** and completion around **2019**; I am not fully certain of the exact posted dates, so treat as approximate/unknown.

**Sponsor track record**
- Otsuka is a large, established psychiatric-drug developer (e.g., aripiprazole/Abilify, brexpiprazole/Rexulti, and others). Solid track record in CNS.

**Later development status (important context)**
- The subsequent **Phase 3 program (DIAMOND trials)** of ulotaront in schizophrenia **failed to separate from placebo** on primary endpoints. Otsuka/Sunovion subsequently **discontinued** development of ulotaront for schizophrenia (announced around **2023**). So despite promising Phase 2 results, the drug did not replicate efficacy in Phase 3. I'm fairly confident of this, but exact announcement dates are **approximate**.
- Development for Parkinson's disease psychosis was also discontinued (I believe around 2023–2024; **date uncertain**).

**Items I am not sure about (marked unknown):**
- Exact C-SSRS, PANSS, relapse, and AE result values from this specific extension study.
- Exact regulatory designation dates.
- Precise start/completion dates and whether full results were ever posted to ClinicalTrials.gov or published.
